cards.title: P versus NP
cards.formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
cards.why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.

cards.title: P versus PSPACE
cards.formal: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using polynomial working space have a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a machine A and constants C,k such that A decides truth of every closed quantified Boolean formula of encoded length n in at most $C(n+1)^k$ steps?
cards.why: This asks whether reusing a feasible amount of memory can provide computational power beyond feasible running time. It is a central unresolved separation even when the allowed language class is enlarged from NP to all of PSPACE, and it organizes the complexity of quantified reasoning, games, and verification.

cards.title: L versus P
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\)? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have a deterministic algorithm that always halts and uses \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits of working memory on an input of binary encoding length n?
cards.why: This is a fundamental question about how much memory efficient computation needs. It asks whether all of polynomial-time reasoning can be reorganized around logarithmic working storage, and connects circuit evaluation, graph reachability, recomputation, and the structure of space-bounded complexity.

cards.title: Superlinear Boolean circuit lower bounds
cards.formal:
Does there exist one total, length-preserving, deterministic polynomial-time function
\[F:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad |F(x)|=|x|,\]
whose unrestricted Boolean circuit complexity is not linear? Precisely, writing \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{n}\) for its restriction to inputs of length \(n\), the requested lower bound is
\[\forall C>0\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N:\quad \operatorname{CC}(F_n)>Cn.\]
Here \(C\) is real and \(N,n\) are integers. Preserve the card's polynomial-time meaning of “explicit” and its allowance of \(n\) output bits. The lower bound need only exceed every fixed linear bound at arbitrarily large lengths.
cards.why: A superlinear lower bound would establish a basic limitation on unrestricted nonuniform computation for an efficiently computable function. It would surpass every fixed linear gate count, even when a circuit can reuse work freely across outputs, and expose structure that simple counting does not identify.

cards.title: L versus NL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\)? Equivalently, do there exist a single deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and a constant \(C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), directed graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(s,t\in[n]\), the machine halts, correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), and visits at most
\[C\left\lceil\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil\]
work-tape cells? The graph is given explicitly by its adjacency matrix; the input is read-only. The machine and constant must work for all input sizes.
cards.why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.

cards.title: NP versus coNP
cards.formal:
Do there exist a single deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and constants \(C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, for every explicitly encoded Boolean CNF formula \(F\),
\[F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\ |\pi|\le C(|F|+1)^k\ \text{ and }\ V(F,\pi)=1?\]
In addition, require soundness on certificates of every length: \(V(F,\pi)=0\) for every satisfiable \(F\) and every binary string \(\pi\). Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\)? All constants and the verifier are fixed independently of the formula.
cards.why: This asks whether every nonexistence claim with an efficiently verifiable positive counterpart also has concise evidence. It is a central bridge between computational complexity, the length of mathematical proofs, and the limits of automated reasoning.

cards.title: NP versus P/poly
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\)? More explicitly, does there exist one language \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) such that \[\forall C,k,N\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}\ \exists n\geq N:\quad\operatorname{CC}(L_n)>C(n+1)^k,\] where \(n\) is an integer, \(L_n\) is the characteristic function of \(L\) on \(n\)-bit strings and \(\operatorname{CC}\) is minimum Boolean circuit size in the model below?
cards.why: This is the central unrestricted Boolean circuit lower-bound question for efficiently verifiable languages. It asks whether NP remains hard even when a separate circuit can be chosen for each input length without an effective construction rule. A separation would strengthen Boolean P versus NP and illuminate the limits of nonuniform computation, with connections to the polynomial hierarchy, pseudorandomness and learning.

cards.title: Strictness of the polynomial hierarchy
cards.formal: For every integer \(k\ge0\), is \(\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\subsetneq\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}\)? In other words, must each additional fixed block of polynomially bounded alternating Boolean quantifiers enable a decision language that cannot be expressed with k blocks? The classes are the uniform, unrelativized classes defined below.
cards.why: This is the organizing conjecture behind the computational cost of alternating existential and universal reasoning. It strengthens the basic P-versus-NP distinction across all fixed quantifier depths and underlies many conditional lower bounds in complexity, verification, and graph problems with nested solution requirements.

cards.title: Polynomial-size circuits for EXP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\)? More explicitly, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), decidable by one deterministic exponential-time algorithm, whose circuit complexity \(s_L(n)\) satisfies \[\forall C\geq1\;\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\forall N\geq1\;\exists n\geq N:\quad s_L(n)>C(n+1)^{k}?\]
cards.why: This is a central test of whether explicit computation can be proved to require large unrestricted Boolean circuits. Resolving it would cross the gap between uniform time hierarchy theorems and lower bounds that defeat arbitrary nonuniform circuit families.

cards.title: Exponential circuit lower bounds for 3-SAT
cards.formal:
For the explicitly encoded \(n\)-variable 3-SAT function \(\mathrm{SAT}_n\) below, do there exist constants \(c>0\) and integer \(n_0\ge1\) such that
\[\forall n\ge n_0,\qquad \operatorname{CC}(\mathrm{SAT}_n)\ge 2^{cn}?\]
The circuit lower bound is against arbitrary nonuniform Boolean circuits of fan-in at most two. Its exponential parameter is the number \(n\) of variables, not the number of input bits in the clause-incidence encoding. The card retains this previously recorded variable-parameter specialization of the source’s exponential-SAT conjecture.
cards.why: An exponential unrestricted circuit lower bound for 3-SAT would establish a quantitative limit on even nonuniform solutions to a canonical NP-complete problem. Fixing the variable parameter makes its relationship to exponential-time hypotheses precise without assuming that algorithmic and circuit lower bounds are interchangeable.

cards.title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) versus \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subsetneq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\) for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family \(f=(f_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\})\) in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) such that for every fixed depth \(d\ge 1\), exponent \(k\ge 1\), and constant \(M\ge 1\), there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing \(f_{n}\) exactly has size greater than \(M(n+1)^{k}\)?
cards.why: One of the central small-circuit questions: whether a constant number of counting layers can perform every logarithmic-depth Boolean computation. A resolution would clarify the power of threshold circuits, finite-group computation, and the role of sequential dependence in parallel computation.

cards.title: NEXP versus nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\)
cards.formal: Is there a language \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NEXP}\) such that, for every fixed circuit depth \(d\ge 1\), every fixed exponent \(k\ge 1\), every constant \(C\ge 1\) and every \(N\ge 1\), some \(n\ge N\) has no depth-at-most-d Boolean circuit of size at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) with AND, OR, NOT and majority gates that computes L correctly on every n-bit input? Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subset \mathrm{TC}^{0}\) for nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\)?
cards.why: Tests whether the algorithmic approach to circuit lower bounds can cross the threshold-gate barrier.

cards.title: KRW formula-size conjecture with constant loss
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(\alpha>0\) such that for every pair of positive integers \(n,m\) and every pair of nonconstant total Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), \(g:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\),
\[L(g\circ f)\ge\alpha L(g)L(f)?\]
Here \((g\circ f)(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})=g(f(x^{(1)}),\ldots,f(x^{(m)}))\) on \(m\) disjoint \(n\)-bit blocks, and \(L\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf size. The constant is chosen before all dimensions and functions.

This card retains the constant-factor formula-size version displayed as Conjecture 5.13 in the source book. It is stronger than versions permitting a growing multiplicative loss. The original KRW paper formulates a depth-composition question; the card does not identify that question, weakened quantitative versions, and the displayed constant-loss formula statement as equivalent.
cards.why: A formula for a composition can substitute an inner computation wherever an outer input is used, multiplying the leaf counts. A universal matching lower bound would show that alternative Boolean factorizations cannot save more than a constant factor on arbitrary block compositions. This is a strong structural statement about formulas, closely connected to the source’s superpolynomial formula lower-bound question.

cards.title: Majority outside constant-depth modular circuits
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{MAJ}\notin\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)? Precisely, for every fixed modulus \(m\geq2\), depth bound \(d\geq1\), constants \(C\geq1\), \(k\geq1\), and \(N\geq1\), is there an input length \(n\geq N\) for which no depth-at-most-\(d\) circuit over AND, OR, NOT and \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\), with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates, computes \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}\) exactly?
cards.why: Majority is a basic threshold operation. Showing that constant-depth modular circuits cannot compute it would separate ordinary threshold counting from the full fixed-modulus ACC⁰ model on a simple explicit function.

cards.title: Berman–Hartmanis conjecture
cards.formal: For every pair of languages \(A,B\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* that are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, does there exist a bijection \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that f and \(f^{- 1}\) are computable in deterministic polynomial time and, for every string \(x, x\in A\) if and only if \(f(x)\in B\)?
cards.why: A fundamental test of what NP-completeness means beyond mutual reducibility: does it impose one efficiently reversible structure on all complete decision problems? It links padding, cryptographic inversion, uniformity and the limitations of relativizing methods.

cards.title: Directed reachability in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space
cards.formal:
Is there one deterministic algorithm that decides directed reachability using polynomial time and polylogarithmic working space simultaneously?

Precisely, does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing decider \(M\) and fixed positive integers \(a,k,c\) such that, for every encoded instance \((G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), it correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), while
\[\operatorname{time}_M(G,s,t)\le c(N+2)^a\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{space}_M(G,s,t)\le c\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil^k?\]
Both bounds must hold for the same computation on every input. This is the question whether directed reachability belongs to the class SC.
cards.why: Directed reachability captures nondeterministic logarithmic space and is a basic model of exploring a large state graph. The question asks whether exploration can be both computationally efficient and extremely economical in reusable memory. Its resolution would clarify the relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic space while separating a genuine simultaneous resource bound from two individually achievable guarantees.

cards.title: PH versus PSPACE
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{PH}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? Equivalently, is there a fixed integer \(k\ge 0\) such that the truth problem for fully quantified Boolean formulas belongs to \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\)?
cards.why: Separates unbounded polynomial-space computation from a bounded number of polynomial-time alternations.

cards.title: P versus NP intersect coNP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates for both membership and nonmembership, but no uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm?
cards.why: This asks whether computational difficulty can persist even when every yes answer and every no answer has a short efficiently checkable proof. It isolates a basic boundary between verification and decision that is finer than the usual one-sided NP condition.

cards.title: NL versus UL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\)? Equivalently, do there exist one nondeterministic Turing machine \(M\) and constants \(C,D,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, on every explicitly encoded directed-reachability input \(x=(G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), every computation branch halts within \(D(N+2)^k\) steps and visits at most \(C\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work-tape cells, and
\[\#\{\text{accepting computation branches of }M(x)\}=
\begin{cases}1,&t\text{ is reachable from }s\text{ in }G,\\0,&\text{otherwise}?\end{cases}\]
The constants and machine are independent of the input. Unreachable and malformed inputs must have no accepting branch.
cards.why: Determine whether the multiplicity of accepting computations adds power to logarithmic-space computation.

cards.title: Polynomial formulas versus linear circuits
cards.formal:
Does there exist a family of total Boolean functions \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for integers \(n\ge1\), such that
\[S(f_n)=O(n)\qquad\text{but}\qquad L(f_n)\notin n^{O(1)}?\]
Here \(S\) is minimum bounded-fan-in De Morgan circuit gate count and \(L\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf count. Both are nonuniform and require exact correctness on every input. Precisely, the question asks for one family and a finite constant \(C>0\) satisfying \(S(f_n)\le Cn\) for all \(n\ge1\), while
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge N:\quad L(f_n)>n^k.\]
This is the source's absence-of-any-polynomial-upper-bound claim. It does not silently strengthen that claim to a lower bound beating each polynomial at every sufficiently large length.
cards.why: Circuits can reuse intermediate values and formulas must duplicate the computation when it is needed again. This question asks whether reuse can turn a task requiring superpolynomial tree size into a circuit of only linear size. It isolates a fundamental limitation of formulas while allowing the circuit computation to have unrestricted depth.

cards.title: CLS versus FP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\)? Equivalently, does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm solve the following Either-Solution problem: given an End-of-Line instance and an independent Localopt instance, return a valid solution of at least one of them?
cards.why: Determine the tractability of the common core of fixed-point search and potential-based local optimization.

cards.title: Does NP-hardness of MCSP imply circuit lower bounds for EXP?
cards.formal: If the Minimum Circuit Size Problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, must \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly? The hypothesis uses unrestricted ordinary polynomial-time reductions, with no locality, uniform-\(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) or naturalness promise.
cards.why: Whether ordinary NP-hardness of circuit minimization entails exponential-time circuit lower bounds is a central connection between metacomplexity and nonuniform lower bounds.

cards.title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space
cards.formal:
Does there exist one computable compiler \(\mathcal C\) that maps every deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) to a reversible multitape machine \(R=\mathcal C(M)\) with the following simultaneous guarantees? For every \(M\), there are a constant \(c_M\ge1\) and an integer \(d_M\ge1\) such that, on every input \(x\) on which \(M\) halts, \(R\) halts with exactly the output pair \((x,M(x))\), clears its auxiliary tapes, and satisfies
\[S_R(x)\le c_M S_M(x),\qquad T_R(x)\le c_M T_M(x)^{d_M}.\]
On every input on which \(M\) does not halt, \(R\) must also fail to halt. The same \(R\) must meet both bounds on every halting input. This is the previously selected polynomial-time, linear-space version of the source's broader simulation tradeoff question.
cards.why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), stable ternary compaction \(S_n:\{0,1,2\}^n\to\{0,1,2\}^n\) is computable by a Boolean circuit with at most \(Cn\) gates? The function deletes all symbols \(2\), retains all symbols \(0,1\) in their original relative order, and appends the deleted number of \(2\)s on the right. Circuits use the binary alphabet encoding and bounded-fan-in basis specified below, with no depth or uniformity restriction.
cards.why: This is an elementary deterministic rearrangement whose output preserves an arbitrary binary subsequence. Its sequential simplicity contrasts with the difficulty of arranging all output bits in a fixed circuit. Resolving linear circuit size would sharpen the boundary between data movement with input-dependent access and unrestricted bounded-fan-in Boolean computation.

cards.title: Minimum Circuit Size Problem
cards.formal:
Is the Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP), with a complete truth table as input, NP-complete under uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time function \(g\) such that
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad x\in\mathrm{SAT}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g(x)\in\mathrm{MCSP}?\]
Use the exact circuit model and language below. The target is unconditional and unrelativized. A reduction may not use random bits, advice, an oracle, a gap promise, a partial truth table or an implicitly represented truth table.
cards.why: MCSP asks how hard it is to recognize computational simplicity from complete data. Its classification connects NP-completeness with circuit lower bounds, learning and cryptography. A proof or refutation of standard NP-hardness would settle a central question about whether circuit minimization has the same reduction-based difficulty as general NP search.

cards.title: Ruling out quasilinear-time SAT without a space restriction
cards.formal:
Is Boolean-formula satisfiability outside deterministic quasilinear time, with no independent bound on the algorithm’s working memory? In the uniform random-access model below, the exact target is
\[\mathrm{SAT}\notin\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left[N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k\right],\]
where \(N\) is the full bit length of the explicitly written formula and \(\mathbb N\) includes zero. Thus every fixed polynomial-logarithmic factor must be excluded. On 16 September 2026 the user selected this meaning of the source’s “near-linear time”; the stronger exclusion of all \(N^{1+o(1)}\)-time algorithms is not required.
cards.why: An unconditional time-only lower bound for SAT in a general random-access model would cross a fundamental barrier in complexity theory. Even this comparatively weak exclusion remains separate from the substantial lower bounds known when memory is restricted.

cards.title: Existence of TFNP-complete problems
cards.formal:
Does the class of total polynomially bounded search problems with polynomial-time verifiable answers contain a complete problem under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions?

Writing this class as \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) and the reduction as \(\le_m^p\), the target is
\[\exists Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \forall R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\le_m^p Q.\]
The same fixed relation \(Q\) must work for every \(R\). For each \(R\), a reduction computes one \(Q\)-instance from the input and converts every valid answer to that instance into a valid \(R\)-answer. The question is unrelativized and concerns the whole class, including problems whose totality follows from different mathematical principles.
cards.why: A complete problem would give one universal task against which the difficulty of every efficiently verifiable total search problem could be compared. Its nonexistence would establish a structural limitation on extending the completeness framework from decision problems to all total search. This is a central question connecting complexity classes defined by semantic conditions, mathematical existence principles and the strength of formal proof systems.

cards.title: \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\)
cards.formal:
Is
\[\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}=\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\]
in the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered real field, with arbitrary real inputs and arbitrary finitely many fixed real machine constants? Equivalently, does every set of finite real tuples with polynomial-length real witnesses checkable in polynomial BSS time have a deterministic polynomial-time BSS decider? The decider and its finite constants may depend on the set, but must be fixed for all input lengths.
cards.why: This is the central determinism-versus-verification question for exact algebraic computation. It would classify the cost of real polynomial feasibility in a model that isolates arithmetic complexity from finite-precision representation, linking complexity theory to real algebraic geometry.

cards.title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(b\ge 2\) and every real \(x\in\)[0,1), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?
cards.why: A proof would impose a strong arithmetic restriction on numbers generated at the fastest possible asymptotic output rate. The checked 2024 source also records that the conjecture would rule out linear-time integer multiplication on multitape Turing machines.

cards.title: Exponential lower bounds for unrestricted threshold-of-threshold circuits
cards.formal: Does there exist an explicit Boolean function family \((f_n)_{n\geq1}\), in the source’s sense \(\mathrm{NP}\), and constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\), such that every unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit computing \(f_n\) has at least \(2^{cn}\) gates for every \(n\geq n_0\)?
cards.why: Depth-two threshold circuits are a basic model of two layers of weighted Boolean decisions. An exponential lower bound with unrestricted real weights would establish a strong limit on this expressive shallow architecture for an explicitly verifiable computational task.

cards.title: Subquadratic deterministic simulation of nondeterministic space
cards.formal: For every space-constructible function \(s:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) with \(s(n)\ge \lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\), is every language in \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) decidable deterministically in \(o(s(n)^{2})\) space? Equivalently, for each such s and each language L accepted by an \(O(s(n))\)-space nondeterministic machine, must there exist one deterministic decider D for L whose maximum workspace \(g_{D}(n)\) on n-bit inputs satisfies \(\lim (n\to \infty ) g_{D}(n)/s(n)^{2}=0\)?
cards.why: Would improve the general memory overhead for eliminating nondeterminism beyond a theorem that has stood since 1970. Even a slowly vanishing improvement would sharpen a basic relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic computation, including the logarithmic-space regime.

cards.title: Exponential depth-three \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) lower bounds for E
cards.formal:
Does there exist a language \(L\in\mathrm E\) whose characteristic functions require exponential-size depth-at-most-three Boolean AND/OR circuits, with arbitrary fan-in and input negations, at infinitely many input lengths?

Let \(f_{L,n}(x)=1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), and let \(S_3(f)\) be the minimum number of AND/OR gates in such a circuit computing \(f\) exactly. The question is
\[\exists L\in\mathrm E\ \exists\delta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N:\quad S_3(f_{L,n})>2^{\delta n}.\]
Here \(N,n\) are integers. This makes the source’s class lower-bound target precise as failure of subexponential-size depth-three computation for one language in E. No almost-every-length strengthening is imposed.
cards.why: Exponential lower bounds against very shallow Boolean circuits remain a substantial explicitness problem, even when the target language may use deterministic exponential time. Resolving this question would sharply advance the distinction between an arbitrary hard truth table and one generated by a uniform computation. The source also identifies this lower bound as an obstacle to extending certain circuit-minimization hardness arguments to ordinary depth-three AND/OR circuits.

cards.title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) perfect matching
cards.formal:
Does perfect-matching decision for general undirected graphs have nonuniform Boolean circuits of polynomial size and logarithmic depth?

For each integer \(v\ge2\), let \(\mathrm{PM}_v:\{0,1\}^{\binom v2}\to\{0,1\}\) indicate whether the encoded graph has a perfect matching. The target is the existence of fixed positive integers \(a,b,d\) and circuits \((C_v)_{v\ge2}\) such that
\[\forall v\ge2,\quad |C_v|\le a(v+1)^b,\qquad\operatorname{depth}(C_v)\le d\lceil\log_2(v+2)\rceil,\]
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{\binom v2},\qquad C_v(x)=\mathrm{PM}_v(x).\]
The gates have fan-in at most two, and negation is allowed. The circuits need not be generated uniformly, and the output is only the decision bit.
cards.why: Perfect matching is a central polynomial-time graph problem whose exact bounded-fan-in depth remains poorly understood. A negative answer would separate nonuniform NC-one from P/poly using a concrete polynomial-time task. A positive answer would put the decision problem at a much shallower level than the broad polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithms studied in most matching work.

cards.title: Sliding-scale PCP conjecture
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(a,b,d,q\), real constants \(c>0\) and \(K>0\), and one uniform deterministic oracle Turing machine \(V\) satisfying the following conditions? For every encoded 3-CNF formula \(F\) of bit length \(N\), set
\[
 r_N=\left\lceil a\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil,\qquad
 M_N=(N+2)^b,\qquad \Sigma_N=\{0,1,\ldots,M_N-1\}.
\]
Given \(F\), a uniformly random string \(R\in\{0,1\}^{r_N}\), and oracle access to a fixed proof \(\pi\in\Sigma_N^{M_N}\), the verifier makes at most \(q\) symbol queries, halts in at most \(K(N+2)^d\) bit operations, and accepts or rejects. It must have perfect completeness and inverse-polynomial soundness:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 F\text{ satisfiable}&\ \Longrightarrow\ 
   \exists\pi\ \forall R:\ V^\pi(F,R)=1,\\
 F\text{ unsatisfiable}&\ \Longrightarrow\ 
   \forall\pi:\ \Pr_R[V^\pi(F,R)=1]\le (N+2)^{-c}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All constants and the verifier are independent of \(F\) and \(N\).
cards.why: Achieving very small verification error while reading only a constant number of logarithmic-size proof symbols would strengthen the quantitative reach of PCP theory and its hardness-of-approximation consequences.

cards.title: \(\exists\mathbb{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Is \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{NP}\) in the ordinary bit-cost Turing model? Equivalently, is truth of every finitely encoded existential sentence over the ordered real field certifiable by a polynomial-length binary string checked in deterministic polynomial time?

For the language ETR defined below, the concrete target is the existence of one deterministic Turing verifier \(V\) and polynomial bounds \(p,q\) such that, for every binary string \(u\),
\[u\in\mathrm{ETR}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|u|)}:\ V(u,w)=1,\]
with \(V\) halting within \(q(|u|)\) steps on every permitted pair. The question is unconditional and has no oracle or advice.
cards.why: The answer would decide whether a broad class of geometric and algebraic existence problems has ordinary efficiently checkable finite certificates. It tests the boundary between discrete verification and exact continuous witnesses, with consequences across every problem complete for the existential theory of the reals.

cards.title: Supercubic uniform formula lower bounds for SAT
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon >0\) such that no LOGTIME-uniform De Morgan formula family computing \(\mathrm{SAT}_{n}\) for every n has \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) leaves?
cards.why: Would cross the cubic exponent for uniform De Morgan formula lower bounds on SAT. This quantifies a limitation of tree-shaped Boolean computation on an NP-complete problem without demanding a full separation from every polynomial-size family.

cards.title: Depth-three lower bounds beyond the log-depth simulation threshold
cards.formal:
Does there exist an explicit Boolean function family \((f_n)_{n\ge1}\) such that
\[S_3(f_n)=2^{\omega(n/\log\log n)}?\]
Here explicit means membership in NP, as in the source, and \(S_3\) counts gates in the smallest unrestricted-fan-in AND/OR circuit of depth three with negations available on inputs. Both top-gate orientations are covered. To avoid undefined small-length logarithms, the precise scale in the quantifiers is \(h(n)=n/\log_2\log_2(n+4)\), which has the stated asymptotics. This is Research Problem 11.2's quantitative target; the inherited description in terms of a switching-lemma barrier did not specify its much stronger exponent.
cards.why: This is the depth-three threshold that would exclude linear-size circuits of logarithmic depth for an explicit problem. It asks for a quantitative jump beyond the square-root exponent frontier, while retaining arbitrary sharing and unrestricted bottom fan-in in the shallow circuit. It therefore connects a very restricted depth model to a longstanding lower-bound goal for more general computation.

cards.title: Depth-three circuit lower bounds beyond the square-root exponent
cards.formal:
Does there exist an explicit family of total Boolean functions \((f_n)_{n\ge1}\) for which
\[S_{\Sigma_3}(f_n)=2^{\omega(\sqrt n)}?\]
The source's explicitness convention is NP membership. The minimum \(S_{\Sigma_3}\) is taken over all OR–AND–OR circuits with unrestricted fan-in and sharing, with negations allowed on input variables, and counts every gate. The target is a superconstant improvement in the exponent over \(\sqrt n\), not merely a larger fixed coefficient. It retains Research Problem 11.15's \(\Sigma_3\) orientation; it does not silently demand a simultaneous \(\Pi_3\) lower bound for the same function.
cards.why: Depth three is the first AND/OR depth at which elementary exponential lower bounds for normal forms no longer settle the complexity landscape. Beating the square-root exponent for an explicit family would improve a basic lower-bound frontier, even without reaching the much stronger exponent needed for the logarithmic-depth simulation consequence.

cards.title: Doubly efficient \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
cards.formal: For every uniform deterministic polynomial-space decider \(M\) and every time-constructible bound \(T(n)\ge n+2\) on its running time, does the language \(L(M)\) have a uniform classical single-prover interactive proof with a verifier running in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time and an honest prover running in \(\operatorname{poly}(T(n))\) total time, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\) against every cheating prover? The quantifier covers the full time range, rather than only \(T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}\).
cards.why: The class equality IP = PSPACE says that polynomial space can be verified efficiently, but does not by itself control the cost of generating the proof relative to the original computation. The target asks whether that prover overhead can always be polynomial while retaining soundness against an unlimited adversary.

cards.title: Randomized evasiveness conjecture
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge 2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and every nonconstant monotone graph property \(P\) on n vertices, its randomized adjacency-query complexity with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) satisfies \(R_{1/3}(P)\ge c n^2\)? Both c and \(n_0\) must be independent of P. This card asks for the bounded-error randomized evasiveness conjecture.
cards.why: This conjecture asks whether monotonicity and invariance under vertex names force essentially complete inspection even when random errors are allowed. It is a broad structural lower-bound question covering many graph recognition tasks at once. Its resolution would sharply delimit the power of randomized access to an exact graph property and explain why proximity testing can behave so differently.

cards.title: Independence of P versus NP from ZFC
cards.why: This asks whether the standard set-theoretic foundations used for ordinary mathematics can prove either outcome of P versus NP. Fixing full ZFC makes the question precise and separates limitations of particular proof methods from a limitation of the entire axiom system. A positive answer would establish incompleteness for a central natural problem about finite computation.

cards.title: Nonlinear-gate advantages for binary linear operators
cards.formal:
Can arbitrary Boolean gates give an unbounded wire saving over XOR gates for computing a binary linear operator? Determine whether
\[\forall K>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\setminus\{0\}:\quad
C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)>K\,C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A).\]
Both models allow unrestricted fan-in, fan-out and depth and must compute the entire same map \(x\mapsto Ax\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) on every input. GEN permits an arbitrary Boolean function at each gate and charges its incoming wires, not the gate's internal implementation. This adopts the unbounded-factor meaning of “help” made explicit by the constant-factor comparison following Problem 7.18.
cards.why: The final map is linear, but a general circuit may pass through nonlinear intermediate values. The question asks whether such intermediate computation can ever save an unbounded number of wires relative to staying linear throughout. It tests a basic structural limitation of circuit computation over the two-element field, where familiar linearization statements from infinite-field settings cannot simply be imported.

cards.title: Black-Box Hypothesis
cards.formal:
Is every semantic property of Boolean functions that is decidable in randomized polynomial time from a circuit description also decidable in randomized polynomial time from only input-output queries and a circuit-size bound?

More precisely, for every family of total predicates \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{2^n}\to\{0,1\}\), does
\[F\in\mathrm{wbBPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ F\in\mathrm{bbBPP}\]
hold under the definitions below? The reverse implication follows from polynomial-time circuit evaluation, so this is the usual equality formulation of the Black-Box Hypothesis. The property is defined on every truth table, and a white-box algorithm must be correct for every circuit description of that truth table.
cards.why: The hypothesis asks whether reading an efficient program can reveal any efficiently decidable fact about its function that could not also be learned efficiently by running the function on selected inputs. It connects the limits of program analysis with circuit complexity and obfuscation. Its truth would imply that NP is not contained in BPP, while restricted failures have known consequences for the complexity of circuit satisfiability.

cards.title: Is ARRIVAL solvable in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Does the deterministic decision problem \(\mathrm{ARRIVAL}\) defined below belong to \(\mathrm P\)? Equivalently, is there one deterministic Turing algorithm and constants \(K,c>0\) that, on every valid explicitly encoded switch graph of bit length \(L\), decides whether its token reaches destination \(d_1\) before \(d_0\) within \(K(L+1)^c\) bit steps? The two-destination termination condition and initial switch settings are part of the definition.
cards.why: ARRIVAL isolates the complexity of a finite deterministic process with one bit of memory at each switch. Its outcome has short verifiable evidence on both sides, but a general efficient decision algorithm would need to go beyond following the potentially exponential trajectory.

cards.title: Graph nonisomorphism in BPP
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that M halts on every binary input x and every random outcome within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions, and outputs the correct membership bit for \(\mathrm{GNI}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each x? The language \(\mathrm{GNI}\) consists of valid encodings of two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs. This asks whether \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\).
cards.why: This asks whether random computation alone can efficiently decide a canonical structural equivalence problem. Nonisomorphism has efficient interactive verification, but the help of an unbounded prover is an additional resource. Settling the BPP question would locate ordinary graph comparison more precisely between efficient deterministic algorithms, randomized algorithms and stronger forms of verification.

cards.title: UNSAT multi-prover proofs with efficient SAT-oracle provers
cards.formal:
Does UNSAT have a classical multi-prover interactive proof with a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and uniform probabilistic polynomial-time honest provers that may query SAT? The verifier has no oracle. For one fixed protocol, every unsatisfiable formula must be accepted with probability at least \(2/3\) when all provers are honest, while every satisfiable formula must be accepted with probability at most \(1/3\) for every collection of computationally unbounded, noncommunicating classical provers.

This restores the complement bar on SAT in the original Conjecture 6.2. The imported card lost that bar and incorrectly named SAT as the language to be proved; the oracle available to the honest provers is still SAT.
cards.why: This asks whether the output of a solver for an NP-complete problem can be checked using only the computational power of that solver. It connects the trustworthiness of hard computation to interactive proofs and to the limits of reductions between NP and total search.

cards.title: Excluding one-sided randomized quasilinear-time log-space SAT
cards.formal:
Is it true that no uniform randomized random-access algorithm decides Boolean satisfiability with one-sided error while using both quasilinear time and logarithmic workspace? More precisely, for every integer \(k\ge0\), is
\[\mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{RTISP}\!\left[N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k,\ \log_2(N+2)\right]?\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length. The two bounds hold simultaneously for one machine on every input and every sequence of coin flips. The error is allowed only on satisfiable inputs: each is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), whereas an unsatisfiable input is never accepted.
cards.why: This asks whether the known obstruction to extremely fast, very low-memory SAT algorithms survives useful one-sided randomness. An unconditional answer would advance lower bounds for a central NP-complete problem in a general computation model.

cards.title: Cost of restricting linear circuits to depth two
cards.formal:
Determine the asymptotic order, up to constant factors, of each of the three depth-restriction penalties
\[D_L(n)=\max_{A\in\mathcal M_n}\frac{C_{L,2}(A)}{C_L(A)},\qquad L\in\{\mathrm{OR},\mathrm{SUM},\mathrm{XOR}\}.\]
The numerator restricts a circuit to two leveled addition layers and the denominator allows arbitrary depth, with the same operation and matrix in each ratio. Size counts wires, fan-in is unrestricted, and matrices are square of dimension \(n\). This quantifies Problem 7.6 for the three linear-computation systems in the book; it does not ask only whether a gap can grow.
cards.why: Sharing through many intermediate stages can make a linear transformation substantially cheaper than a single layer of shared sums followed by outputs. These three functions quantify that saving for merging, exact addition, and parity cancellation. They isolate the role of depth without changing the operation or the target matrix.

cards.title: Downward self-reducibility of PLS-complete problems
cards.formal:
Is every PLS-complete total search problem downward self-reducible with respect to the bit length of its input? Precisely, for every binary relation \(R\) that is PLS-complete under polynomial-time search many-one reductions, must there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time oracle algorithm that finds an \(R\)-solution on every input \(x\), using an oracle for the same relation \(R\) only on strings \(z\) with \(|z|<|x|\)? It must work for every valid choice of solutions returned by that oracle.

The SODA 2026 result identifies this universal statement with \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\). This is an equivalence with an unresolved complexity-class equality, rather than an unconditional affirmative or negative resolution of the card.
cards.why: The question tests whether a recursive structure characterizes every representation of hard local search. The newer equivalence shows that its unconditional resolution would also resolve whether all PLS problems can be solved in polynomial time.

cards.title: NEXP circuit lower bounds from uniform obfuscation
cards.formal:
Prove or refute the following implication:
\[\text{a uniform polynomial-time, perfectly correct, uniformly secure IO exists}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}.\]
IO means indistinguishability obfuscation for general Boolean circuits, with the source's security definition specified below. Security is required only against uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms. On 16 September 2026 the user selected this particular circuit lower bound from the source's broader question. The target keeps perfect correctness and removes the stronger nonuniform-security hypothesis under which the source already proves this conclusion.
cards.why: This implication asks whether cryptographic security against one effective algorithm at a time already forces a language in nondeterministic exponential time to resist every polynomial-size circuit family. It isolates the role of nonuniform adversaries in a known connection between obfuscation and circuit lower bounds.

cards.title: Closure of UL under complement
cards.formal:
Is unambiguous logarithmic space closed under Boolean complement?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*,\qquad L\in\mathrm{UL}\ \Longrightarrow\ \{0,1\}^*\setminus L\in\mathrm{UL}.\]
Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{UL}=\mathrm{coUL}\)? A language is in \(\mathrm{UL}\) if one uniform nondeterministic machine decides it using logarithmic work space and has at most one accepting computation path on every input.

The complementing machine must also have at most one accepting path on every input and logarithmic space with its own fixed constants. The question concerns ordinary uniform machines with no advice or oracle and arbitrary binary input languages, not only planar graph problems.
cards.why: Unambiguity retains existential computation while limiting each positive instance to a unique accepting history. Complement closure asks whether the same economy is available for negative instances. Its resolution would clarify a basic structural property between deterministic and nondeterministic logarithmic space and the interpretation and composition of functions computed using unambiguous subroutines.

cards.title: Unconditional exclusion of linear-time CNF satisfiability
cards.formal: Is CNF satisfiability outside deterministic linear time on multitape Turing machines: does no deterministic machine decide every explicitly encoded CNF formula in \(O(L)\) time, where \(L\) is its full input bit length and no additional workspace restriction is imposed?
cards.why: An unconditional lower bound for satisfiability would establish a limitation of general computation for a central natural problem, beyond limitations of a solver family or consequences of a conjecture. Even a modest bound is significant when it applies without an extra memory restriction. Its precise computational model is part of the mathematical achievement.

cards.title: Formula versus circuit noise thresholds
cards.formal: Put \(\beta=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\). For \(0\le p<1/2\), let \(\mathcal C_p(n)\) be the finite noisy circuits defined below. Define reliable computation at noise \(p\) by \[\operatorname{Reliable}(p)\iff \exists\delta\in(0,1/2]\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}\ \exists C\in\mathcal C_p(n)\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\Pr[C(x)=f(x)]\ge1/2+\delta.\] Is the following proposition true? \[\forall p\in[0,1/2):\quad \operatorname{Reliable}(p)\iff p<\beta.\] In particular, the proposition includes impossibility at \(p=\beta\).
cards.why: The problem asks how much unreliable local computation can be tolerated when arbitrary redundancy and reuse are available. It would determine whether sharing intermediate noisy values changes the fundamental threshold already known for formulas.

cards.title: A counting characterization of P with NP access
cards.formal:
Does there exist one total counting function \(f\in\#\mathrm P\) such that
\[\mathrm P^f=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{SAT}}?\]
The oracle for \(f\) returns its exact nonnegative integer value in binary. Both sides are classes of decision problems with deterministic, adaptive polynomial-time oracle access. This asks about the ordinary, unrelativized classes; no auxiliary oracle or complexity separation is assumed.
cards.why: The question asks whether existential search has a precise counting counterpart at the level of computational power. Resolving it would clarify the boundary between deciding existence, counting witnesses and the polynomial hierarchy, while a negative answer would also separate P from NP.

cards.title: Improving the log-space SAT time exponent beyond 2 cos(π/7)
cards.formal:
Let \(\alpha=2\cos(\pi/7)\), approximately \(1.8019377\). Does there exist a rational constant \(q>\alpha\) such that no uniform deterministic random-access algorithm decides SAT using both \(O(N^q)\) time and \(O(\log N)\) workspace on every input of bit length \(N\)? In symbols, is
\[\exists q\in\mathbb Q,\quad q>2\cos(\pi/7)\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{DTISP}[N^q,\log N]?\]
This is the fixed positive improvement explicitly proposed in Problem 1. The two resource bounds must belong to the same machine.
cards.why: A fixed improvement would cross a precisely understood limit of the established proof framework for unconditional SAT time-space lower bounds. It would strengthen our understanding of how little memory constrains computation on an NP-complete problem.

cards.title: Largest separation between SUM and OR circuits
cards.formal:
Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the largest possible SUM-over-OR wire-complexity gaps
\[G(n)=\max_{A\in\mathcal M_n}\frac{C_{\mathrm{SUM}}(A)}{C_{\mathrm{OR}}(A)},\qquad
G_2(n)=\max_{A\in\mathcal M_n}\frac{C_{\mathrm{SUM},2}(A)}{C_{\mathrm{OR},2}(A)}.\]
The first ratio allows both circuits arbitrary depth; the second restricts both to the source's two-layer addition model. This retains the two comparisons explicitly motivating Problem 7.1. It compares two ways of evaluating the same zero-one coefficient matrix, not the largest SUM complexity and largest OR complexity on separately chosen matrices.
cards.why: OR can merge repeated contributions while ordinary addition must count each contribution exactly once. The largest possible size difference quantifies how much this idempotence helps when many outputs share partial computations. Separating the unrestricted and depth-two gaps tests how this advantage interacts with the number of computational layers.

cards.title: Unbounded XOR-over-OR complexity separations
cards.formal:
Can XOR wire complexity exceed OR wire complexity by an unbounded factor on the same zero-one matrix? Precisely, is the following statement true?
\[\forall K>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists A\in\mathcal M_n:\quad
C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)>K\,C_{\mathrm{OR}}(A).\]
Both circuit depths are unrestricted. Their outputs use the same coefficient matrix, but OR outputs are Boolean unions and XOR outputs are sums modulo two. No explicitness or efficient matrix-generation condition is imposed. This is the unrestricted ratio question in Problem 7.11, not its depth-two analogue.
cards.why: XOR can cancel duplicate contributions, while OR can merge them. There is no immediate pointwise ordering between the most efficient circuits for these different output semantics. An unbounded gap in this direction would show a systematic limitation of parity computation relative to idempotent merging, even when both can use arbitrary depth.

cards.title: Real quantifier alternation versus summation
cards.formal: For every fixed \(t\ge1\), does the truth problem for closed real-arithmetic sentences with at most \(t\) alternating quantifier blocks admit a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to \(\Sigma\text{-}\mathrm{ETR}\), the existential theory of the reals with Boolean summation binders? Equivalently, is every fixed level of the real polynomial hierarchy contained in \(\exists\mathbb R^\Sigma\) as defined below? The polynomial-time reduction and its degree may depend on \(t\); the number of real variables in each block is unrestricted. Either existential or universal first blocks are included.
cards.why: Alternating real quantifiers express geometric and optimization conditions beyond pure existence. Finite summation over Boolean choices adds a form of counting without introducing new real quantifier blocks. Comparing these resources would clarify whether a single strengthened existential theory captures all fixed levels of the real hierarchy.

cards.title: Closure of SZK under truth-table reductions
cards.formal:
Is statistical zero knowledge closed under deterministic polynomial-time truth-table reductions, using the promise-problem and three-valued circuit semantics of the source? In symbols,
\[\forall A,B,\qquad B\in\mathrm{SZK}\ \land\ A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A\in\mathrm{SZK}.\]
The reduction writes all queries before obtaining their answers and combines those answers with an arbitrary polynomial-size Boolean circuit. Its circuit need not have logarithmic depth or be a polynomial-size formula. Queries outside the oracle’s promise are permitted under the explicit rules below.
cards.why: A positive answer would make statistical zero knowledge robust under a broad form of efficient nonadaptive composition. A negative answer would reveal a basic limitation on combining individually private verification tasks, despite the known strong formula closure.

cards.title: Complete problem for Search-SZK
cards.formal:
Does Search-SZK, the class of promise search problems with statistical zero-knowledge protocols defined below, have a complete problem under the authors' deterministic polynomial-time Levin reductions? Precisely, is there one promise search problem \(R^{\star}\) such that
\[R^{\star}\in\mathrm{Search\text{-}SZK}\quad\text{and}\quad \forall R\in\mathrm{Search\text{-}SZK},\ R\le_{\mathrm L}^{\mathrm P}R^{\star}?\]
The user selected the statistical version on 16 September 2026. The source also asks the separate computational-zero-knowledge version; that question is not an additional required target here.
cards.why: A complete problem would provide a single representative of statistical zero-knowledge search, as complete decision problems do for familiar complexity classes. The issue tests whether privacy of a revealed solution admits a common reduction-based structure even when protocols can produce many different legal outputs.

cards.title: Subexponential derandomization with two-way random-tape access
cards.formal:
Can every bounded-error randomized logspace decision algorithm with two-way access to polynomially many random bits be simulated by a deterministic algorithm in time \(2^{o(n)}\)?

Precisely, does every language \(L\in\mathrm{2\text{-}wayBPL}\) admit one deterministic decider \(D\) whose worst-case running time \(T_D(n)\) satisfies
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2(T_D(n)+2)}{n}=0?\]
There is no additional space restriction on \(D\). This card uses the single-decider \(2^{o(n)}\) meaning of subexponential time, matching the explicit time scale discussed in the source. The source question is about arbitrary two-way random-tape access, even though the paper’s main advice theorem concerns a bounded number of one-way passes.
cards.why: Rereading random bits costs no additional writable memory in this model, but it creates dependencies that ordinary one-way randomized-space simulations do not directly handle. Even a subexponential deterministic simulation would clarify how much computational power persistent randomness supplies under a logarithmic memory bound. The problem is a concrete derandomization question between ordinary randomized logspace and unrestricted polynomial-time randomness.

cards.title: FBPP versus negligible-error FBPP
cards.formal:
Under the following relational error conventions, is
\[\mathrm{FBPP}\subseteq\mathrm{FBPP}_{\mathrm{negl}}?\]
In \(\mathrm{FBPP}\), a uniform randomized algorithm receives a precision parameter \(m\ge1\) in unary, must produce a valid answer with probability at least \(1-1/m\), and may take time polynomial in \(|x|+m\). In \(\mathrm{FBPP}_{\mathrm{negl}}\), one uniform randomized algorithm receives only \(x\), runs in time polynomial in \(|x|\), and has error smaller than every inverse polynomial for all sufficiently long inputs.

Both classes range over the same polynomially bounded binary relations. Relations may be partial and need not have decidable membership. The inclusion quantifies over every such relation; a negligible-error algorithm may depend on the relation but must be one fixed algorithm for all input lengths and all inverse-polynomial comparisons.
cards.why: For a decision problem, repeated trials concern one correct bit. A relation may instead allow many different valid answers without any procedure for recognizing them. This question tests whether adjustable inverse-error running time can always be replaced by negligible failure at one fixed polynomial cost, clarifying which error-reduction properties survive in general randomized search.

cards.title: UEOPL versus EOPL
cards.formal: Does EndOfPotentialLine reduce to UniqueEOPL by a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction for total search problems? Equivalently, is UEOPL=EOPL? Instances contain explicit Boolean circuits, and the reduction may inspect their descriptions. The question concerns the ordinary classes without an oracle.
cards.why: Would determine whether uniqueness with efficiently detectable violations defines a strictly easier form of total search inside \(\mathrm{PLS}\cap\)PPAD, affecting the classification of fixed-point, orientation and game problems captured by UEOPL.

cards.title: \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\) versus MA
cards.formal:
Do the following two classes of ordinary decision languages coincide?
\[\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{MA}.\]
An \(\mathrm{MA}\) language has a polynomial-length classical witness and a polynomial-time randomized verifier: a yes-instance has some witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and every witness to a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\).

For \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\), the witness predicate must additionally be an ordinary BPP language on pairs. Its acceptance probability is therefore always at most \(1/3\) or at least \(2/3\), including for every unsuccessful witness on a yes-instance. The equality asks whether every MA language admits some verifier with that stronger all-pairs gap, possibly with a different witness encoding and polynomial length bound.
cards.why: Existential witnesses and randomized verification interact differently depending on whether every witness must induce a valid bounded-error decision. Resolving this equality would determine whether the additional gap requirement changes computational power or only the presentation of a verifier. The distinction is fundamental when probabilistic predicates are nested beneath quantifiers in classical and quantum complexity hierarchies.

cards.title: Effective enumeration of BPP
cards.formal:
Does there exist a total computable function \(E\) which, for every index \(i\in\mathbb N\), outputs the finite description of a randomized polynomial-time decision machine \(M_i\), such that
\[\forall i\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^*,\quad\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1],\]
and every language in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) is decided by at least one of these machines?

With \(L_i=\{x:\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\ge2/3\}\), the coverage condition is exactly
\[\{L_i:i\in\mathbb N\}=\mathrm{BPP}.\]
Repeated languages and repeated machine descriptions are allowed. The enumeration must include at least one suitable algorithm for each BPP language; it need not list every bounded-error program. There is no efficiency bound on computing \(E(i)\). Each \(M_i\) may have its own polynomial runtime bound, and the enumerator is not additionally required to output that bound.
cards.why: Polynomial running time can be guaranteed syntactically by a clock, but bounded error is a condition on every possible input. The question asks whether a computably generated family can still capture all feasible randomized decision problems while guaranteeing that condition. A resolution would clarify the relationship between semantic complexity classes, programming formalisms and what arithmetical theories can certify about randomized computation.

cards.title: Polynomial-time weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that decides weighted falsifiability for every unambiguous DNF? Given
\[F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j,\qquad w_1,\ldots,w_n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,\]
it must decide whether
\[\exists a\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\qquad F(a)=0\quad\land\quad\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t.\]
Each term \(T_j\) is explicitly listed, and the weights and threshold are binary integers. Unambiguity means that no assignment satisfies two distinct term occurrences. The threshold is “at least,” not exact equality.
cards.why: The problem isolates whether a representation with easy exact counting also supports optimization over its complement. Binary weights create a sharp distinction from the unweighted and unary cases, with consequences for the operations supported by compact Boolean representations.

cards.title: Deterministic query complexity of tournament kings
cards.formal: Determine the asymptotic order of \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\), the minimum worst-case number of edge-orientation queries needed by a deterministic decision tree to output one king of every tournament on \([n]\). The domain is the integers \(n\ge 2\). The required precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to absolute constant factors: supply a positive function \(f\) and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge 2\) such that \(c f(n)\le D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\le C f(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\).
cards.why: This is a longstanding total search problem in which existence is elementary but the information needed for deterministic discovery is unresolved. It isolates a substantial gap between deterministic and randomized access to a graph, without the computational cost of processing already known edges. A tight bound would explain how much pairwise information is inherently required to identify a vertex with global two-step reachability, a tournament solution motivated by pairwise competition and social choice.

cards.title: DNF versus d-DNNF succinctness
cards.formal: Is the following nonuniform size separation true? For every \(C\geq1\), integer \(k\geq1\) and \(N\geq1\), there is a DNF formula \(F\) of size \(s\geq N\) such that every d-DNNF circuit computing exactly the same Boolean function on the same input variables has size greater than \(C(s+1)^{k}\). Equivalently, is there no single polynomial bound on the size of a d-DNNF representation of an arbitrary DNF? No efficient construction or conversion algorithm is required on either side of this size comparison.
cards.why: The question measures an inherent space cost of making overlapping explanations disjoint while retaining decomposable structure. It determines whether the simplest compact disjunctive representation can always remain compact in a form suited to exact counting, independently of how difficult that form is to find.

cards.title: Polynomial-size closure of d-DNNF under negation
cards.formal:
Do constants \(c>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, for every finite variable set \(X\) and every d-DNNF circuit \(C\) over \(X\), there is a d-DNNF circuit \(D\) over \(X\) with
\[s(D)\le c\bigl(s(C)+1\bigr)^k\quad\text{and}\quad\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\ f_D(a)=1-f_C(a)?\]
The constants are universal: they cannot depend on \(X\), \(C\) or its Boolean function. No algorithm, uniformity or bound on the time needed to find \(D\) is required. Its internal decompositions may differ from those of \(C\), with no global variable-tree restriction on either circuit.
cards.why: This question isolates whether Boolean negation inherently destroys the succinctness of a central tractable representation. It separates a representational obstruction from the algorithmic difficulty of discovering a representation. A negative answer would exhibit a fundamental asymmetry between compact descriptions of a set of assignments and its complement; a positive answer would establish polynomial-size robustness under negation.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
cards.why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

cards.title: Optimal size of four-additive graph spanners
cards.formal: Determine \(s_{4}(n)=\max _{G} \min _{H} |E(H)|\) up to universal multiplicative constants for integers \(n\ge 2\), where G ranges over connected simple undirected unweighted graphs on n vertices and H ranges over their spanning subgraphs satisfying \(d_{H}(u,v)\le d_{G}(u,v)+4\) for all vertices u,v.
cards.why: The +4 additive-spanner regime is the classical remaining constant-error sparsity-exponent gap, making it a central distance-compression problem rather than a peripheral parameter choice.

cards.title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.

cards.title: Size-bounded approximate multicommodity-flow sparsifiers
cards.formal: Does there exist a function \(f:\{2,3,\ldots\}\times(0,1)\to\mathbb N\) such that every finite undirected capacitated graph \(G\) with a labelled set \(T\) of \(k\) terminals admits a finite undirected capacitated graph \(H\), containing the same labelled terminals and at most \(f(k,\varepsilon)\) vertices, for which \[\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\le\operatorname{cong}_G(d)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\] holds simultaneously for every nonnegative terminal demand vector \(d\)? Here \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and new nonterminal vertices and arbitrary capacities in \(H\) are permitted.
cards.why: This tests whether terminal flow behavior admits an arbitrarily accurate finite summary independent of the original network.

cards.title: Hypergraph cut sparsifiers with \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H\) on \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) admit a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H'\) on the same vertices with \(|E'|\le Cn/\varepsilon^2\) and \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\le\operatorname{cut}_{H'}(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\)?
cards.why: Tests whether preserving all cuts of a multiway interaction system requires any more hyperedges than the graph sparsification upper bound. It separates the number of retained interactions from their incidence storage and from the cost of computing them.

cards.title: Near-linear output-sensitive Subset Sum
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm that lists all attainable subset sums up to a given threshold in time near-linear in the explicit input size plus the number of distinct output values?

More precisely, for integers \(n,t\ge1\) and an input list \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{1,\ldots,t\}^{n}\), put
\[
S(X,t)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I}x_i:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\right\}
\cap\{0,\ldots,t\},\qquad q(X,t)=|S(X,t)|.
\]
Does there exist one finite program \(A\), a fixed integer \(d\ge1\), a constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(b\ge0\), chosen independently of every input, such that on the word RAM defined below, with
\[
w=d\left\lceil\log_2(n+t+2)\right\rceil,
\]
both of the following hold for every valid \(n,t,X\)?
\[
\forall r\quad T_{A,d}(X,t;r)
\le C\bigl(n+q(X,t)\bigr)\bigl(\log_2(n+t+2)\bigr)^b,
\]
\[
\Pr_r\!\left[\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\right]\ge \frac23.
\]
Here success means that the complete output lists every element of \(S(X,t)\) exactly once and no other value. The time bound applies to every random execution, including unsuccessful executions. The algorithm is not given \(q(X,t)\) or any subset-sum information as additional input.

This card retains the previously selected bounded-error, worst-case word-RAM formulation of the source's near-linear output-sensitive question. Its explicit instruction set and requirement on every random execution are editorial model conventions; the source's expected-time or high-probability bounds are reported separately below.
cards.why: The question tests whether a basic dynamic-programming problem can be solved at essentially the cost of reading its input and writing its distinct answers. A positive resolution would avoid paying for a large unused numerical range even when the input contains repeated items. A negative resolution would establish an additional computational cost beyond input and output size for a fundamental exact problem. This is a general algorithmic endpoint, not a request to count solutions or to improve one implementation.

cards.title: Small Implicit Graph Conjecture
cards.formal: Does every hereditary small graph class \(\mathcal C\) admit an adjacency labeling scheme using at most \(K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits per vertex on every \(n\)-vertex graph in \(\mathcal C\), for some constant \(K\) depending only on \(\mathcal C\)?
cards.why: A short global description of every graph does not by itself make adjacency locally decodable from two short vertex descriptions. The conjecture asks whether a precise growth restriction and induced-subgraph closure suffice to bridge this gap.

cards.title: Quadratic-size submodular hypergraph sparsifiers
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that every submodular hypergraph on \(n\geq1\) vertices and every \(0<\varepsilon<1\) admit a reweighted sub-hypergraph with at most \(C n^{2}/\varepsilon^{2}\) hyperedges that simultaneously approximates every cut value within factors \(1-\varepsilon\) and \(1+\varepsilon\)?
cards.why: The question asks whether rich higher-order cut objectives always have representations using quadratically many original terms, independent of their complexity and value ranges. Such a theorem would provide a general compression guarantee across submodular optimization models.

cards.title: Quasipolynomial dependence on vertices for hypergraph isomorphism
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that decides isomorphism of two explicitly represented hypergraphs in time \[2^{C(\log_2(n+2))^{a}}\,N^{b},\] for fixed constants \(C,a,b\geq1\), where \(n\) is the maximum number of underlying vertices and \(N\) is the combined input bit length?
cards.why: This asks whether symmetry testing can depend quasipolynomially only on the underlying universe, while remaining polynomial in the amount of set-system data. It matters for hypergraphs with many large edges and for algorithms that encode structural graph information as set systems.

cards.title: Optimal additive error of linear-size spanners
cards.formal: Determine the optimal worst-case additive error \(A_c(n)\) of a spanner with at most \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) edges, up to multiplicative constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), for every fixed real constant \(c\geq1\). The graph is arbitrary, undirected and unweighted; the edge budget is genuinely linear, without hidden factors depending on \(n\).
cards.why: The linear edge regime compresses a graph to a constant number of retained edges per vertex. Determining its unavoidable distance loss would quantify a fundamental limit on how accurately arbitrary graph metrics can survive such strong sparsification.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial planar minimum-cost flow
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm for minimum-cost flow in a planar directed graph whose worst-case number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is \(o(n^{2}\log(n+2))\), where \(n\) is the number of vertices? The algorithm must return an exact minimum-cost feasible flow, or correctly report infeasibility, for all rational capacities, costs and vertex supplies.
cards.why: This asks how much planarity can accelerate exact flow optimization when numerical magnitudes cannot enter the operation count. It separates combinatorial graph structure from progress that relies on bounded capacities and costs.

cards.title: Isomorphism dichotomy for finitely forbidden hereditary classes
cards.formal: For every finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite graphs, is graph isomorphism restricted to graphs containing no induced copy of a member of \(\mathcal F\) either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or complete for general graph isomorphism under polynomial-time many-one reductions?
cards.why: A finite list of forbidden induced patterns is a simple and widely used graph-class description. The conjecture asks whether such finite structural restrictions always make symmetry testing tractable or retain the full difficulty of unrestricted graph isomorphism.

cards.title: Spanners matching Thorup–Zwick emulator tradeoffs
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), do there exist constants \(C_{k},D_{k}>0\) such that every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(n=|V|\ge1\), has a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,E_{H})\), \(E_{H}\subseteq E\), satisfying
\[
|E_{H}|\le C_{k}n^{\,1+1/(2^{k+1}-1)}
\]
and, simultaneously for all distinct vertices \(u,v\) in the same connected component of \(G\),
\[
d_{H}(u,v)\le d_{G}(u,v)+D_{k}\,d_{G}(u,v)^{\,1-1/k}?
\]
The constants may depend on \(k\), but not on the graph, its size or the vertex pair. This is the fixed-\(k\) size and distance-error tradeoff achieved by Thorup–Zwick emulators, now required of an actual subgraph.
cards.why: Spanners retain real routes in the original network, while emulators can encode long routes as weighted shortcuts. Matching their size/error tradeoffs would establish that this structural restriction costs only constant factors at every fixed level of sublinear distance accuracy. The later almost-matching theorem makes the exact remaining loss especially concrete.

cards.title: Complexity of general vertex-connectivity augmentation
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a simple undirected graph \(G\) and a target \(1\leq\lambda<|V(G)|\), computes the minimum number of new edges needed to make \(G\) \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected, when every missing edge is available at unit cost?
cards.why: The question asks whether optimal resilience to vertex failures can be added efficiently when all new links have the same cost and are freely available. These simple input conditions isolate the difficulty of vertex connectivity itself from costly or forbidden links.

cards.title: Linear-time exact inversion counting
cards.formal: Do there exist one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly listed permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(A\) outputs \[\operatorname{Inv}(\pi)=|\{(i,j)\in[n]^2:i<j\ \text{and}\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}|\] exactly, using at most \(Cn\) machine instructions in the worst case? The word length and allowed instructions are specified below. The constant and the program must be independent of \(n\) and \(\pi\).
cards.why: Exact inversion counting compresses a permutation’s pairwise disorder into one integer and is a fundamental offline aggregation task. Its complexity remains separated from the cost of sorting already rank-bounded integers. The 2025 hardness connections show that a linear-time solution would also change the algorithmic frontier for packed-string processing.

cards.title: Near-linear-time approximation of reachability diameter
cards.formal:
Is there an integer constant \(C\ge1\) and a single uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite unweighted directed graph \(G\), returns an integer \(\widehat D\) satisfying
\[
\Pr\!\left[D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)\right]\ge 2/3
\]
and always halts in near-linear time? Here
\[
D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):u,v\in V(G),\ d_G(u,v)<\infty\}
\]
is the reachability diameter. The graph representation, machine and worst-case time bound are specified below. This retains the card's near-linear constant-factor specialization of the source's broader approximation-versus-time question; it does not ask to determine that entire tradeoff.
cards.why: This asks whether a basic distance statistic of an arbitrary directed network can be estimated without computing distances from every vertex. It captures information that conventional directed diameter loses when directions are disconnected, and appears in assessing diameter reduction by reachability-preserving shortcut edges. A resolution would establish a general algorithmic principle or limitation for directed reachability and distance estimation.

cards.title: Set-system sparsifiers of size proportional to chain length
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for every integer \(m\ge 1\), every family \(S\subseteq 2^{[m]}\), every weight vector \(w\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) and every \(0<\varepsilon <1\), there is a reweighting \(\tilde\{w\}\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) with at most \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) nonzero coordinates and satisfying \((1- \varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\le \sum _{i\in A}\tilde\{w\}_{i}\le (1+\varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\) simultaneously for every \(A\in S\)?
cards.why: Would give a sharp structural bound for simultaneous multiplicative compression of arbitrary weighted set families. It asks whether chain length and squared inverse accuracy fully account for the necessary support, without logarithmic losses.

cards.title: Complexity of planar 3-edge-colorability
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple planar graph \(G\), decides whether its edges can be properly colored with three colors?
cards.why: This is a basic unresolved coloring decision problem on planar graphs with very small maximum degree. A resolution would clarify exactly how far the algorithmic consequences of the Four-Color Theorem extend beyond regular planar graphs.

cards.title: Three disjoint directed shortest paths
cards.formal: Does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm decide whether a directed graph with positive rational arc lengths and three prescribed source-target pairs contains three mutually vertex-disjoint paths, each individually shortest between its own endpoints?
cards.why: Three pairs form a small and sharply defined test of whether directed shortest-path constraints can be coordinated efficiently. A resolution would distinguish the difficulty of selecting individually optimal routes from ordinary shortest-path computation and from undirected routing.

cards.title: Polynomial-time detection of fixed pivot- and vertex-minors
