cards.formal: For each relation \(\rho\in\{\text{pivot-minor},\text{vertex-minor}\}\) and each fixed finite simple graph \(H\), does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple graph \(G\), decides whether some \(\rho\) of \(G\) is isomorphic to \(H\)?
cards.why: Efficient fixed-pattern detection would make local-transformation graph structure algorithmically accessible, with consequences for graph classes and graph-state transformations.

cards.title: Planarity dichotomy for induced subdivision detection
cards.formal: Assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), is it true that for every fixed finite subcubic graph \(H\), detecting an induced subdivision of \(H\) in an arbitrary input graph belongs to \(\mathrm P\) if and only if \(H\) is planar?
cards.why: A resolution would give one structural explanation for the complexity of an entire family of induced pattern-detection problems. It asks whether the geometry of the fixed pattern, rather than just its bounded degree, controls tractability.

cards.title: Polynomial-time minimum-total-length disjoint paths for fixed k
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an undirected unweighted graph G and k prescribed terminal pairs \((s_{i},t_{i})\), outputs pairwise vertex-disjoint paths \(\mathrm{P}_{i}\) from \(s_{i}\) to \(t_{i}\) minimizing \(\sum _{i}|E(\mathrm{P}_{i})|\), or correctly reports that no such collection exists? Randomized algorithms with success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input are admitted in this reading, consistently with the randomized \(k=2\) baseline cited by the source. Polynomial degree and constants may depend on k; an FPT bound with exponent independent of k is not requested.
cards.why: Would determine whether exact length optimization preserves the polynomial-time solvability of undirected disjoint routing with a fixed number of prescribed terminal pairs.

cards.title: Polynomial-time independent set under a forbidden forest
cards.formal: For every fixed finite forest \(H\) whose connected components each have at most three leaves, does Maximum Weight Independent Set on \(H\)-free graphs admit a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm? Precisely, must there exist an algorithm \(A_{H}\) and constants \(c_{H},C_{H}>0\) that, for every \(H\)-free vertex-weighted graph \((G,w)\) of encoding length \(L\), output a maximum-weight independent set in at most \(C_{H}(L+1)^{c_{H}}\) steps?
cards.why: This conjecture would complete a natural complexity classification of a central optimization problem by forbidden induced structure. It asks whether the large family now admitting quasipolynomial algorithms actually permits polynomial-time exact optimization, including graphs of unrestricted density.

cards.title: A dichotomy for edge deletion with finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs
cards.formal: For every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is the following decision problem either in \(\mathrm P\) or \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and integer \(k\geq0\), decide whether there is \(S\subseteq E\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) has no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of \(\mathcal F\).
cards.why: Edge deletion is a basic graph-repair operation whose tractability changes with the desired hereditary property. A dichotomy for every finite forbidden list would explain this variation across many graph classes and locate a general boundary between efficient repair and NP-completeness.

cards.title: Near-linear constant-factor minimum-degree spanning trees
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\), absolute constants \(K,C\ge1\), and an integer \(b\ge0\) such that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\) with \(n\ge2\) and \(m=|E|\), the algorithm outputs a spanning tree \(T\subseteq G\) satisfying \(\Delta(T)\le K\Delta^\star(G)\) in at most \(C(m+n)(\log_2(n+2))^b\) word-RAM operations? Here \(\Delta(T)=\max_{v\in[n]}\deg_T(v)\) and \(\Delta^\star(G)=\min\{\Delta(T):T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}\). All constants and the program must be independent of the graph. This is a static construction problem; the graph is supplied once, and no update sequence is part of the input.
cards.why: A low-degree spanning tree supplies a connected backbone while limiting the largest number of connections handled by one vertex. A constant approximation in near-linear time would make a strong structural guarantee available at a cost close to reading the graph. The target is substantially weaker than exact degree minimization, but stronger than bounds whose approximation grows with the graph size. This is a static construction frontier, despite the dynamic setting of the seminar collection.

cards.title: Complexity of directed detours
cards.formal: Classify the worst-case complexity of the following decision problem on unrestricted finite directed graphs: given distinct vertices s and t, is there a simple directed s-to-t path with at least \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s,t)+1\) edges? The requested distinction is polynomial-time solvability versus NP-completeness. This is the fixed \(k=1\) case of Longest Detour, not the problem with k supplied as part of the input.
cards.why: Pinpoints whether even the smallest departure from shortest-path length creates NP-complete difficulty under the simple-path constraint, a basic boundary in directed path algorithms.

cards.title: Linear-time directed bottleneck paths and trees
cards.formal: Do the directed bottleneck path and rooted bottleneck spanning-tree problems admit comparison-based algorithms with expected running time \(O(n+m)\) on every input, always returning an exact optimum? The input has \(n\) vertices and \(m\) weighted directed edges. Randomization is allowed; deterministic linear time would also answer positively. The source writes \(O(m)\) after the usual removal or treatment of irrelevant vertices. The requested guarantee is total running time, including graph processing and output, with weights accessible only through comparisons.
cards.why: Determines the exact cost of fundamental directed min-max optimization when numerical information is available only by comparison. Removing the overhead would close a long-standing gap for sparse graphs; distinguishing the input model prevents an already-solved variant from being presented as open.

cards.title: Near-linear-query reconstruction of bounded-degree graphs
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(\Delta\geq2\), is there a randomized exact reconstruction algorithm \(A_{\Delta}\) and constants \(C_{\Delta}>0\), \(k_{\Delta}\geq0\) such that every hidden connected simple unweighted undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\) labeled vertices with maximum degree at most \(\Delta\) can be reconstructed using \[\mathbb E[Q(A_{\Delta},G)]\leq C_{\Delta}\,n(\log(n+2))^{k_{\Delta}}\] queries to an oracle that returns the shortest-path distance between one requested pair of vertices?
cards.why: The problem asks how much pairwise distance information is inherently needed to discover an entire sparse network. A near-linear worst-input guarantee would show that distances allow almost output-sized exact reconstruction despite hiding every edge, without relying on randomness in the network itself.

cards.title: Maximum reset threshold of synchronizing automata
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\), determine \(T(n)=\max\){\(rt(A): A\) is a synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n states and any finite nonempty alphabet}, where \(rt(A)\) is its shortest reset-word length.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(\mathrm{L}(D)=\mathrm{L}(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

cards.title: Generalized star-height problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \Sigma\)* such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
cards.why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.

cards.title: Decidability of equivalence for unambiguous context-free grammars
cards.formal: Is it decidable, given two finite context-free grammars \(G_1,G_2\) over the same finite terminal alphabet and promised that both are unambiguous, whether \(L(G_1)=L(G_2)\)?
cards.why: This basic equivalence problem tests the algorithmic power of unique parsing beyond deterministic context-free language descriptions.

cards.title: First-order definability of regular tree languages
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a finite bottom-up automaton A for finite unranked ordered labeled trees, always halts and decides whether some first-order sentence \(\varphi\) using label predicates, strict descendant and sibling order satisfies A accepts t if and only if \(t\models \varphi\) for every finite input tree t?
cards.why: The tree analogue of effective first-order definability for regular word languages.

cards.title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
cards.why: Determine whether bounded logical alternation can be recognized effectively throughout a fundamental hierarchy of regular languages.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
cards.why: Locate the decidability boundary for equivalence of terminating recursive tree programs with copying and nested output parameters.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, on every pair \((G,H)\) of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether \[\operatorname{Tree}(G)=\operatorname{Tree}(H)?\] Both schemes may have arbitrary finite type order, with their orders supplied by their finite descriptions. Equality is exact equality of the possibly infinite ordered value trees, including the nullary divergence symbol \(\bot\). No safety or productivity promise is imposed.
cards.why: This is a central comparison problem for finite programs with higher-order recursion. Their complete output can be an infinite tree, and strong logical properties of each individual tree are already decidable. Deciding equality would establish an effective method for identifying identical observable recursive behavior across different finite descriptions; undecidability would locate a fundamental boundary beyond single-program verification.

cards.title: Linear-time minimization of deterministic finite automata
cards.formal: For every fixed alphabet size \(a\ge2\), is deterministic minimization of complete finite automata over \([a]=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) possible in \(O(n)\) worst-case time on the word-RAM defined below? More explicitly, the target is \[\forall a\ge2\ \exists M_a,C_a,n_a\ \forall n\ge n_a\ \forall A\text{ with }n\text{ states},\quad M_a(A)\text{ outputs a smallest equivalent complete DFA in at most }C_a n\text{ steps}.\] Here \(M_a\) is a single finite program independent of \(n\); \(C_a\) and \(n_a\) may depend on \(a\), and \(n_a\ge a\) may be assumed. The task is exact language-preserving minimization, with no prescribed canonical naming of output states.
cards.why: DFA minimization is a basic preprocessing step for recognizers, regular-language operations and finite-state verification. Its classical algorithm is almost linear, and the logarithmic factor has resisted removal for general transition graphs. Resolving the target would distinguish an inherent cost of the problem from the cost of the partition-refinement paradigm.

cards.title: Decidability of the nondeterministic tree-automaton index problem
cards.formal: Is it decidable, given a nondeterministic parity automaton A on infinite full binary trees and a nonempty integer priority interval J={i,…,j}, whether some nondeterministic parity tree automaton over the same alphabet, using only priorities in J, recognizes exactly the same language as A?
cards.why: The index problem measures how much acceptance complexity is inherently needed to describe a tree language.

cards.title: Separating words problem
cards.formal:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), let \(s(n)\) be the largest, over pairs of distinct binary words of length \(n\), minimum number of states in a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that accepts exactly one of the two words. The automaton model is specified in Definitions and model below.

Determine the polynomial growth exponent
\[
x_* = \inf\bigl\{r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:s(n)=O(n^r)\bigr\}
\]
to absolute error at most \(1/100\). The asymptotic bound inside this definition is quantified explicitly below; the target is the exponent, rather than the entire function up to constant factors.
cards.why: Determining the polynomial exponent would quantify the worst-case finite-state memory needed to distinguish two long binary words, while separating polynomial growth from finer logarithmic factors.

cards.title: Primitive words and context-freeness
cards.formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) with \(|\Sigma|\ge2\), is the language \[\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)=\{w\in\Sigma^+ : \text{there are no }u\in\Sigma^+,\ k\ge2\text{ with }w=u^k\}\] not context-free?
cards.why: The primitive-word language is a basic boundary case linking periodicity of words with the expressive power of context-free grammars.

cards.title: Two-dimensional cellular-automaton limit sets
cards.formal: Characterize exactly which two-dimensional subshifts are ordinary limit sets of cellular automata, allowing finitely many auxiliary states that disappear from the limit set. Equivalently, determine the realizability function \(R(q,S)\in\{0,1\}\) on the full domain of finite alphabet sizes \(q\ge1\) and subshifts \(S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,q-1\}^{\mathbb Z^2}\) defined below. Its value is 1 exactly when some cellular automaton on a finite alphabet containing those \(q\) symbols has ordinary limit set exactly \(S\), and is 0 otherwise. This is a whole-class characterization, with no computability or time requirement on the answer function.
cards.why: A cellular automaton has a finite local description but can retain complex global configurations indefinitely. An exact realizability classification would identify which translation-invariant spatial constraints can arise in that long-term behavior. It concerns every possible initial configuration, including exceptional configurations that probabilistic descriptions may discard.

cards.title: Complement closure of conjunctive languages
cards.formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every conjunctive grammar G over it, does there exist a conjunctive grammar H over the same terminal alphabet with \[L(H)=\Sigma^*\setminus L(G)\,?\]
cards.why: This asks whether grammar conjunction and recursion can express negation without an explicit negation operation.

cards.title: Dense periodic behavior in surjective one-dimensional cellular automata
cards.formal: For every finite nonempty alphabet A, radius r≥0 and local rule \(f:A^{2r+1}\to A\), let \(F:A^{\mathbb Z}\to A^{\mathbb Z}\) be defined by \(F(x)_i=f(x_{i-r},\ldots,x_{i+r})\). If F is surjective, must its temporally periodic configurations be dense in \(A^{\mathbb Z}\)?
cards.why: The conjecture connects reversible coverage of configurations with recurrence in a basic discrete computation model.

cards.title: State complexity of complementing unambiguous automata
cards.formal: For each integer \(n\geq1\), define \[C(n)=\max_{A}\ \min\{\lvert Q_B\rvert: L(B)=\{0,1\}^{*}\setminus L(A)\},\] where \(A\) ranges over all unambiguous finite automata with between 1 and \(n\) states over the binary alphabet, and \(B\) ranges over nondeterministic finite automata over that alphabet with at least one state. Determine the asymptotic growth of \(C(n)\) up to multiplicative constant factors. The output automaton is allowed to be ambiguous.
cards.why: Unambiguity limits the number of positive certificates without directly describing negative certificates. The optimal cost of complementing this representation measures how much succinctness is lost under logical negation and tests the reach of communication-based lower bounds for finite-state models.

cards.title: Polynomial-time universality for unambiguous context-free grammars
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that decides whether \(L(G)=\Sigma^{*}\) for every context-free grammar \(G\) promised to be unambiguous, in time polynomial in the bit length of its explicit description? The algorithm must have one polynomial running-time bound on all input strings; correctness is required on the promised grammars. The terminal alphabet is part of the input. This card selects the polynomial-time endpoint of the source’s broader question about the exact complexity.
cards.why: Unique parse trees suffice to make universality decidable, but they do not give deterministic control of parsing. A polynomial-time procedure, or a proof excluding one, would locate the computational cost of this fundamental coverage test between finite-state reasoning and general context-free behavior.

cards.title: A \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) dichotomy for visibly pushdown languages
cards.formal: For every visibly pushdown language \(L\) of well-matched finite words, is \(L\in\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) or is \(L\) complete for \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) under constant-depth truth-table reductions? The circuit families and reductions are nonuniform, as defined below; the alternatives are inclusive.
cards.why: This asks whether visible stack structure admits a complete boundary between constant-depth threshold computation and general logarithmic-depth circuits. Such a theorem would explain parallel complexity across an infinite language family, beyond deciding individual automata or proving one circuit lower bound.

cards.title: Equivalence of discounted-sum automata
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides, given a rational \(\lambda\) with \(0<\lambda<1\) and two total nondeterministic discounted-sum automata \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) over the same finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), whether \[\forall w\in\Sigma^\omega,\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\mathcal B(w)?\] Both automata have rational transition weights and use the same discounted-sum value function \(\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}\). Their word values are the suprema of their run values. The input factor is arbitrary rational, with no reciprocal-integer restriction.
cards.why: Exact equivalence is a basic correctness test for quantitative specifications: it asks whether replacing one finite-state description by another preserves the value of every possible infinite behavior. Discounting makes each value convergent but leaves a difficult interaction between exact arithmetic and nondeterministic choices. Resolving equivalence for the basic rational single-factor model would establish a central algorithmic boundary for quantitative automata.

cards.title: Complexity of the Game of Life limit set
cards.formal: Is the finite-pattern language of the limit set of Conway's Game of Life \(\Pi^0_1\)-complete under total computable many-one reductions? Let \(F:\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z^2}\to\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z^2}\) be the usual B3/S23 update, and set \[\Omega(F)=\bigcap_{n\ge0}F^n(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z^2}),\qquad L_\Omega=\{\operatorname{code}(p):[p]\cap\Omega(F)\ne\varnothing\}.\] Here \(p\) is any finite binary pattern on an explicitly specified finite domain. Membership in \(\Pi^0_1\) is known; the question is whether the matching completeness bound holds for this fixed cellular automaton.
cards.why: The limit set records which local observations are compatible with arbitrarily long past histories. Matching the co-computably-enumerable upper bound would make this concrete two-state rule as hard as any universal nonhalting condition under computable reductions. The currently known polynomial-space lower bound leaves a major gap between finite resource complexity and undecidability.

cards.title: Deciding pattern avoidance over a prescribed alphabet
cards.formal: Is the following set decidable: pairs (p,k), where p is a nonempty finite word of variables and k≥2, such that there exists an infinite word \(w\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^{\mathbb N}\) containing no nonerasing substitution instance of p as a contiguous factor?
cards.why: This distinguishes decidability with a prescribed alphabet from the easier unrestricted-alphabet existence question.

cards.title: Nondeterminism versus determinism with two two-way heads
cards.formal: Is there a finite alphabet Sigma and a language L⊆Sigma* recognized by a nondeterministic two-way two-head finite automaton but by no deterministic two-way two-head finite automaton, under the nonsensing model below?
cards.why: This isolates the power of nondeterminism at a fixed number of heads, rather than the state cost of simulation.

cards.title: Zeroness of rational weighted context-free grammars
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that always halts and decides whether \(f_G(w)=0\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), given a context-free grammar in the weighted normal form below with rational production weights? Here \(f_G(w)\) is the sum, over all parse trees with yield \(w\), of the product of their production weights. Rational weights may be negative. This card selects the rational weighted-grammar case of the source’s broader zeroness agenda.
cards.why: This is an identity test for recursive numerical descriptions, extending finite-state weighted equivalence to context-free composition. It isolates the difficulty of exact cancellation across arbitrarily deep but finitely parsed derivations, a basic obstacle behind comparing quantitative grammars and counting their parses.

cards.title: Periodic configurations in low-complexity two-dimensional shifts of finite type
cards.formal: For every finite nonempty alphabet \(A\), finite nonempty shape \(D\subset\mathbb Z^2\), and set of allowed patterns \(P\subseteq A^D\) with \(|P|\leq|D|\), let \(X(D,P)=\{x:\mathbb Z^2\to A:\ (d\mapsto x(t+d))\in P\text{ for every }t\in\mathbb Z^2\}\). If \(X(D,P)\neq\varnothing\), must there exist \(x\in X(D,P)\) and a vector \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\) such that \(x(t+v)=x(t)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb Z^2\)?
cards.why: This is a boundary question for how little local diversity can still enforce complete absence of global repetition. It links symbolic dynamics with the decidability of planar tiling constraints and isolates the arbitrary-shape obstruction beyond the established convex case.

cards.title: Decidability of discounted-sum universality over infinite words
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm that, given a complete nondeterministic discounted-sum automaton \(\mathcal A\) with rational weights and a rational discount factor \(0<\lambda<1\), and a rational threshold \(t\), decides whether \(\mathcal A(w)\leq t\) for every infinite word \(w\in\Sigma^\omega\)? Here \(\mathcal A(w)\) is the infimum of the discounted sums of its runs on \(w\).
cards.why: Universality asks whether a quantitative finite-state specification can keep every possible infinite input below a threshold. Its decidability is a basic unresolved boundary for verification with rational discounting, where arbitrarily small tail contributions can still decide exact threshold equality.

cards.title: Recognizing good-for-games and good-for-MDP automata
cards.formal: Determine the exact worst-case computational complexity of each of the following two recognition languages: \[\mathrm{GFG}_{\mathrm{par}}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-games parity automaton}\},\qquad \mathrm{GFM}_{\mathrm B}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-MDP Büchi automaton}\}.\] The input is an explicit finite nondeterministic automaton, and the number of parity priorities is unbounded and part of the first input. The requested classification is for each language separately, with matching complexity-class upper and hardness bounds under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The source's two recognition tasks are retained; no particular class membership conjecture is substituted for either classification.
cards.why: These recognition problems measure the cost of checking whether a compact nondeterministic specification supports composition with an adversarial system or with a probabilistic controller. Their semantic definitions quantify over infinitely many behaviors, although their inputs are finite graphs. Matching classifications would explain the computational price of certifying these useful restrictions on nondeterminism and the difference between their game and probabilistic settings.

cards.title: Isomorphism of tree-automatic ordinals without addition
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm which, given two injective finite-tree-automatic presentations promised to describe well-orders using only their domain and strict order relations, decides whether those well-orders are isomorphic?
cards.why: The problem tests whether ordinal structure can be compared algorithmically without an additional automatic addition operation.

cards.title: Deterministic separability of nondeterministic timed languages
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given two nondeterministic timed automata \(A,B\) with epsilon transitions over the same finite alphabet, always halts and decides whether there exists a deterministic timed automaton \(S\) such that \(L(A)\subseteq L(S)\) and \(L(S)\cap L(B)=\varnothing\)? Languages contain finite timed words. The separator may use any finite number of clocks and any finite integer constants: no resource bound is supplied or fixed in advance.
cards.why: Deterministic timed descriptions support complement and monitoring operations that arbitrary nondeterministic descriptions do not. Settling unrestricted separability would identify whether the existence of such a classifier can be decided without an advance bound on the memory of time represented by clocks.

cards.title: Containment of finitely ambiguous probabilistic automata
cards.formal: Is quantitative containment decidable for pairs of finitely ambiguous probabilistic automata? Given two rational probabilistic automata \(A,B\) over the same finite alphabet, each promised to admit its own uniform finite bound on the number of positive accepting runs per word, decide whether \(p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\). Neither automaton is required to be unambiguous, and the sought algorithm is unconditional.
cards.why: Pointwise probability comparison is a basic refinement test for stochastic finite-state descriptions. Resolving this case would determine whether a constant bound on accepting multiplicity suffices to make exact comparison effective, just below a model in which linear growth of that multiplicity already permits undecidability.

cards.title: Does adding modular predicates preserve decidable first-order definability?
cards.formal: For every effective first-order fragment \(\mathcal F\) satisfying the closure conditions below, does decidability of \(\mathcal F[<]\)-definability of regular finite-word languages imply decidability of \(\mathcal F[<,\mathrm{MOD}]\)-definability? Each decision algorithm takes a finite alphabet and a deterministic finite automaton as input; the fragment is fixed.
cards.why: This asks whether adding elementary arithmetic tests to word logics preserves the ability to recognize their expressive power algorithmically. A general transfer theorem would replace separate definability arguments for many fragments; a counterexample would identify limits of that expectation even for effective, substitution-closed syntax.

cards.title: Deciding first-order definability of orbit-finite automata
cards.formal: Is it decidable, given a finitely presented deterministic orbit-finite automaton over an infinite equality-only data alphabet \(D\), whether its language \(L\subseteq D^*\) is definable by a first-order sentence using the order of word positions and equality of their data values?
cards.why: Over finite alphabets, first-order definability has a classical effective algebraic characterization. This problem asks whether that connection remains decidable when finite memory stores data from an infinite set, beyond the narrower orbit-finite-monoid setting.

cards.title: Recognizable separability of automatic relations
cards.formal: Is the following recognizable-separability problem undecidable, as asserted by Conjecture 7.1 of the source? Given a finite alphabet \(A\) and two nondeterministic finite automata representing binary automatic relations \(R_1,R_2\subseteq A^*\times A^*\), decide whether there exist \(k\in\mathbb N\) and regular languages \(L_1,\ldots,L_k,K_1,\ldots,K_k\subseteq A^*\) with \[R_1\subseteq S,\qquad S\cap R_2=\varnothing,\qquad S=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}(L_i\times K_i).\] The number \(k\) and the sizes of all component automata have no prescribed finite bound. Undecidability means that no deterministic Turing machine halts and gives the correct answer on every finite input description of this kind.
cards.why: Automatic relations allow a finite machine to compare positions in two unbounded strings. Recognizable relations replace this synchronization with finitely many independent regular tests. Deciding whether such a replacement can separate two specifications is a basic abstraction question connected to regular colorings of infinite graphs and to simplifying relational constraints. Its answer would locate an effective boundary between two elementary finite descriptions of infinite relations.

cards.title: Decidability of stochastic resolvability for \(\omega\)-automata
cards.formal: For each of the two acceptance conditions \(c\in\{\mathrm{B\ddot uchi},\mathrm{coB\ddot uchi}\}\), is stochastic resolvability decidable for finite nondeterministic word automata with condition \(c\)? More precisely, does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on every encoded automaton \(\mathcal A\) of that type, halts and decides whether there exists a finite-memory stochastic resolver \(\mathcal R\) such that \[\forall w\in L(\mathcal A),\qquad \Pr_{\mathcal R,w}[\text{the constructed run of }\mathcal A\text{ is accepting}]=1?\] The resolver is chosen before the word and must work for every accepted word; the word is fixed independently of its random choices. The source asks both the Büchi and coBüchi questions, and their decidability statuses are to be determined separately.
cards.why: This problem asks when nondeterministic specifications can be executed online with finite memory and reliable random choices. It isolates a precise gap between deterministic resolution against an adaptive environment and probabilistic behavior on every fixed input. A decision procedure would recognize which existing automata admit such execution; an undecidability theorem would establish a limitation even for two elementary acceptance conditions on finite graphs.

cards.title: Decidability with two parametric clocks and arbitrarily many integer parameters
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which always halts and decides finite reachability for discrete-time parametric timed automata with at most two parametric clocks and an arbitrary finite number of nonnegative integer parameters? For the finite input automaton \(A\), the predicate to decide is \[\exists\mu:P\to\mathbb N\ \exists k\in\mathbb N\ \exists\text{ a legal }k\text{-transition run under }\mu\text{ from }(q_0,\mathbf0)\text{ to }(q_f,v).\] The parameter valuation is chosen once for the whole run; neither its values nor the run length have a supplied bound. Arbitrarily many clocks compared only with numerical constants remain allowed.
cards.why: Timing parameters turn verification of a fixed timed system into the search for a working assignment of unknown delays and deadlines. With one parametric clock reachability is decidable, while three parametric clocks already yield undecidability. The two-clock case with unrestricted parameter count is a precise boundary between these behaviors, with connections to counter machines and arithmetic with divisibility.

cards.title: Unconditional containment of unambiguous probabilistic automata
cards.formal: Is quantitative containment decidable when the left automaton \(A\) is unambiguous and the right automaton \(B\) is finitely ambiguous? In other words, does a single unconditional terminating algorithm decide \(\forall w\in\Sigma^{*},\ p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every promised pair of rational probabilistic automata as defined below? This selects the direction of bounded-ambiguity containment whose known decidability proof uses Schanuel’s conjecture; the reverse direction is already decidable unconditionally.
cards.why: This asks whether a basic exact comparison between small stochastic models can be decided from a finite bound on accepting behavior, without a conjecture in transcendental number theory. The asymmetry between one probability product and a bounded sum isolates the unresolved arithmetic obstacle in an otherwise effective verification setting.

cards.title: Universality of unambiguous register automata over ordered integers
cards.formal:
Is universality decidable for unambiguous register automata with guessing over \((\mathbb Z,<,=)\) and finitely many named integer constants? Given a finite automaton description in the model below, promised to have at most one accepting run on every finite data word, must there be an algorithm deciding whether
\[L(\mathcal A)=(\Sigma\times\mathbb Z)^*?\]
The finite alphabet, number of registers, control states, guards and binary-encoded constants are all part of the input. This card makes the guessing convention explicit, using the relational register model discussed in the cited literature. Its main target is the decidability part of the source question; a tight complexity classification is a further question if the answer is positive.
cards.why: Unambiguity often preserves much of nondeterministic expressive power while recovering decidable equivalence or universality. This question tests that phenomenon over discrete ordered data with constants and guessed register values. Its resolution would identify how far the successful algorithms for equality and dense order extend toward integer-valued verification models.

cards.title: Determinacy of Wadge games for Muller tree languages
cards.formal: Let \(D_{\mathrm{tree}}\) be the statement that, for every pair \(A,B\) of finite nondeterministic Muller automata on infinite full binary labeled trees, the Wadge game \(W(L(A),L(B))\) is determined. Is \(D_{\mathrm{tree}}\) provable in Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice, ZFC? The target is provability from these axioms, not an algorithm for finding the winning player.
cards.why: Asks how much set theory is needed to compare properties described by finite automata. A resolution would clarify whether the topological organization of all regular infinite-tree languages rests on ordinary ZFC or needs stronger foundations.

cards.title: Greibach normal form for conjunctive grammars
cards.formal: Does every conjunctive language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) with \(\varepsilon\notin L\) have an equivalent conjunctive grammar all of whose rules are of the form \[A\to a\beta_1\mathbin{\&}\cdots\mathbin{\&}a\beta_k,\qquad a\in\Sigma,\quad k\ge1,\quad\beta_i\in N^*\,?\]
cards.why: A Greibach form would impose input-consuming recursion on a broad extension of context-free grammar.

cards.title: Complement closure of deterministic finite-testable counter languages
cards.formal: For every one-way deterministic finite-testable multicounter machine M with a right endmarker, is there another such machine N over the same input alphabet Sigma with \(L(N)=\Sigma^*\setminus L(M)\)?
cards.why: This asks whether a limited zero-test resource preserves a basic language-theoretic closure property.

cards.title: Complementing unambiguous partially blind counter languages
cards.formal: For every unambiguous one-way partially blind multicounter machine M, does some nondeterministic one-way partially blind multicounter machine N satisfy \(L(N)=\Sigma^*\setminus L(M)\) over the same input alphabet?
cards.why: This isolates the interaction between unambiguity, weak counters and negation.

cards.title: Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every input consisting of an integer \(k\ge1\), integer coefficients \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), and integer initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(u_t=0\) for some integer \(t\ge0\), where the infinite sequence is uniquely defined by \[u_{t+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j u_{t+j}\qquad(t=0,1,2,\ldots)?\] The order \(k\) is part of the input and is unrestricted; no time or space bound is requested.
cards.why: Skolem asks whether exact reachability of zero is decidable for the simplest class of discrete linear recurrences with finite integer descriptions. The question connects arithmetic with verification of linear loops, matrix dynamics, automata and stochastic systems, and serves as a common unresolved decision problem to which other verification tasks are compared.

cards.title: Parity games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\geq1\) such that, for every encoded finite parity game \(G\) and starting vertex \(s\), \(A\) decides whether Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps, where \(L\) is the full input length defined below?
cards.why: Parity games are a central algorithmic component of model checking and reactive synthesis: they express recurring obligations in infinite executions by a finite arena. Their winner problem is polynomial-time equivalent to model checking the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Determining whether general parity games admit polynomial time would resolve a basic complexity boundary for these verification tasks and for a natural problem in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\).

cards.title: Word equations with linear length constraints
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input consisting of a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite system of word equations \(U_i=V_i\) and a finite conjunction of integer linear equalities and inequalities on variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when they admit a simultaneous solution in the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\)? The alphabet, equations, variables and arithmetic coefficients are all part of the input. No bound on the running time is prescribed.
cards.why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.

cards.title: A logic capturing polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a logic L with decidable syntax and isomorphism-invariant semantics on finite relational structures such that its sentences define exactly the polynomial-time decidable Boolean properties, and an effective compiler maps each sentence to a correct polynomial-time evaluation algorithm with a polynomial running-time bound?
cards.why: The central descriptive-complexity question of characterizing feasible computation without supplying an arbitrary order.

cards.title: Internal semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
cards.formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and restriction maps \(r_{n}:S(n+1)\to S(n)\) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes \(D_{n}\)?
cards.why: Determine whether ordinary HoTT can express a fundamental unbounded coherent structure internally, a basic issue for higher categories and foundational proof languages.

cards.title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
cards.formal: Is the first-order theory of the standard real exponential field \(\mathbb R_{\exp}=(\mathbb R;0,1,+,-,\times,<,\exp)\) decidable? Precisely, does there exist one ordinary deterministic Turing machine \(D\) which halts on every encoded first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in this fixed language and outputs \(1\) exactly when \(\mathbb R_{\exp}\models\varphi\), and \(0\) otherwise? The exponential function is defined on all real numbers, and the required conclusion is unconditional.
cards.why: A central boundary in exact algorithmic reasoning over real numbers: polynomial real arithmetic is decidable, while adding one standard analytic function connects logical truth to unresolved transcendence questions. Its resolution would determine whether a uniform symbolic decision procedure can handle all finite first-order specifications involving real exponentiation, with consequences for verification problems already reducible to this theory.

cards.title: Positivity problem for linear recurrences
cards.formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, on every input consisting of an integer \(d\ge 1\), integer initial values \(u_{0},\ldots ,u_{d- 1}\), and integer coefficients \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{d- 1}\), halts and decides whether \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for every \(n\ge 0\), where \(u_{n+d}=\sum _{i=0}^{d- 1}a_{i} u_{n+i}\)? The order d is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound.
cards.why: A basic infinite-time safety question for finite linear descriptions. Its resolution would establish a major decidability boundary connecting verification, discrete dynamical systems and effective number theory, and would also settle general Skolem decidability.

cards.title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold \(r\in [0,1]\), decide whether \(v_{G}(s)>r\), where \(v_{G}(s)=\sup _{\sigma} \inf _{\tau} \Pr _{s}^{\sigma ,\tau}\)[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
cards.why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.

cards.title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Is the exact mean-payoff winner language \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?

A valid instance is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge1\), at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition \(V=V_{\mathrm{Max}}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{Min}}\), an integer weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\), and a start vertex \(s\in V\). Its encoding is in \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) exactly when
\[\exists\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\ \forall\tau\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}},\qquad
\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\ge0,\]
where \(v_0=s\) and the unique infinite play \((v_t)_{t\ge0}\) follows the two strategies. Weights have the binary encoding specified below, and equality zero counts as winning for Max. Give a complete Lean proof of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\in\mathrm P\) or of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\notin\mathrm P\).
cards.why: Mean-payoff games model sustainable long-run rewards when an adversary controls part of a finite system. Their exact winner problem has short certificates for both answers, yet its unrestricted polynomial bit complexity remains an important question in quantitative verification and graph-game theory.

cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.formal:
For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is first-order model checking fixed-parameter tractable with a computable parameter dependence?

Precisely, does every such \(\mathcal C\) admit a single deterministic algorithm \(A_{\mathcal C}\), a total computable function \(f_{\mathcal C}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and a constant integer \(d_{\mathcal C}\ge0\) such that, for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every first-order graph sentence \(\varphi\), the algorithm outputs whether \(G\models\varphi\) within
\[f_{\mathcal C}(|\varphi|)\,(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{\mathcal C}}\]
steps? The algorithm receives only the graph and the sentence, in the encodings below, and must halt on every input. The exponent may depend on the class but not on the sentence. The effective structural hypothesis is the computable powerset-obstruction bound defined below.
cards.why: First-order formulas express a broad family of graph queries, but direct evaluation lets the graph-size exponent grow with the query. The proposed structural condition aims to explain when that dependence can be confined to a computable function of the query alone, even on dense graph classes. Settling this tractability direction would complement the established hardness of hereditary classes that can logically encode arbitrary graphs.

cards.title: Asser’s problem
cards.formal:
Is the class of finite first-order spectra closed under complement within the positive integers?

For every finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) and every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over \(\tau\), does there exist a finite relational vocabulary \(\sigma\) and a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over \(\sigma\) such that
\[\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\quad \bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\sigma\text{-structure satisfying }\psi\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \neg\bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\tau\text{-structure satisfying }\varphi\bigr)?\]
The vocabulary and sentence \((\sigma,\psi)\) may depend on \((\tau,\varphi)\), but must work simultaneously for every positive size \(n\). They need not use the original vocabulary. No effective procedure for obtaining \(\psi\), or bound on its length, is required.
cards.why: A first-order sentence can describe rich finite structures, while its spectrum keeps only the possible domain sizes. Asser’s question asks whether the sizes excluded by one such description can always be the sizes admitted by another. Its equivalence with closure of nondeterministic exponential time under complement makes this a fundamental meeting point of finite model theory and computational complexity.

cards.title: NP membership of word-equation satisfiability
cards.formal:
Let \(\mathrm{WE}\) be the language of encodings of satisfiable word equations \(u=v\) over finite free monoids, as defined below. Is
\[
\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}?
\]
Explicitly, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(V\), a constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(V\) halts on every pair of bit strings \((e,w)\) within \(C(|e|+|w|+1)^k\) steps and, for every valid equation encoding \(e\) of length \(N\),
\[
e\in\mathrm{WE}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ 
\bigl(|w|\le C(N+1)^k\ \text{and}\ V(e,w)=1\bigr)?
\]
The verifier rejects invalid equation encodings. The same machine and constants work for all alphabets, equations and variable sets.
cards.why: Word equations are a basic model of string constraints and associative unification. Their decidability is established, but the gap between NP-hardness and polynomial-space algorithms leaves the complexity of short verifiable evidence unresolved. NP membership would place the unrestricted satisfiability problem at the familiar NP-complete boundary.

cards.title: Decidability of multiplicative-exponential linear logic
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite propositional MELL sequent \(\Gamma\) in the calculus below, halts and answers yes exactly when \(\vdash \Gamma\) has a finite derivation? There is no promised bound on formula size or exponential nesting and no requested time bound beyond termination on every input.
cards.why: MELL combines resource-sensitive composition with controlled reuse. Its decision problem connects automated proof search to branching counter systems and tests a fundamental boundary of algorithmic reasoning about resources.

cards.title: A logic capturing logarithmic space
cards.formal: Does there exist one effective logic \(\mathcal L\), in the precise sense below, whose sentences define exactly all deterministic logarithmic-space Boolean properties of finite unordered relational structures, for every finite relational vocabulary?
cards.why: This asks whether all order-independent queries evaluable with logarithmic working memory have an effective logical language with exactly that expressive power. It would connect a central low-space computation model to a complete account of queries on finite relational data, beyond the familiar setting where an input order is supplied.

cards.title: Decidability of Presburger arithmetic with primes
cards.formal: Is the full first-order theory of the fixed structure \[\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}=(\mathbb Z;0,1,+,-,<,\mathrm{Pr})\] decidable, where \(\mathrm{Pr}(n)\) means that \(n\ge2\) is a positive prime? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every finite encoded sentence \(\varphi\) of this language and returns YES exactly when \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}\models\varphi\)? The question is unconditional and permits arbitrary finite first-order quantifier alternation.
cards.why: Addition and order alone admit a complete decision procedure, while the prime predicate brings the distribution of primes into quantified arithmetic without directly adding multiplication. This is a classical boundary question linking effective first-order reasoning, definability and deep number theory. The standard ordered structure can express prime-pattern assertions, so a truth decider would have consequences far beyond individual primality tests.

cards.title: Continuous Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, given any dimension \(d\ge 1\), rational matrix \(A\in \mathbb Q^{d\times d}\), and rational column vectors \(b,c\in \mathbb Q^{d}\), always halts and correctly decides whether \(c^{T}\exp (tA)b=0\) for some real \(t\ge 0\)?
cards.why: A minimal exact reachability question for continuous linear systems whose decidability remains unresolved, linking algorithmic verification to real analysis, transcendence and effective number theory.

cards.title: Scott-continuous lambda models with theory \(\lambda \beta\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a pointed directed-complete partial order D and Scott-continuous maps \(F:D\to [D\to D]\) and \(\mathrm{L}:[D\to D]\to D\) with \(F\circ \mathrm{L}=id\) such that, for every pair of finite untyped lambda terms M,N, equality of their interpretations for every environment in D holds if and only if M and N are beta-convertible?
cards.why: A foundational completeness question for denotational semantics: does the mathematical structure used to describe approximation and recursion inevitably identify programs beyond beta-conversion, or can it preserve every distinction made by that computation rule?

cards.title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture
cards.formal: For every pure type system \((S,A,R)\) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
cards.why: Normalization connects computation with the metatheory of typed proofs. This conjecture asks whether the pure-type-system rules turn the existence of a terminating computation for every typable term into termination under every reduction order.

cards.title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every finite modal formula \(\varphi\) and decides whether there exists a substitution \(\sigma\) for its propositional variables such that \(\sigma (\varphi )\) is valid on every Kripke frame?
cards.why: Determines whether automated reasoning can decide the existence of a validity-making substitution in the basic normal modal logic, despite the decidability of checking each individual instance and the poorly behaved structure of its unifiers.

cards.title: Decidability of termination for one-rule string rewriting
cards.formal: Is global termination of a one-rule string rewriting system decidable? The input is a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two explicitly written words \(\ell,r\in\Sigma^{*}\). Define \(u\to v\) when \(u=x\ell y\) and \(v=xry\) for some \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\). Decide whether there exists no infinite sequence \(w_0\to w_1\to w_2\to\cdots\) of finite words. The quantifier includes every starting word and every choice of replacement position.
cards.why: A single literal replacement is among the simplest possible descriptions of an unbounded computation. Settling its global termination problem would locate a sharp limit on automatic reasoning about repeated symbolic transformations, without relying on a large instruction set or richer term syntax.

cards.title: Ultimate Positivity problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every finite description of a rational linear recurrence sequence \((u_n)_{n\ge0}\), halts and correctly decides whether \[\exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\ge N,\qquad u_n\ge0?\] The input consists of \(k\ge1\), rational coefficients \(a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\), and rational initial terms \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\); subsequent terms satisfy \[u_{n+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}a_j u_{n+j}\qquad(n\ge0).\] The supplied recurrence length \(k\) is unrestricted, and repeated characteristic roots are allowed. “Positivity” in this problem's established name means nonnegativity.
cards.why: Ultimate Positivity asks whether finitely specified linear dynamics eventually remain on one side of a boundary. It connects recurrence sequences, eventual program behavior and precise approximation questions in number theory. A resolution would determine whether eventual sign stability is algorithmically recognizable even when repeated roots introduce polynomial factors and several oscillating contributions interact.

cards.title: Termination of linear-constraint loops
cards.formal: Determine separately, for each state domain \(D\in\{\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}\), whether termination of single-path linear-constraint loops over \(D\) is decidable. An input is \(d\ge1\) and an explicitly given system of rational linear inequalities \[A x+B y\le c,\qquad A,B\in\mathbb Q^{m\times d},\quad c\in\mathbb Q^m,\] defining allowed consecutive states \(x,y\in D^d\). Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine for that fixed domain which always halts and decides whether \[\neg\exists (x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in(D^d)^{\mathbb N}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\qquad A x_n+B x_{n+1}\le c?\] Thus termination means that every execution from every initial state is finite, irrespective of the allowed successor choices. The three domain variants are retained separately, with no assumption that their decidability statuses coincide.
cards.why: This question asks how much nondeterminism can be introduced into elementary linear dynamics while preserving decidable universal termination. A single system of inequalities allows infinitely many possible successors but retains a strong convex structure over the reals. Resolving its domain-specific cases would locate a central boundary between complete verification algorithms for affine programs and undecidability in more expressive program models.

cards.title: Commutativity of the full probabilistic powerdomain monad
cards.formal: Editorial subprobability variant: for all dcpos X,Y, all continuous subprobability valuations mu on X and nu on Y, and every Scott-continuous \(f:X\times Y\to[0,\infty]\), must \[\int_X\!\left(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)\right)d\mu(x)=\int_Y\!\left(\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\right)d\nu(y)\,?\] This is commutativity of the full continuous-subprobability valuation monad.
cards.why: Commutativity determines whether a central denotational model supports unrestricted exchange of probabilistic effects.

cards.title: Fagin’s binary-relation spectrum problem
cards.formal: For every first-order sentence phi in a finite vocabulary, is there a first-order sentence psi using only equality and one binary relation symbol R such that \[\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi)=\operatorname{Spec}(\psi)\,?\]
cards.why: This asks whether a minimal relational vocabulary suffices to express all finite-model cardinality phenomena.

cards.title: Effective syntax for order-invariant first-order queries
cards.formal: Editorial effective-syntax variant: for every finite relational vocabulary tau, is there a decidable set S_tau of finite sentence codes, a total computable evaluator E_tau, and a total computable compiler C_tau into order-invariant first-order sentences, satisfying the soundness and expressive-completeness requirements below, uniformly in tau?
cards.why: An effective syntax would make semantic order invariance available as a usable formal language.

cards.title: Decidability of branching-VASS reachability
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm deciding reachability in branching vector addition systems with states when the dimension is part of the input? Given a finite system \(B\) as defined below and a target configuration \(q(x)\), decide whether \(q(x)\) is the root of a finite valid derivation tree of \(B\).
cards.why: Branching VASS extend the Petri-net style of counter computation to recursive combinations of resources. Settling exact reachability in arbitrary dimension would identify a central decidability boundary between path computations and branching derivations in infinite-state verification.

cards.title: Consistency of excluded middle and Church’s thesis in Coq
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathcal T+\mathrm{LEM}+\mathrm{CT}\) logically consistent, where \(\mathcal T\) is Coq's ordinary cumulative inductive core calculus specified below, and the two added propositional axioms are
\[\mathrm{LEM}:\quad\forall P:\mathrm{Prop},\ P\lor\neg P,\]
\[\mathrm{CT}:\quad\forall f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N,\ \exists e:\mathbb N,\ \forall x:\mathbb N,\ \exists s:\mathbb N,\ T(e,x,s)=\mathrm{Some}(f(x))?\]
Here \(T\) is the fixed bounded evaluator for ordinary register-machine programs defined below. Consistency means that there is no finite well-typed closed proof term of \(\mathrm{False}\) in the extended calculus. The existence quantifiers in CT are in Prop; they are not computational dependent pairs.
cards.why: This would clarify whether classical reasoning about propositions can coexist with the claim that every internal numerical function is computable, while retaining a rich dependent type theory. The distinction matters for synthetic computability developments that use Church’s thesis as an axiom and for the foundational role of separating propositions from computational data.

cards.title: Inductive-inductive types from inductive types without UIP
cards.formal: In the intensional Martin-Löf type theory \(\mathsf T\) specified below, can every finitary inductive-inductive signature be implemented using the existing type formers, with its full dependent eliminator and propositional constructor computation equations? More precisely, is there a uniform effective derived-rule construction which, for every finite well-formed signature \(S\), every well-formed external parameter context and every permitted universe instance, produces the sorts and constructors of an \(S\)-algebra \(A_S\) and, for every displayed \(S\)-algebra \(D\) over \(A_S\), a section of \(D\) with a proof of each constructor equation? All these terms and proofs must be derivable in \(\mathsf T\). This is the user-selected intensional specialization, approved on 16 September 2026, of the source's broader question about a UIP-free setting; it does not ask to settle every possible UIP-free foundation.
cards.why: Inductive-inductive definitions express dependent syntax directly, including contexts and the types valid in each context. A generic reduction would identify which primitives a proof assistant needs to support such syntax while retaining identity types with higher structure. The issue concerns expressive power and dependent elimination, not merely implementation convenience: an encoding can supply all the apparent constructors yet lose the induction principle needed to use the data.

cards.title: Constructive simplicial model with univalent universes
cards.formal: Does the constructive set theory \(\mathsf S\) specified below support a full simplicial interpretation of intensional Martin-Löf type theory with \(0,1,\mathbb N,\Pi,\Sigma,\mathsf{Id}\) and a cumulative sequence of univalent universes, in which every type former, term former and eliminator is strictly stable under substitution? The required universes classify the small Kan fibrations between cofibrant Kan complexes described below. Work in CZF with a sequence \((I_i)_{i\in\mathbb N}\) of constructive inaccessible sets, \(I_i\in I_{i+1}\), and the explicit small-subset principle \[\forall i\ \forall a,b\; (a\subseteq b\ \land\ b\in I_i\ \Rightarrow\ a\in I_i).\] Do not assume excluded middle or an axiom of choice. This is the full-model target selected by the user on 16 September2026; a univalent fibration with only weakly stable type operations is insufficient.
cards.why: Simplicial sets provide a standard geometric language for homotopy theory and classical univalent semantics. A constructive full model would connect that language with foundations that track how mathematical objects are built. The unresolved coherence and size issues determine whether partial semantic structures actually interpret dependent type-theoretic substitution and universes.

cards.title: Univalence, impredicativity and propositional resizing
cards.formal: Does there exist a nondegenerate model of ordinary dependent type theory, with the type formers and computation rules specified below, containing a univalent impredicative universe \(U\) of data types into which every homotopy proposition can be resized?
cards.why: Determine compatibility of univalence, impredicative data-type universes and propositional resizing under ordinary dependent computation rules, clarifying a substantive boundary in foundations for proof assistants.

cards.title: Decidability and completeness of concurrent Kleene algebra with parallel iteration
cards.formal: Settle both parts of the source question for the full concurrent Kleene-algebra signature, including unbounded finite parallel iteration. For finite expressions \(e,f\), write \(e\preceq f\) when \(\downarrow\llbracket e\rrbracket\subseteq\downarrow\llbracket f\rrbracket\), using the pomset refinement semantics below. (1) Is there a total computable procedure deciding \(e\preceq f\) on every pair of such expressions? (2) Are the stated Kleene-algebra axioms for both products, together with weak interchange, complete for this semantics: \[\forall e,f,\quad e\preceq f\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{CKA}\vdash e+f=f?\] The already settled fragment without parallel iteration is recorded in the context. The two remaining questions are separate: neither an algorithm alone nor an axiomatic completeness theorem alone is a complete answer to this paired target.
cards.why: The two questions ask whether unrestricted finite spawning of concurrent computations remains algorithmically comparable, and whether every valid refinement can be justified by a fixed algebraic calculus. Parallel iteration crosses the bounded-width boundary where existing decision and completeness results apply. Resolving the full signature would clarify the expressive and proof-theoretic cost of unbounded concurrency.

cards.title: Singly exponential shortest solutions of word equations
cards.formal:
Do positive integers \(c,k\) exist such that every satisfiable word equation \(u=v\), over every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of constant letters and a disjoint finite set \(\mathcal X\) of variables, has a solution \(h\) satisfying
\[\max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|\le 2^{c(n+1)^k},\qquad n=|u|+|v|?\]
Here \(\mathcal X\) consists exactly of the variables occurring in the equation, each occurrence contributes one to \(n\), and the maximum over no variables is zero. A solution replaces each variable consistently by a finite word over \(\Sigma\), possibly empty, fixes the constant letters and makes the two expanded words identical.

The same constants \(c,k\) must work independently of the equation, the alphabet and the number of variables. This is the polynomial-exponent meaning of singly exponential. A linear exponent is welcome but is not required.
cards.why: Very short equations can describe solutions whose expanded words are enormous. A universal singly exponential shortest-solution bound would constrain this hidden growth and, by the source’s compression theorem, imply NP membership of general word-equation satisfiability. This links a basic combinatorial question about strings to the unresolved complexity of exact string constraints.

cards.title: Greedy CDCL without restarts versus resolution
cards.formal: Does greedy CDCL without restarts p-simulate resolution in the asserting-learning model below? Precisely, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a constant \(C>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that for every finite CNF formula \(F\) and every valid resolution refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\), on the explicit binary input \((F,\pi)\) of length \(L\), \(M\) halts within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps and outputs a legal greedy CDCL refutation of the same \(F\), without restarts, of at most \(C(L+1)^k\) bits? The single program and polynomial must work for all formulas and supplied proofs.
cards.why: Restarts are a central operation in modern clause-learning SAT solvers. This target isolates whether their removal causes an unavoidable loss in proof generation even when the solver may choose decisions, propagation order and learned asserting clauses with full knowledge of a supplied resolution proof. A resolution would connect an exact operational restriction of search with the polynomial simulation structure studied in proof complexity.

cards.title: Madlener–Otto plain-group conjecture
cards.formal: Let A be a finite alphabet and R a finite confluent length-reducing string-rewriting system. If the quotient monoid \(A^*/{\equiv_R}\) is a group G, must there be finite groups \(H_1,\ldots,H_s\) and an integer r≥0 with \[G\cong H_1*\cdots*H_s*F_r\,?\]
cards.why: The conjecture would characterize exactly which group word problems admit this finite normalization mechanism.

cards.title: NP membership of context unification
cards.formal: Is satisfiability of finite systems of context equations in NP, with uncompressed input terms, an input finite ranked signature, ordinary variables, and arbitrarily repeated one-hole context variables?
cards.why: This asks for short certificates at the central remaining complexity boundary for context unification.

cards.title: Deciding MSO-definable choice on the infinite binary tree
cards.formal: Given a monadic second-order formula phi(X,Y) over the full infinite binary tree, is it decidable whether there is an MSO formula theta(X,Y) defining a partial function with exactly the same domain as phi and with graph contained in phi?
cards.why: Definable choice connects logical specification to the existence of uniform witnesses.

cards.title: Satisfiability with two variables and one transitive relation
cards.formal: Is satisfiability decidable for first-order sentences with equality, only two reusable variable symbols, and one distinguished binary relation required to be transitive, when models may be finite or infinite?
cards.why: The target isolates a basic boundary between finite-model and unrestricted decidability.

cards.title: Successor-invariant first-order model checking on nowhere dense graphs
cards.formal:
For every effectively nowhere dense class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{\mathcal C}\), a total computable function \(f_{\mathcal C}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), and an integer constant \(c_{\mathcal C}\ge1\) such that, given a graph \(G\in\mathcal C\) and a successor-invariant first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in the signature \(\{E,S\}\), the algorithm decides
\[
(G,S_G)\models\varphi
\]
in at most
\[
f_{\mathcal C}(|\varphi|)(L+2)^{c_{\mathcal C}}
\]
bit operations? Here \(S_G\) is any successor relation on the vertices, \(L\) is the full input encoding length, and both effectiveness and successor invariance are defined below. The exponent may depend on the graph class but not on the sentence or graph.
cards.why: An auxiliary successor can join distant parts of a sparse graph and disrupt the local structure used by model-checking algorithms. Invariance allows that successor to be chosen freely, but it is unknown whether this freedom always preserves tractability throughout the nowhere dense frontier.

cards.title: Cai–Fürer–Immerman definability in choiceless polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the parity query for Cai–Fürer–Immerman graphs over arbitrary connected unordered base graphs definable in Choiceless Polynomial Time with counting? In the source’s construction below, is there one CPT program \(P\) that, for every finite connected base graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every \(T\subseteq V\), accepts the unordered input graph \(G^{T}\) exactly when \(|T|\) is odd?
cards.why: CFI parity is a central test of whether computation that preserves all input symmetries can match ordinary polynomial time. A negative answer would separate CPT with counting from polynomial time; a positive answer would remove an important candidate obstruction without by itself proving that CPT captures every polynomial-time property.

cards.title: Eliminating an invariant order on bounded-degree structures
cards.formal: For every finite relational vocabulary tau, every integer D≥0 and every globally order-invariant first-order sentence phi over tau together with an extra binary relation <, does there exist an FO(tau) sentence psi equivalent to phi on every finite nonempty tau-structure of Gaifman degree at most D?
cards.why: The collapse would show that auxiliary order adds no expressive power in a broad sparse setting.

cards.title: Word problem for the S-combinator
cards.formal: Is convertibility of closed S-combinator terms decidable? Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the least set with \(S\in\mathcal{T}\) and \((uv)\in\mathcal{T}\) whenever \(u,v\in\mathcal{T}\). The sole rewrite rule, applicable inside any term context, is \[(((Sx)y)z)\longrightarrow ((xz)(yz)),\qquad x,y,z\in\mathcal{T}.\] Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that halts on every pair \(p,q\in\mathcal{T}\) and decides whether they are connected by a finite sequence of forward or backward applications of this rule?
cards.why: The S-only fragment retains duplication and nonterminating behavior with just one combinator. Its word problem tests whether symbolic equality becomes decidable after removing the other primitives of combinatory logic, beyond the already-known ability to recognize normalizing terms.

cards.title: Decidability of fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching
cards.formal: Is fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching decidable in the source's closed range formulation? Given finite simple types \(\sigma,\tau\) and closed simply typed lambda terms \(F:\sigma\to\tau\) and \(N:\tau\), with \(\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\le5\), decide whether \[\exists M\;\bigl(\varnothing\vdash M:\sigma\ \land\ F\,M=_\beta N\bigr).\] The unknown \(M\) is a finite closed term. One deterministic Turing machine must halt and decide this predicate for every such input, with no time bound. Type order starts at one, exactly as in the source.
cards.why: Matching is a central restricted form of higher-order unification, with uses in rewriting and symbolic reasoning. The fifth-order boundary asks exactly how much higher-order functional structure is needed for beta-only matching to encode undecidable behavior. It also exposes the substantive effect of extensional eta equality: a change in the equality relation, rather than just the input size, changes the general decidability result.

cards.title: One-dimensional piecewise-affine reachability
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides, given a one-dimensional rational piecewise-affine map \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) and rational points \(s,t\in[0,1]\), whether \[\exists n\in\mathbb N,\qquad f^n(s)=t?\] The map is specified by finitely many rational linear guards and one rational affine expression on each guard, as defined below. The number of pieces is part of the input and is not bounded by a fixed constant. The question is exact point reachability after finitely many iterations, including zero iterations.
cards.why: This is an elementary finite description of potentially complicated discrete dynamics: one rational number evolves by affine updates selected through interval tests. Exact reachability is the basic question behind checking whether such an iteration ever attains a specified state. A resolution would locate a decidability boundary between the tractable affine orbit problem and the already undecidable higher-dimensional piecewise-affine setting.

cards.title: Effective homotopy canonicity with propositional resizing
cards.formal: Does the fixed univalent De Morgan cubical type theory \(\mathsf T_R\) defined below, with individual propositional resizing between adjacent universe levels, satisfy both consistency and effective homotopy canonicity? For each \(i\ge0\), add the scheme \[R_i:\prod_{P:\mathcal U_{i+1}}\mathsf{isProp}(P)\to\sum_{Q:\mathcal U_i}(Q\simeq P).\] Require one ordinary computable algorithm which, from any finite derivation of a closed judgment \(\vdash t:\mathbb N\) in \(\mathsf T_R\), halts and returns a numeral \(\overline k\) and a checked object-theory derivation of \[\vdash e:\mathsf{Path}_{\mathbb N}(t,\overline k).\] Consistency here includes that there is no closed derivation of \(\mathsf{Path}_{\mathbb N}(0,\mathsf s0)\). The selected requirement is effective equality to a numeral, with no additional request for judgmental normalization of all terms.
cards.why: Resizing permits logical propositions to move into smaller universes while univalence identifies equivalent types. An effective numeral-and-identity theorem would explain how this useful size principle can coexist with an ordinary computational account of closed programs, beyond merely postulating a consistent axiom.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time equivalence testing for d-DNNFs
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given two d-DNNF circuits \(C,D\), returns yes exactly when
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_C(a)=f_D(a),\]
where \(X\) is the union of the variables appearing in the two inputs?

The algorithm must work for all promised pairs, without any requirement that their internal decompositions or variable trees agree. It must give the exact yes/no answer in worst-case time polynomial in their total binary encoding length. The two circuits are supplied explicitly; no truth table, equivalence certificate, common compiled representation or source formula is supplied.
cards.why: Equivalence testing checks whether two compiled representations express the same Boolean knowledge despite different decompositions. A deterministic polynomial-time test would support exact comparison and verification of representation changes without a probabilistic failure event. The gap between known randomized testing and the deterministic target also links this concrete compilation task to broader derandomization questions.

cards.title: Two-sided distributive unification with a unit
cards.formal: Let \(E\) be exactly the four identities \[x\cdot(y+z)=(x\cdot y)+(x\cdot z),\qquad (x+y)\cdot z=(x\cdot z)+(y\cdot z),\qquad x\cdot1=x,\qquad1\cdot x=x.\] Is general first-order \(E\)-unification decidable? Namely, does one deterministic Turing machine halt on every finite signature and finite list of equations \(s_i\doteq t_i\), under the conventions below, and return YES exactly when a single finite-term substitution \(\sigma\) satisfies \(s_i\sigma=_E t_i\sigma\) for every \(i\)?
cards.why: Distributivity couples two operations, so the standard decomposition methods for disjoint equational theories do not immediately apply. The multiplicative unit creates additional identifications between expanded and unexpanded expressions. Determining decidability for exactly this small axiom set would clarify a longstanding boundary in symbolic constraint solving, between known distributive fragments and stronger theories with undecidable unification.

cards.title: Continuous-time synthesis for Metric Interval Temporal Logic
cards.formal: For the future-time MITL signal semantics below, is it decidable whether an input specification phi admits a causal operator F from finitely variable input signals to finitely variable output signals such that the combined signal (I,F(I)) satisfies phi at time zero for every input I?
cards.why: The problem asks whether metric real-time specifications can be automatically realized as causal behavior.

cards.title: Polynomial-time quantitative stochastic parity verification
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether \[\sup_\sigma\inf_\tau\Pr^{\sigma,\tau}_v[\text{the least priority occurring infinitely often is even}]\ge q\] for every finite turn-based stochastic parity game and binary-encoded rational threshold q∈[0,1]?
cards.why: This combines randomness, adversarial control and infinite-run specifications in a central quantitative verification task.

cards.title: Probabilistic Newman lemma with ordinary local confluence
