cards.why: Asks whether the existence of a short familiar refutation can make unsatisfiability efficiently recognizable even when finding a refutation in that same calculus is hard. This isolates an unresolved limitation of proof search and the theoretical analysis of SAT solvers.

cards.title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege lower bounds
cards.formal:
For every prime integer \(p\), does there exist a single polynomial-time constructible family of DNF tautologies \((\tau_{p,n})_{n\ge1}\) of length polynomially related to \(n\), such that its proofs in the fixed modular Frege calculus below exceed every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth? Precisely, require for each \(p\) a finite deterministic machine \(M_p\) and integers \(C_p,k_p\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) the machine outputs a DNF \(\tau_{p,n}\) within \(C_p(n+2)^{k_p}\) bit steps, this formula is a tautology, and
\[n\le |\tau_{p,n}|\le C_p(n+2)^{k_p}.\]
The required lower bound is
\[\forall d,r,N\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge N\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{Proof}_{p,d}(\pi,\tau_{p,n})\Rightarrow |\pi|>n^r\bigr).\]
The machine and the family may depend on \(p\) but not on \(d,r,N\); the witness \(n\) may depend on all three. No effective procedure producing \(M_p\) from \(p\) is required. The family consists of genuine tautologies, not formulas whose lack of short proofs might be due to falsity. The lower bound is infinitely often, not necessarily eventually for every \(n\).
cards.why: This is a central unresolved comparison between the expressive power of shallow formulas and the length of rigorous deductions. Ordinary bounded-depth Frege lower bounds are known, but modular gates permit compact reasoning about arithmetic counts, including parity. Proving the stated lower bounds would move a major proof-complexity frontier beyond shallow reasoning without modular counting.

cards.title: Frege lower bounds from circuit hardness
cards.formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{Frege is not polynomially bounded}.\]
Precisely, assuming that some NP language has no polynomial-size Boolean circuit family, must it be true that for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every constant \(C\ge1\), there is a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\), in the fixed system below, has
\[|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+1)^k?\]
This asks for a conditional connection between two lower-bound statements. It does not separately require proving the circuit-hardness premise.
cards.why: General Boolean circuit lower bounds and Frege proof lower bounds are two major barriers in complexity theory. A positive implication would make progress on the former sufficient for the latter, even without an explicit hard-tautology construction. It would clarify whether these difficulties are formally linked or whether proof complexity requires an additional source of hardness.

cards.title: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic
cards.formal:
Are there integers \(i>j\ge1\) and a closed first-order arithmetic sentence \(\theta\) such that
\[T_2^i\vdash\theta\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_2^j\nvdash\theta?\]
The theory \(T_2^r\) is BASIC together with induction for every \(\Sigma_r^b\) formula in the language defined below. The question asks for a separation as sets of provable sentences, with no assumed separation of computational complexity classes and no additional oracle symbols. One pair of levels is enough; it need not be fixed in advance, and proving strictness at every pair is not required.
cards.why: These theories organize arithmetic reasoning by the logical complexity permitted in induction hypotheses. Showing that even two positive levels prove different sentences would establish an unconditional difference in the strength of those reasoning principles. It would clarify how computational complexity is reflected in provability, beyond the known conditional connections.

cards.title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)\) lower bounds
cards.formal:
Is resolution over parities not polynomially bounded on unsatisfiable Boolean CNF formulas? Precisely, is the following proposition true?
\[
\forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists F\quad
\bigl[F\text{ is an unsatisfiable CNF}\ \land\
L_{\oplus}(F)>C\bigl(N(F)+1\bigr)^k\bigr].
\]
Here \(L_{\oplus}(F)\) is the minimum number of lines in any unrestricted \(\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)\) refutation of \(F\), with the rules below, and \(N(F)\) is its full combinatorial input size. Earlier proof lines may be reused arbitrarily. There is no restriction on depth, width, regularity or space.
cards.why: A central lower-bound challenge for a small extension of resolution that can reason directly about parity. Resolving it would establish whether this algebraic ability suffices to give short refutations of every unsatisfiable CNF, or whether even unrestricted reuse of parity information leaves an unavoidable superpolynomial proof-size barrier.

cards.title: Complete disjoint NP pairs
cards.formal:
Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), and let
\[
\mathcal D=\{(A,B):A,B\subseteq\Sigma^{*},\ A,B\in\mathrm{NP},\ A\cap B=\varnothing\}.
\]
Does there exist a disjoint NP pair that is complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions of pairs? Precisely, is
\[
\exists(A,B)\in\mathcal D\ \forall(C,D)\in\mathcal D\ \exists f\in\mathrm{FP}\
\forall x\in\Sigma^{*}\
\bigl[(x\in C\Rightarrow f(x)\in A)\land(x\in D\Rightarrow f(x)\in B)\bigr]
\]
true? Here \(\mathrm{FP}\) consists of total polynomial-time functions \(\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}\), as specified below. The target pair is fixed before the source pair is chosen; the reduction and its polynomial running-time bound may depend on the source pair.
cards.why: A complete pair would be a universal promise problem for two disjoint cases that each have efficiently checkable certificates. The question links the structure of promise problems to the possible existence of a strongest propositional proof system and to feasible versions of incompleteness.

cards.title: Unprovability of polynomial circuit upper bounds in \(S_2^1\)
cards.formal:
Is the following unconditional unprovability statement true?
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists\eta\ \forall c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\qquad S_2^1\nvdash\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta].\]
Here \(\eta(x,y)\) must be a \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula for which \(S_2^1\) proves that every \(x\) has exactly one output \(y\). It therefore represents a polynomial-time function. The sentence \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\), defined below with explicit coding, asserts that the predicate “the output is nonzero” has exact Boolean circuits of description size at most \(c n^k\) on every positive input length \(n\).

For each fixed exponent, the same represented function must resist provability for every fixed coefficient. The question concerns what this formal theory can prove; it does not ask directly for a circuit lower bound in the standard natural numbers or for unprovability of all possible upper bounds for one fixed function.
cards.why: Circuit upper bounds assert that small nonuniform computations exist, even when no efficient method for finding them is supplied. This question asks whether a theory designed to formalize polynomial-time reasoning can certify fixed-polynomial circuit bounds for every polynomial-time predicate. A positive result would expose an unconditional limitation on the power of such proofs without requiring the corresponding unconditional circuit separation.

cards.title: Unprovability of NP circuit upper bounds in \(T_2^1\)
cards.formal:
Is the following unconditional statement true?
\[
\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists\theta(x)\in\Sigma_1^b\
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\qquad
T_2^1\nvdash\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\theta].
\]
The formula \(\theta\) represents an NP predicate. The sentence \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\theta]\), defined below, says that this predicate has deterministic Boolean circuits of description size at most \(c n^k\) on every positive input length. Thus for each fixed exponent one represented NP predicate must resist every fixed coefficient. The theory, formula class, circuit encoding and formal upper-bound sentence are all specified below.
cards.why: This asks whether a theory that supports induction over NP predicates can certify fixed-polynomial circuits for every NP language. An unconditional negative limitation on its proving power would strengthen a central connection between bounded arithmetic and circuit complexity, beyond the known weaker-theory or larger-language-class cases.

cards.title: \(PV_1\) nonprovability of polynomial-time SAT solvers
cards.formal: Is it true that, for every unary function symbol \(g\) in the syntactically generated language \(L_{PV}\) below, \[PV_1\not\vdash\Phi_g,\qquad \Phi_g=\forall F\,\forall a\bigl(\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\to\operatorname{Sat}(F,g(F))\bigr)?\] The theory, admissible symbols and arithmetic formula \(\operatorname{Sat}\) are fixed in the definitions. This is an unconditional assertion about finite first-order proofs.
cards.why: The question isolates whether reasoning restricted to efficiently computable concepts can certify a polynomial-time algorithm for an NP-complete search task. It is a foundational test of the strength of feasible mathematics and separates the truth of an algorithmic assertion from the existence of a proof in a particular theory.

cards.title: Lovász–Schrijver simulation of Cutting Planes
cards.formal:
Does the basic Lovász–Schrijver system \(\mathrm{LS}\) polynomially simulate Cutting Planes \(\mathrm{CP}\) in the following real-coefficient, line-count sense?

There exist a real constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), every \(m\ge0\), every finite initial system
\[
\Phi=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}x_j\ge b_i:1\le i\le m\right\},
\qquad a_{ij},b_i\in\mathbb R,
\]
and every CP refutation \(\Pi\) of \(\Phi\), there is an LS refutation \(\Lambda\) of the same initial system satisfying
\[
|\Lambda|\le C\bigl(n+m+|\Pi|+1\bigr)^k.
\]
All variables are Boolean. The proof systems and the length measure are defined below. The constants are independent of the initial coefficients and both proofs.
cards.why: Cutting Planes derives integer consequences by rounding, while LS derives consequences using Boolean identities and quadratic inequalities. Establishing or separating their remaining simulation direction would clarify whether the latter rules can always match concise arguments based on rounding. The known reverse separation makes this a concrete boundary between major proof systems.

cards.title: Cutting Planes versus polynomial-coefficient Cutting Planes
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(C,k\) such that, for every CNF formula \(F\) and every Cutting Planes refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\), there is a Cutting Planes refutation \(\pi'\) of the same formula satisfying
\[
L(\pi')\le C\bigl(N(F)+L(\pi)\bigr)^k,\qquad
M(\pi')\le C\bigl(N(F)+L(\pi)\bigr)^k?
\]
Both refutations use exactly the rules and variables defined below. The original coefficients are unrestricted, proof lines may be reused, and there is no space restriction. A negative answer is the full quantified negation: for every pair \(C,k\ge1\), some \(F,\pi\) admit no replacement satisfying both bounds. The violating instance may depend on \(C,k\).
cards.why: A resolution would determine whether the numerical size of coefficients is an essential resource for concise integer-inequality proofs, independently of memory. This is a central comparison among propositional proof systems and clarifies what short pseudo-Boolean certificates can express. It does not by itself guarantee an efficient algorithm for discovering those certificates.

cards.title: Linear-space Cutting Planes refutations
cards.formal:
Does there exist one constant \(C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that every unsatisfiable CNF formula on \(n\) Boolean variables has a Cutting Planes refutation using total space at most \(C(n+1)\), with the exact rules and space measure below?
\[
\exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_0\
\forall F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\
\left(\operatorname{Unsat}(F)\ \Longrightarrow\
\exists\Pi\
\left[\operatorname{Ref}_{\mathrm{CP}}(F,\Pi)
\land\operatorname{TotSp}(\Pi)\le C(n+1)\right]\right).
\]
Here \(n\) counts variables, rather than clauses, literal occurrences or the binary length of the whole input. There is no restriction on the number of clauses, proof length or coefficient magnitudes. The same constant \(C\) must work for every \(n\) and \(F\); the finite refutation \(\Pi\) may depend on \(F\). The \(n+1\) convention includes formulas with no variables and is equivalent to the source's asymptotic linear bound.
cards.why: The question tests a basic memory limit of a central arithmetic proof system used to study pseudo-Boolean reasoning. Counting only inequalities hides the cost of large coefficients, whereas total space records that cost. A resolution would determine whether the known constant-line-space phenomenon extends to a linear numerical representation budget, or whether some Boolean contradictions force additional simultaneous information even when arbitrarily long proofs are permitted. This is a universal structural question about the proof system, with a separate meaning from lower bounds on proof length.

cards.title: PSPACE-completeness of resolution clause space
cards.formal:
Is the following language \(\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\) PSPACE-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions?
\[\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}=\{\langle F,s\rangle:\ F\text{ has a general resolution refutation in clause space at most }s\}.\]
Here \(F\) is any finite CNF formula, with no fixed bound on input clause width, and \(s\ge0\) is an integer encoded in binary. A refutation starts with no stored clauses and may download an input clause, derive a resolvent or weakening of currently stored clauses, or erase a stored clause. It succeeds when the empty clause is stored. Its clause space is the largest number of simultaneously stored distinct clauses, counting a new conclusion together with its still-stored premises. Proof length and clause width during the derivation are unrestricted.

The question is about general resolution, allowing a retained clause to be reused in arbitrarily many inferences. PSPACE membership is known; the unresolved target is whether the full problem is PSPACE-hard. Satisfiable inputs have no refutation and are no-instances for every finite \(s\).
cards.why: The target asks whether predicting the minimum memory needed by a resolution proof is as hard as arbitrary polynomial-space computation. This would sharpen the distinction between checking a supplied logical derivation and determining whether any derivation fits a memory budget. It also tests how unrestricted reuse of learned information changes the complexity landscape beyond tree-like proof search.

cards.title: Polynomial resolution length from logarithmic clause space
cards.formal:
Does logarithmic clause space imply polynomial refutation length for every fixed input clause width in general resolution?

Precisely, for every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and real constant \(a>0\), do there exist constants \(B>0\) and \(d\ge1\), depending only on \(k,a\), such that every unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\) satisfies
\[\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le a\log_2 N(F)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(F)\le B\,N(F)^d?\]
Here \(N(F)=2+|F|+\sum_{C\in F}|C|\) is formula size, \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\) is the minimum number of clauses simultaneously retained in a resolution refutation, and \(L(F)\) is its minimum number of axiom downloads and inference steps. These two minima are taken independently over all general resolution refutations. The short refutation whose existence is requested has no space restriction.
cards.why: The question asks whether a resolution proof that can be checked with only logarithmically many retained clauses necessarily has a short certificate somewhere in the same proof system. Resolving it would sharpen the relation between proof memory and proof length beyond the known constant-space case, without conflating proof existence with an efficient search algorithm.

cards.title: Simultaneous polynomial-length constant-space refutations
cards.formal: Is the following statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and every family \((F_n)_{n\ge1}\) of unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formulas of size polynomial in \(n\), if there is a constant \(s\) such that every \(F_n\) has a resolution refutation using at most \(s\) clauses simultaneously, then there are constants \(S\ge1\), \(C>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that every \(F_n\) has a single resolution refutation \(\pi_n\) with \[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi_n)\le S\qquad\text{and}\qquad L(\pi_n)\le C(n+1)^d.\] The constants may depend on the family and on \(k,s\), but not on \(n\). In particular, the conclusion may use a larger constant space bound \(S\) than the original bound \(s\).
cards.why: Proof length measures how many lines a refutation generates, and clause space measures how many it must retain at once. The question asks whether a formula that is easy in each measure separately can be hard when both restrictions apply to the same proof. Its constant-space regime makes it a sharp structural question about resolution and the interpretation of proof-memory bounds.

cards.title: Linear versus general resolution
cards.formal:
Is linear resolution strictly weaker than general resolution in polynomial refutation size, for the same input CNF formula? Here linear resolution has no restarts, and the size \(\ell\) is one plus the number of resolution inferences. More precisely, is the following assertion true?
\[
\forall c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_0\
\exists F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\ \exists\pi\
\left[
\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\ \land\
\forall\lambda\
\left(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\Longrightarrow
\ell(\lambda)>c\,\ell(\pi)^{k}\right)
\right].
\]
The classes of formulas and the two syntactic refutation predicates are defined below. This asserts failure of every polynomial bound on the extra proof length needed by linear resolution. The constants \(c,k\) range independently over positive integers; \(n,F,\pi\) may depend on them. The comparison concerns existence of proofs, with no requirement that a conversion between proofs be computable in polynomial time. It does not prescribe an exponential separation or an effectively generated family of formulas.
cards.why: This compares two longstanding, complete refinements of a foundational propositional proof system. It isolates the effect of how deductions are organized and reused, with the inference rule and input formula held fixed. A separation would identify an intrinsic proof-length cost of the linear discipline; a polynomial simulation would show that arbitrary resolution structure can always be reproduced within polynomial length. The result would clarify the strength hierarchy of resolution refinements, independently of how efficiently a solver can discover the proofs.

cards.title: Short tree-like resolution from small proof space
cards.formal: For \(\mu\) equal to resolution clause space CSpace or PCR monomial space \(MSpace_{K}\), does there exist a constant \(a\ge 1\) and \(C>0\) such that every unsatisfiable CNF F on \(n\ge 2\) variables satisfies \(\log _{2}(S_{T}(F)+1)\le C((\mu (F)+1)\log _{2}(n+1))^{a}\)? Determine the validity of this comparison in each of the two cases in the source’s Problem 5.1. For monomial space, K is an arbitrary fixed field and the constants may depend on K, but not on F or n. Here \(S_{T}\) is minimum tree-like resolution leaf count. The opposite comparison, bounding each space measure by logarithmic tree-like size up to these polynomial/logarithmic losses, is known.
cards.why: Would determine whether low working memory in propositional refutations fundamentally limits repeated work, clarifying strong size-space trade-offs and the cost of converting reusable proofs into trees.

cards.title: Optimal proof systems outside NP
cards.formal: Does there exist a nonempty language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with \(L\notin\mathrm{NP}\) that has an optimal Cook–Reckhow proof system, where optimality compares proof lengths and does not require an efficient translation between systems?
cards.why: Determines whether a proof language can be best up to polynomial proof-length overhead even when membership has no uniformly short certificates. It separates optimality relative to all competing proof systems from the existence of short proofs themselves.

cards.title: Sharp resolution length bounds at fixed width
cards.formal:
Do there exist integers \(c\ge1\) and \(w_0\ge\max\{3,c+1\}\) such that, for every integer \(w\ge w_0\), there are constants \(a_w,b_w,d_w>0\), an integer \(n_w\ge1\), and a family of unsatisfiable 3-CNF formulas \((F_{n,w})_{n\ge n_w}\) satisfying, for every integer \(n\ge n_w\),
\[
a_wn\le s(F_{n,w})\le b_wn,\qquad
W(F_{n,w})\le w,\qquad
L(F_{n,w})\ge d_wn^{\,w-c}?
\]
Here \(W\) is minimum refutation width and \(L\) is minimum refutation length without a width restriction. The absolute constant \(c\) is common to every width. The family and the other constants may depend on \(w\), which is fixed before \(n\) tends to infinity.
cards.why: A sharp answer would quantify the inherent exponent cost of narrow resolution, a foundational resource in SAT proof complexity. It would distinguish the optimal dependence on width from the already known qualitative exponential dependence, and sharpen what resolution-based proof search can achieve even when it is free to use wider clauses.

cards.title: Effective polynomial simulation of Extended Frege by Resolution
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic transformation R and fixed polynomials p,q such that, for every propositional formula F and every integer \(s\ge 1, R\)(F,1ˢ) outputs a CNF formula in at most p(|F|+s) bit operations, F is a tautology if and only if R(F,1ˢ) is unsatisfiable, and whenever F has an Extended Frege proof of length at most s, R(F,1ˢ) has a Resolution refutation of length at most q(|F|+s)?
cards.why: Determines whether allowing efficient preprocessing fundamentally changes the apparent gap between elementary clause reasoning and proof systems that can name arbitrary intermediate Boolean computations. This affects what proof-size separations say about algorithms for finding proofs.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) proof systems for directed reachability
cards.formal:
For \(n\ge2\), let
\[
R_n=\{A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}:
\text{the directed graph encoded by }A\text{ has a path from }1\text{ to }n\}.
\]
Does there exist an integer \(D\ge0\) such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) there are a nonnegative integer \(m_n\) and a Boolean circuit
\[
C_n:\{0,1\}^{m_n}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n^2}
\]
of depth at most \(D\), using AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two and NOT gates, for which
\[
\{C_n(z):z\in\{0,1\}^{m_n}\}=R_n?
\]
The right side is identified with row-major adjacency-matrix encodings. Equivalently, every proof string must produce a graph with the required directed path, and every graph with that path must be produced by some proof string.
cards.why: The question asks whether a global directed-path property can be guaranteed by generating each edge from only constantly many proof bits, while still representing every yes-instance. The contrast with known local proof systems for undirected reachability and directed unreachability isolates the role of direction and global consistency in very weak proof systems.

cards.title: Does uniform randomized circuit learning imply P equals NP?
cards.formal: Does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time learner for arbitrary Boolean circuits under the uniform input distribution, with membership queries and the resource bounds below, imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\)?
cards.why: Asks whether the difficulty of predicting efficiently computable functions follows from worst-case NP hardness alone. The question probes the gap between worst-case complexity, learning and the average-case hardness used in cryptography; its significance depends on keeping their models and quantifiers distinct.

area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

cards.title: Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture
cards.formal:
Does there exist a positive integer \(C\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\), every integer \(1\le d\le n\), and every real multilinear polynomial \(f\) in \(n\) variables of degree at most \(d\),
\[\bigl[\forall x\in\{-1,1\}^n,\ 0\le f(x)\le1\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists i\in[n]:\ \operatorname{Inf}_i(f)\ge\left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(f)}d\right)^C?\]
Variance and squared \(L_2\) influence use the uniform distribution on the entire Boolean cube, with the normalization below. The same exponent \(C\) must work for all dimensions, degrees, coefficients and variances.
cards.why: A central structural question about real-valued Boolean-cube functions, with direct consequences for when quantum query algorithms can have large classical simulation costs.

cards.title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist one finite real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every positive integer \(n\) and every function \(f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}\), \[H(f)\le C I(f),\] where \(H(f)\) is the Shannon entropy in bits of the squared Fourier spectrum and \(I(f)\) is total influence for uniformly distributed inputs? The same \(C\) must work for all dimensions and all Boolean functions.
cards.why: A central structural conjecture connecting sensitivity to spectral information. Its resolution would sharpen our understanding of Boolean functions and spectral learning, while testing a relation that fails without the Boolean constraint.

cards.title: Mansour’s conjecture
cards.formal:
Does there exist an absolute real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), integer \(s\ge2\), function \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, and real \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), there is a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) for which
\[
 |\mathcal F|\le\left\lceil s^{C\log_2(1/\varepsilon)}\right\rceil,
 \qquad
 \sum_{S\subseteq[n],\ S\notin\mathcal F}\widehat f(S)^2\le\varepsilon?
\]
The coefficients are the ordinary Walsh–Fourier coefficients under the uniform distribution. The same constant \(C\) must work for every dimension, term count, formula and accuracy.
cards.why: A fundamental bridge between short logical formulas, sparse spectral representations, and learning with queries. The strong accuracy parameter makes the question a precise test of how much analytic structure small DNF size forces.

cards.title: Interactive compression with logarithmic input-length overhead
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\) such that every two-party protocol \(\pi\) on \(n\)-bit inputs, under every joint input distribution \(\mu\), has a simulation \(\rho\) with distributional error at most \(1/100\) and worst-case communication at most
\[
K\bigl(I_{\mu}(\pi)+1\bigr)\bigl\lceil\log_2(n+2)\bigr\rceil\quad\text{bits}?
\]
Here \(n\ge1\), the protocol and simulation model, internal information cost \(I_{\mu}\), and joint-transcript error are defined below. There is no restriction on the finite communication cost of \(\pi\), and \(K\) must be independent of \(n,\mu,\pi\).

This is an explicitly selected editorial version of the source's proposed logarithmic-loss question. The source's surrounding paragraph concerns two-party internal information, despite the article's multiparty title. It already reports that compression without an overhead is impossible. The particular logarithmic factor, constant error, additive regularization and worst-case transcript-simulation guarantee below are specified here rather than attributed verbatim to its informal sentence.
cards.why: The question asks how much communication is forced by interaction beyond the information actually transferred. A general small-overhead simulation would strengthen the connection between information-theoretic lower bounds and communication complexity, with consequences for direct-sum phenomena. A matching obstruction would show why correlated inputs prevent a near-information-cost account of interactive communication.

cards.title: Polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication
cards.formal: Are randomized classical and entanglement-assisted quantum communication polynomially related for every total Boolean function? Precisely, do universal constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that \[R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\le C\bigl(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1\bigr)^k\] for every pair of nonempty finite sets \(X,Y\) and every function \(F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\)?
cards.why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

cards.title: Maximum influence of polynomial threshold functions
cards.formal:
Determine, up to universal multiplicative constant factors jointly in \(n\) and \(d\), the function
\[M(n,d)=\max\{I(f):f\in\mathcal F_{n,d}\},\qquad n,d\in\mathbb N,\quad n\ge1,\quad1\le d\le n,\]
where \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) is the class of Boolean functions represented by the sign of a real polynomial of total degree at most \(d\) with no zero on \(\{-1,1\}^n\), and \(I(f)\) is total influence under the uniform distribution, defined below. The answer must give a positive growth function \(h(n,d)\) and constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), independent of both parameters, such that \[\forall n\ge1\ \forall d\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad c\,h(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le C\,h(n,d).\] No particular formula for \(h\) or extremizing Boolean function is prescribed.
cards.why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.

cards.title: Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on \([n]\) to \(\{0,1\}\) that is invariant under every permutation of \([n]\) and monotone under adding edges, is \(D(f)=n(n- 1)/2\), where \(D(f)\) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
cards.why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.

cards.title: Formula size versus partition complexity
cards.formal: Are there universal constants \(C\ge1\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that every nonconstant Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for every \(n\ge1\), satisfies \(L(f)\le C\,\chi(f)^d\)? Here \(L(f)\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf size, and \(\chi(f)\) is the minimum number of disjoint coordinate-monochromatic rectangles partitioning \(f^{-1}(1)\times f^{-1}(0)\). The polynomial bound must depend only on \(\chi(f)\), with no additional factor depending on \(n\).
cards.why: A formula organizes computation hierarchically, whereas a rectangle partition only gives a disjoint collection of valid local distinctions between accepting and rejecting inputs. The question asks whether this absence of an imposed hierarchy can yield more than polynomial savings. A resolution would determine how closely a central combinatorial lower-bound measure captures general formula size.

cards.title: Linearization conjecture for depth-two circuits
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute integer \(C\ge1\) with the following property?

For every \(n\ge1\), every matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times n}\), and all integers \(w,d\ge0\), if the linear map \(x\mapsto Ax\) is computed exactly by a depth-two circuit with arbitrary Boolean gates, width at most \(w\), and degree at most \(d\), then it is computed exactly by a linear depth-two circuit with width at most \(Cw\) and degree at most \(Cd\).

Width counts middle-layer gates. Degree counts, for each output separately, only the direct wires from the original input variables; it does not count wires through middle-layer gates. Both notions and the gate models are defined below. The constant \(C\) is independent of the matrix, dimensions and resource bounds.
cards.why: A short nonlinear summary of the input might help answer many linear queries even when no equally short linear summary is available. The conjecture asks whether that advantage disappears up to constant factors when the only other resource is a few direct input bits per output. It would connect matrix-based lower bounds more closely to unrestricted Boolean computation.

cards.title: Quadratic decision-tree bounds from block sensitivity
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for every integer \(n\ge1\), satisfies \[D(f)\le C\,\operatorname{bs}(f)^2?\] Here \(D(f)\) is deterministic worst-case bit-query complexity and \(\operatorname{bs}(f)\) is block sensitivity, with both measures defined below. The constant must be independent of \(n\) and of the function, and no logarithmic or dimension-dependent multiplier is allowed.
cards.why: The two quantities measure different aspects of the information needed to determine a Boolean output: the worst adaptive query cost and the number of disjoint ways to change the output at one input. Their known cubic general upper bound and quadratic examples leave a basic gap. A uniform quadratic relation would sharpen the structure of query complexity across every total Boolean function.

cards.title: Constant-factor randomized direct sums for total Boolean functions
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) such that, for every pair of nonempty finite input sets \(X,Y\), every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), \[R_{1/3}(f^{\otimes k})\ge c\,k\,R_{1/3}(f),\] where communication is public-coin, worst-case and measured with one global error probability?
cards.why: Direct sums ask whether communicating about many tasks together can save a substantial fraction of the single-task cost. They connect communication lower bounds with interactive compression and the distinction between information revealed and bits transmitted. The exact error and task conventions determine which savings are possible.

cards.title: Number-on-forehead disjointness complexity
cards.formal:
Determine, up to absolute constant factors, the randomized number-on-forehead communication complexity
\[
R(n,k)=R_{1/3}^{\mathrm{pub}}(\operatorname{DISJ}_{n,k})
\]
for all integers \(n\ge1\) and \(k\ge2\).

The input consists of \(k\) arbitrary subsets \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\subseteq[n]\). Player \(i\) sees every set except \(S_i\). The common output must be
\[
\operatorname{DISJ}_{n,k}(S_1,\ldots,S_k)
=\mathbf 1\!\left[\bigcap_{i=1}^k S_i=\varnothing\right].
\]
Players use public randomness and unrestricted interactive broadcasts, with error at most \(1/3\) on every input and communication measured by the maximum total number of broadcast bits.

The requested characterization is a specified noncircular asymptotic function \(g(n,k)>0\) and constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), independent of both \(n\) and \(k\), such that
\[
c\,g(n,k)\le R(n,k)\le C\,g(n,k)
\qquad(n\ge1,\ k\ge2).
\]
cards.why: Each player knows almost the entire input, which makes communication lower bounds much harder than in the ordinary split-input model. Set disjointness gives a concrete way to measure how this overlap and additional players change the power of randomized interaction. A full answer would clarify a basic limitation used in several connections between communication, circuits and proofs.

cards.title: Large zero rectangles in low-rank real matrices
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) of rank \(r\) with at least \(n^2/2\) zero entries, there are nonempty sets \(I,J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying \[A_{ij}=0\quad(i\in I,\ j\in J),\qquad |I|\,|J|\ge n^2\exp(-C\sqrt r)?\]
cards.why: The question asks whether low real rank forces a large exact combinatorial pattern when zeros are dense. This connects linear-algebraic complexity to the rectangles that control communication protocols, while extending beyond Boolean matrices. Its value is the proposed general structural principle; the question is not merely to speed up a search for a rectangle.

cards.title: Sign-rank bounds from constant margin
cards.formal: For every real \(\rho \in\)(0,1], does there exist a finite integer \(d(\rho )\), independent of matrix dimensions, such that every finite sign matrix A with margin \(m(A)\ge \rho\) has sign-rank at most \(d(\rho )\)? This is the dimension-free bounding-function question written in the source as rank±\((A)\le \eta (m(A)^{- 1})\); no polynomial or computable bound on \(\eta\) is requested.
cards.why: Asks whether robust high-dimensional point–halfspace representations can always be replaced by bounded-dimensional representations, connecting geometric learning parameters with communication complexity.

cards.title: Fourier rank versus sparsity
cards.formal: Does there exist a sequence of integers \(n_{j}\ge 1\) and Boolean functions \(f_{j}:\{- 1,1\}^{n_{j}}\to \{- 1,1\}\) such that \(k(f_{j})\to \infty\) and \(r(f_{j})/\sqrt{k}(f_{j})\to \infty\) as \(j\to \infty\), where k is Fourier sparsity and r is Fourier rank over \(F_{2}\)? Equivalently, is the ratio \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\) unbounded over all finite-dimensional Boolean functions?
cards.why: Would determine whether sparse Boolean Fourier support necessarily occupies only square-root-many independent parity directions, or whether the familiar quadratic relation misses a growing separation.

cards.title: Fourier Min-Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\), some set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfies \(\widehat f(S)^2\ge 2^{-C I(f)}\)? Here \(I(f)\) is total influence under the uniform distribution. Equivalently, the conjecture asserts \(H_\infty(f)\le C I(f)\), with Fourier min-entropy defined below. The same constant must work for every dimension and every function.
cards.why: Total influence measures how often individual bit changes alter an output, while Fourier min-entropy measures how weak even the strongest parity correlation can be. A universal relation would constrain all Boolean functions without representation or balance assumptions. Its distinction from full Fourier entropy matters: controlling a single coefficient asks for less than controlling the entire spectral information, yet retains a connection to fundamental influence inequalities.

cards.title: Deterministic communication versus monochromatic partition size
cards.formal:
Determine the largest deterministic two-party communication complexity possible for a total Boolean function with a given bound on its monochromatic partition size, up to multiplicative constants.

For a total function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\) on finite nonempty sets, let \(D(f)\) be its minimum worst-case deterministic communication cost in bits. Let \(\chi(f)\) be the smallest number of pairwise disjoint monochromatic combinatorial rectangles whose union is all of \(X\times Y\). Define, for integers \(t\ge0\),
\[H(t)=\max\bigl\{D(f): X,Y\text{ finite and nonempty},\ f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\},\ \chi(f)\le2^t\bigr\}.\]
The target is the asymptotic order of \(H(t)\) as \(t\to\infty\), with matching upper and lower bounds up to constants independent of \(t\). This includes any nonconstant factors below the known quadratic upper bound; determining only the optimal power exponent does not meet this precision.
cards.why: This tradeoff measures how much information a small monochromatic partition fails to capture about an executable communication protocol. Determining it sharply would delineate the power and limitations of a central combinatorial lower bound on deterministic communication, beyond knowing only its quadratic exponent.

cards.title: Influence lower bound for noisy query complexity
cards.formal:
Historical question, resolved affirmatively: for every fixed noise probability \(p\in(0,1/2)\), does there exist a constant \(c_p>0\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) and every total Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\),
\[
\mathsf N_p(f)\ge c_p\,\mathsf I(f)\log_2\mathsf I(f)\ ?
\]
Here \(\mathsf N_p(f)\) is adaptive randomized noisy bit-query complexity with error at most \(1/3\), measured by the worst-input expected number of queries, and \(\mathsf I(f)\) is total influence under the uniform distribution. Both are defined below. The constant may depend on \(p\), but not on \(n\), \(f\) or the algorithm.
cards.why: A Boolean function may change on many single-bit perturbations, yet an adaptive algorithm can concentrate its effort unevenly. The theorem shows that average sensitivity still forces an additional logarithmic query cost under independently repeated noise. It gives a general structural lower bound instead of a separate argument for each computational task.

cards.title: A randomized-communication characterization of ordinary KW games
cards.formal:
Is the following candidate characterization true? For every family of total two-party search relations \((R_n)_{n\ge2}\) with polynomially bounded input and answer lengths and deterministic polylogarithmic communication for verifying a proposed answer, the following are equivalent:

1. \(R_n\) has a public-coin randomized protocol with polylogarithmic communication and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input pair.
2. \(R_n\) is equivalent, under deterministic polylogarithmic-communication mapping reductions in both directions, to the ordinary Karchmer–Wigderson game of a partial Boolean function on at most quasipolynomially many variables.

All bounds, quantifiers, models and reductions are specified below. This is a user-selected editorial candidate, not a conjecture asserted verbatim by the source.
cards.why: An intrinsic characterization would explain which total communication search tasks arise from ordinary Boolean function separation. It would connect randomized communication with the structural reductions behind circuit-depth games, while distinguishing ordinary games from their monotone counterparts.

cards.title: Two-sided versus one-sided randomized communication
cards.formal:
For total Boolean two-party function families, is
\[
\mathrm{BPP}^{\mathrm{cc}}=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{RP}^{\mathrm{cc}}}\,?
\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}^{\mathrm{cc}}\) consists of families with public-coin randomized protocols using a polylogarithmic number of communicated bits and error at most \(1/3\) on every input. The class on the right consists of families computed exactly by deterministic protocols with adaptive access to ideal one-sided-error communication oracles, with polylogarithmic total charged cost as defined below.

Equivalently, does every total family \((F_n)_{n\ge1}\), where \(F_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), with
\[
R_{1/3}^{\mathrm{pub}}(F_n)\le C(\log_2(n+2))^a
\]
for some fixed \(C\ge1,a\ge0\), admit deterministic oracle protocols of cost at most
\[
C'(\log_2(n+2))^b
\]
for some fixed \(C'\ge1,b\ge0\) and every \(n\)? The latter constants may depend on the family. There are no promised or undefined inputs.
cards.why: Many randomized communication algorithms use a few kinds of tests that can be wrong in only one direction. The question asks whether arbitrary two-sided randomized interaction can always be organized around such tests while retaining efficient communication. Either outcome would clarify the role of randomness in the structural hierarchy of two-party protocols.

cards.title: Multiparty Clique lower bounds in compression games
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon>0\) and an integer round bound \(r(N)\to\infty\) such that every nonuniform, deterministic, polynomial-party \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\)-compression protocol family deciding Clique with at most \(r(N)\) rounds has cost \(\Omega(N^\varepsilon)\)? Here \(N\) is the graph’s number of vertices. In each round, Alice sends messages to independent computationally unrestricted Bobs, receives their replies, and eventually computes the answer herself with an \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) circuit. Cost is the sum over rounds of the maximum length of an Alice-to-Bob message in that round.
cards.why: This asks whether many unrestricted helpers can compensate for Alice’s constant-depth computation using short messages and an increasing number of interactions. The source connects a positive answer for Clique to a major nonuniform circuit lower bound. The unusual communication measure makes precise model recovery essential to that connection.

cards.title: Sharp low-degree Fourier weight of halfspaces
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every linear threshold function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}\), is \(\mathrm{W}^{\le 1}(f)=\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat\{f\}(\{i\})^{2}\ge 2/\pi\)?
cards.why: A sharp universal low-degree Fourier inequality for all halfspaces describes the spectral structure of a foundational Boolean function class.

cards.title: Zero-error query complexity of recursive majority-of-three
cards.formal:
Determine, up to multiplicative constants independent of the height \(h\), the zero-error randomized query complexity \(Q(h)\) of the complete height-\(h\) recursive majority-of-three function \(M_h\).

Set \(M_0(x)=x\). For \(h\ge0\), divide an input of length \(3^{h+1}\) into three consecutive blocks \(x^{(1)},x^{(2)},x^{(3)}\) of length \(3^h\) and define
\[M_{h+1}(x)=\operatorname{Maj}_3\bigl(M_h(x^{(1)}),M_h(x^{(2)}),M_h(x^{(3)})\bigr),\]
where \(\operatorname{Maj}_3(a,b,c)=1\) exactly when at least two of its three Boolean arguments are one.

An algorithm adaptively queries individual input bits and must always output the correct value. Its cost is the maximum over inputs of its expected number of queries, with expectation only over its internal randomness. If \(\mathcal T_h\) is the finite set of deterministic decision trees computing \(M_h\) without repeating a query on a path, then
\[Q(h)=\min_{\mu\in\Delta(\mathcal T_h)}\ \max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{3^h}}\ \mathbb E_{T\sim\mu}\bigl[q_T(x)\bigr].\]
Here \(q_T(x)\) is the number of queried bits on the input path, and \(\Delta(\mathcal T_h)\) is the set of probability distributions on these trees. The target is matching upper and lower bounds for this full function as \(h\to\infty\), including any nonconstant factors beyond its exponential growth rate.
cards.why: Determining this complexity would explain the full power of random adaptive evaluation on one of the simplest recursively defined Boolean functions. It is a canonical setting where exact computation gains substantially from randomization, but the best possible savings are still not understood despite decades of improved bounds.

cards.title: Near-linear communication for exact maximum flow with local outputs
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), does there exist a randomized two-party protocol and constants \(K_a\ge1\), integer \(r_a\ge0\), such that for every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge capacities in \([0,n^a]\), whose edges are partitioned between Alice and Bob, the protocol computes an exact maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow with success probability at least \(2/3\) and communicates at most
\[
 K_a n\bigl\lceil\log_2(n+2)\bigr\rceil^{r_a}
\]
bits on every execution? Each party must output the flow on its own edges. Interaction is unrestricted, and local computation, storage and local output are free; all transmitted bits are charged.
cards.why: A dense flow may assign values to quadratically many edges, yet each participant already knows its own part of the graph. The question asks whether this local knowledge lets them coordinate an exact optimum while exchanging only about as many bits as there are vertices.

cards.title: Removing low-influence directions from convex sets
cards.formal: Does there exist a function \(\tau :(0,1)\to [0,1]\) with \(\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0^{+}}\tau (\varepsilon )=0\) such that the following holds for every \(n\ge 1\), every centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(K\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{n}\), every unit vector v and every \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\)? If \(Inf_{v}[K]\le \varepsilon\), then there exists a centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(C\subseteq v\perp\) such that \(\gamma _{n}(K \triangle  (C+\mathbb{R} v))\le \tau (\varepsilon )\). The same \(\tau\) must work in all dimensions and for all such sets and directions.
cards.why: Would make convex influence a robust measure of whether a Gaussian direction matters, strengthening the analogy between symmetric convex sets and Boolean functions with irrelevant variables.

cards.title: PSPACE-hardness of a factor-two gap in decision-tree depth
cards.formal:
Is the following promise problem PSPACE-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? The input is an explicitly given Boolean circuit \(C\) on \(n\ge1\) input variables and an integer \(k\) with \(1\le k\le n\). Writing \(f_C:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) for the function computed by \(C\), the two promised cases are
\[
\text{YES}:D(f_C)\le k,\qquad
\text{NO}:D(f_C)>2k,
\]
where \(D(f_C)\) is the minimum worst-case depth of a deterministic decision tree that computes \(f_C\) exactly on every input.
cards.why: The exact decision-tree depth of a succinctly represented function is PSPACE-hard. A multiplicative-gap result would show that this difficulty survives coarse approximation of the number of input bits that must be inspected, rather than depending on a single critical query.

cards.title: Optimal one-bit cryptogenography success for every number of players
cards.formal:
Determine the function \(p:\{2,3,4,\ldots\}\to[0,1]\), where
\[
 p(k)=\sup_{\Pi}\ \inf_{e}\Pr\bigl[Y_\Pi=X\ \text{and}\ e(T_\Pi)\ne J\bigr].
\]
Here \(X\) is a uniformly random secret bit, \(J\) is an independent uniformly random owner in \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(\Pi\) ranges over the private-randomness public-communication protocols defined below, \(T_\Pi\) is the entire public transcript, and \(Y_\Pi\) is the protocol’s public output bit. The observer’s strategy \(e\) maps the transcript to one accused player and is chosen after the protocol is known. The requested answer is a function \(a\) with
\[
 |a(k)-p(k)|\le1/100\qquad\text{for every integer }k\ge2.
\]
There is no restriction on the time needed to evaluate or specify the answer.
cards.why: This model separates revealing information from revealing who supplied it, without relying on computational secrecy or a private channel. The function measures the best anonymity that cooperation alone can achieve as the group size changes.

cards.title: Optimal time exponent for truth-table decision-tree depth
cards.formal:
Determine the real number
\[
\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}=\inf\mathcal E,
\]
where \(\mathcal E\) is the set of real \(a\ge0\) for which one deterministic word-RAM program computes the minimum decision-tree depth of every Boolean function, from its complete truth table of length \(N\), in worst-case time \(O(N^a)\). The input, output, machine and quantifiers defining \(\mathcal E\) are specified below. Give a real answer \(v\) and a complete Lean proof of
\[
|v-\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
This is the user-selected optimal-exponent refinement of the source's broader request for exact sequential time complexity. It measures the exponent in truth-table length \(N=2^n\), not in the number \(n\) of variables. It does not ask for a constant-factor characterization of the entire running-time function, or for the depth of a parallel circuit solving the task. The infimum need not be attained by any one algorithm.
cards.why: This is a basic question in the complexity of optimizing a computational model when its entire input-output behavior is already explicit. It separates knowing every value of a Boolean function from finding its best adaptive query depth. The source establishes polynomial-time solvability and parallel hardness, leaving a substantial gap in the sequential exponent; narrowing that gap would sharpen our understanding of decision-tree optimization and this form of meta-complexity.

cards.title: A fine-grained reduction from integer APSP to 3SUM
cards.formal:
Is there a bounded-error randomized fine-grained Turing reduction from integer all-pairs shortest paths to integer 3SUM? Specifically, for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a rational \(\delta\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer weight exponent \(c\ge1\), one uniform classical randomized oracle algorithm outputs all shortest-path distances of every promised \(n\)-vertex input graph with probability at least \(2/3\), using an exact 3SUM oracle and charged cost
\[
T+\sum_{j=1}^{q}m_j^{\,2-\varepsilon}\le K(n+2)^{\,3-\delta}
\]
on every execution? The constants \(K\), the machine word-size factor and the algorithm may depend on \(\varepsilon,c\), but \(\delta\) must be common to all \(c\). Input weights, queries and the oracle-cost model are defined below.
cards.why: APSP and 3SUM support two major collections of conditional algorithmic lower bounds. A reduction from APSP to 3SUM would show that a subquadratic breakthrough for 3SUM also breaks the cubic APSP barrier, linking these two currently separate explanations of algorithmic difficulty.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width q may depend on epsilon but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
cards.why: All-pairs distances are a basic graph primitive. A fixed improvement over the cubic exponent would also change the complexity of several equivalent path, matrix and weighted-triangle problems. Their reductions make the exact weight and machine assumptions essential to interpreting claimed improvements.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic algorithms for 3SUM
cards.formal:
Is there a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(B\ge1\), a uniform randomized Las Vegas algorithm solves integer 3SUM with worst-case expected time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) on the word RAM defined below? An input consists of three lists \(A,B',C\), each containing at most \(n\) integers in \([-n^B,n^B]\), and the task is to decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \exists b\in B'\ \exists c\in C:\quad a+b=c.\]
The algorithm and hidden constant may depend on the fixed universe exponent \(B\); the saving \(\varepsilon\) must be independent of \(B\). This selects the polynomial-universe integer version of the source's question, with the expected-time convention used by Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat.
cards.why: 3SUM is a central test of whether apparently quadratic search over pairs can admit a fixed polynomial improvement. Its conjectured hardness supports fine-grained lower bounds for many geometric, graph and data-structure problems. The exact model matters: removing a logarithmic factor, changing integer size or omitting preprocessing costs can make a result look stronger than the improvement asked for here.

cards.title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a constant \(K>0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every integer \(n\ge2\), every Boolean matrix \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\), and every sequence \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n\) supplied online, the algorithm outputs each \(Mv_t\) before receiving \(v_{t+1}\), and outputs \(Mv_n\) at the end, using at most
\[
 K n^{3-\varepsilon}
\]
word-RAM instructions in total on every execution, including preprocessing of \(M\), with probability at least \(2/3\) that all \(n\) output vectors are correct? Products are over the Boolean semiring:
\[
 (Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j\bigr).
\]
The OMv conjecture asserts a negative answer.
cards.why: The conjecture supports many precise lower bounds for dynamic graph and data-structure problems. A general truly subcubic online algorithm would overturn these conditional barriers, while an unconditional lower bound would explain a shared obstacle to faster dynamic algorithms.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic exact edit distance
cards.formal: For the binary alphabet \(\Sigma =\{0,1\}\), do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon \in\)(0,1], a constant \(C>0\) and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm A such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every pair \(x,y\in \Sigma ^{n}, A\) outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance \(ED(x,y)\) in at most \(C(n+1)^{2- \varepsilon}\) operations?
cards.why: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.

cards.title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
cards.formal:
Is it true that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\ \text{no allowed algorithm solves bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors in }O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\text{ time}\]
for all integers \(n\ge2\) on two lists of \(n\) vectors in \(\{0,1\}^{d}\), where \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\)? An allowed algorithm is a uniform randomized classical word-RAM program in the model below. Its running-time bound is worst-case over both inputs and random choices, and its answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. The dimension constant \(c\) may depend on the proposed exponent saving \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed as \(n\) grows.
cards.why: A basic disjointness problem anchors a large part of fine-grained complexity. Settling its uniform exponent barrier would reshape conditional lower bounds for strings, geometry and data structures.

cards.title: Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the min-plus convolution of any two length-\(n\) integer arrays with entries in \([-n^{a},n^{a}]\) in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
cards.why: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.

cards.title: Randomized APSP hypothesis for polynomial integer weights
cards.formal: Is the following hypothesis true? \[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \neg\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] Here \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) means that a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the entire exact distance matrix of every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^c,n^c]\) and no negative-weight cycle, succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input, and has worst-case time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) over all inputs and coin sequences. The word model and the quantifiers hidden in this definition are specified below. The weight exponent \(c\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This makes explicit the weaker quantifier order stated in the 2026 source; the 2018 source's phrase about sufficiently large \(c\) did not specify that dependence.
cards.why: The randomized APSP hypothesis is a principal foundation of fine-grained complexity. Resolving it would determine whether exact distances in general integer-weighted graphs admit a fixed polynomial improvement over cubic time, and would affect a large network of conditional bounds for graph, matrix, sequence and dynamic problems.

cards.title: Algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis
cards.formal:
For each fixed integer \(k\ge3\), let \(\tau(k)\) be the infimum worst-case time exponent for uniform classical randomized algorithms deciding whether an \(n\)-vertex graph contains a \(k\)-clique, in the word-RAM model defined below. Let \(\omega\) be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over \(\mathbb C\). Is
\[
 \liminf_{k\to\infty}\frac{\tau(k)}{k}=\frac{\omega}{3}?
\]
The input size \(n\) tends to infinity with \(k\) fixed when defining \(\tau(k)\); only afterwards does \(k\) grow in the displayed limit inferior.
cards.why: A basic quantitative hardness hypothesis for graph patterns and many reductions in fine-grained complexity, precisely testing whether the matrix-multiplication exponent gives the optimal leading coefficient.

cards.title: Randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal:
Is the following randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis true?
\[
\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists k\in\mathbb N,\ k\ge3:
\quad\text{there is no bounded-error randomized algorithm for }k\text{-SAT}
\text{ with time }O\!\left(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}\operatorname{poly}(L)\right).
\]
Here \(n\) is the number of variables, \(L\) is the complete binary input length, and algorithms are uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machines with worst-case running time over both inputs and coin outcomes, as defined below.

More precisely, for each \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), some fixed width \(k\ge3\) must exclude every machine \(M\) and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) satisfying, for every valid \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\),
\[
\Pr_r[M(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)=\operatorname{SAT}(F)]\ge\frac23,
\qquad
\forall r:\quad
t_M(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)
\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d.
\]
The machine returns a decision bit. The width may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed before the machine and the input are quantified.

This card uses the standard bounded-error Turing-machine formulation explicitly named RSETH in the later primary source’s \(\mathrm{BPTIME}\) definition. The original 2018 survey states its hypothesis under a logarithmic-word RAM convention. The choice of the later formulation is explicit; equivalence to a literal logarithmic-address-space interpretation of that earlier RAM convention is not asserted.
cards.why: This hypothesis is a central proposed barrier for randomized algorithms: it specifies whether exhaustive assignment search becomes essentially optimal as clause width increases. It supports fine-grained conditional lower bounds where randomized target algorithms must also be excluded, and links exact satisfiability complexity to tight complexity questions for other fundamental problems. A proof or refutation would change a major foundation of modern algorithmic hardness, well beyond the performance of one SAT solver.

cards.title: ETH versus Gap-ETH
cards.formal:
Is the implication
\[
 \mathsf{ETH}_{\mathrm{det}}\ \Longrightarrow\quad
 \mathsf{GapETH}_{\mathrm{det}}
\]
true for the following precise hypotheses?
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathsf{ETH}_{\mathrm{det}}
   &:\quad \exists\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ 
           \neg\operatorname{FastSAT}(\eta),\\
 \mathsf{GapETH}_{\mathrm{det}}
   &:\quad \exists B\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ 
           \exists\delta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ 
           \exists\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ 
           \neg\operatorname{FastGapSAT}(B,\delta,\eta).
\end{aligned}
\]
The fast-algorithm predicates below use deterministic bit computation, exponent parameter equal to the number of variables, and a fixed polynomial factor in the whole binary input length. The gap predicate concerns formulas with at most \(Bn\) clauses and the promise of full satisfiability or value at most \(1-\delta\).
cards.why: The implication would show that exponential hardness of exact satisfiability already supplies the sparse constant-gap hardness used in many fine-grained approximation lower bounds.

cards.title: Hyperclique Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is the following bounded-error randomized Hyperclique Hypothesis true? For every fixed pair of integers \(h\ge3\) and \(k>h\), and every constant real \(\epsilon>0\), there is no uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and constant \(T\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge k\) and every simple \(h\)-uniform hypergraph \(H\) on \([n]\), \(A\) outputs one bit deciding whether \(H\) contains a \(k\)-clique, runs for at most \(Tn^{k-\epsilon}\) steps on every execution, and is correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on that input. The dense representation, permitted instructions and word size are fixed below. The program and constants may depend on \(h,k,\epsilon\), but not on \(n\), the input hypergraph or the random outcomes.
cards.why: A principal fine-grained hypothesis for higher-order combinatorial interactions, supporting conditional lower bounds beyond ordinary graph clique and shortest paths.

cards.title: Disjunction of randomized SETH, integer APSP and 3SUM hypotheses
cards.formal:
Is the following disjunction true in the uniform randomized word-RAM models defined below?
\[
H_{\mathrm{SAT}}\ \lor\ H_{\mathrm{APSP}}\ \lor\ H_{\mathrm{3SUM}},
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_{\mathrm{SAT}}&:\quad
 \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists k\ge3:
 \neg\operatorname{FastSAT}(k,\varepsilon),\\
H_{\mathrm{APSP}}&:\quad
 \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists c\ge1:
 \neg\operatorname{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon),\\
H_{\mathrm{3SUM}}&:\quad
 \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1):
 \neg\operatorname{Fast3SUM}(\varepsilon)?
\end{aligned}
\]
The quantified \(k,c\) are integers. The predicates assert algorithms with respective time bounds \(K2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}(L+1)^d\), \(Kn^{3-\varepsilon}\), and \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\), and success probability at least \(2/3\) on each input. Each time bound holds on every random tape.
cards.why: Many precise algorithmic lower bounds rest on one of these three separate assumptions. Establishing their disjunction would support results that are hard under all three while requiring less than any individually chosen hypothesis. Refuting it would require fixed-exponent algorithmic advances across satisfiability, weighted shortest paths and integer sum detection.

cards.title: Linear-size Circuit-SAT below exhaustive search
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a rational \(\delta_c\in(0,1)\), a constant \(K_c\ge1\), an integer \(d_c\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A_c\) that decides satisfiability of every explicitly given Boolean circuit with \(n\ge1\) input variables and at most \(cn\) gates within
\[
K_c\,2^{(1-\delta_c)n}(L+1)^{d_c}
\]
Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(L\) is the full binary encoding length. Gates are binary AND and OR and unary NOT, with unrestricted depth and fan-out. The answer must be correct on every allowed circuit.
cards.why: A broad satisfiability-speedup question connecting fine-grained algorithms with unrestricted circuit lower bounds.

cards.title: Nondeterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal:
Is the Nondeterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis false? Precisely, is there a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every integer \(k\ge3\), there are a uniform nondeterministic machine \(M_k\) and integers \(C_k\ge1,d_k\ge0\) with the following properties?

For every \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\), \(M_k\) has an accepting computation if and only if \(F\) is unsatisfiable, and every computation branch halts within
\[
C_k\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_k}
\]
steps. Here \(n(F)\) is the number of distinct variables, \(L(F)\) is the explicit binary input length, and the machine model is defined below.

The same positive saving \(\varepsilon\) must work for every fixed width \(k\). The machine and its constants may depend on \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on the individual input. The negation of this displayed existence statement is NSETH itself.
cards.why: A nondeterministic computation can guess a certificate that a formula has no satisfying assignment, but it must verify that certificate without random errors. A uniform exponential saving would change the limits of fine-grained reductions and would have consequences for circuit lower bounds. The question therefore tests a barrier that is stronger than the difficulty of finding a satisfying assignment deterministically.

cards.title: Fine-grained comparability of permanent and SETH
cards.formal: Are exact binary-matrix permanent computation and the family of fixed-width satisfiability problems comparable by deterministic fine-grained oracle reductions at the \(2^n\) scale? Ask whether at least one of the following two fixed directions exists. In the SAT-to-permanent direction, for every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), there is a rational \(0<\delta<1\), independent of the clause width, such that for every fixed \(k\ge3\) a reduction decides \(k\)-SAT on \(n\) variables, using an exact binary-permanent oracle, with ordinary bit time \(T\) and queried matrix dimensions \(N_j\) satisfying \[T+\sum_j2^{(1-\varepsilon)N_j}\le C\,2^{(1-\delta)n}(L+1)^a.\] Here \(L\) is the formula encoding length, and \(C,a\) and the reduction may depend on \(\varepsilon,k\). In the permanent-to-SAT direction, for every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), there exist rational \(0<\delta<1\), a fixed \(k\ge3\), and a reduction computing the permanent of every \(N\times N\) binary matrix using a \(k\)-SAT decision oracle, with queried variable counts \(n_j\) and \[T+\sum_j2^{(1-\varepsilon)n_j}\le C\,2^{(1-\delta)N}(N+1)^a.\] In this direction \(\delta,k,C,a\) and the reduction may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(N\) or the matrix. A single direction must satisfy its condition for every \(\varepsilon\).
cards.why: The permanent is a canonical exact counting problem with a natural exponential algorithm, whereas SETH organizes the difficulty of satisfiability decision across clause widths. A quantitatively efficient connection would reveal whether their exponential barriers have a common source. Ordinary counting completeness does not determine how a constant improvement in one exponential base transfers to the other problem.

cards.title: Hitting Set conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the randomized Hitting Set conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(c\ge1\) such that no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides the following problem in worst-case time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)? The input is two lists \(A,B\), each of \(n\) subsets of \([d]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). Decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \forall b\in B:\quad a\cap b\ne\varnothing.\]
The chosen set must be one of the supplied sets in \(A\). This is the source's fine-grained two-list problem, not the general optimization problem of selecting a small hitting set from the universe.
cards.why: This hypothesis captures a quadratic barrier with an existential choice followed by a universal test. It supports fine-grained lower bounds for graph radius, centers and quantified geometric problems where the more familiar two-existential-quantifier orthogonal-vectors hypothesis does not directly match the task. Settling it would clarify the role of quantifier order in fine-grained complexity.

cards.title: Min-Weight k-Clique hypothesis
cards.formal: Is the following hypothesis true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\) and every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is no uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^{100k},n^{100k}]\), outputs a minimum-total-edge-weight \(k\)-clique, or correctly reports that no \(k\)-clique exists, with probability at least \(2/3\), and has worst-case running time \(O(n^{k-\varepsilon})\). The time bound is over both input graphs and all random choices, with \(k\) fixed and \(n\to\infty\). This is the fixed weight-range version of Hypothesis 7 in the cited survey.
cards.why: Weighted clique optimization is a basic way to express interactions among several selected objects. Its conjectured exponent underlies exact-time lower bounds for problems far beyond clique detection. A polynomial exponent improvement would change those conditional barriers, while a proof would establish strong unconditional limits for a family of explicit polynomial-time tasks. The question also separates the difficulty of arbitrary edge costs from that of merely requiring all pairwise adjacencies.

cards.title: NC-SETH for polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits
cards.formal:
Is the following randomized NC-SETH true?

For every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there exists an integer \(k\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized algorithm can decide satisfiability, with error at most \(1/3\) on every instance, for all \(n\)-input Boolean circuits of size at most \((n+2)^k\) and depth at most \(\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^k\) in time
\[
K\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}(L+1)^d
\]
for any fixed constants \(K\ge1\), integer \(d\ge0\) and word-length constant in the specified RAM model. Here \(n\ge2\) counts inputs, \(L\) is the full encoded circuit length, and the runtime bound is worst-case over random tapes.
cards.why: A circuit can express much more computation compactly than a bounded-width formula. The question asks whether even this structured parallel-computation representation can be analyzed for satisfiability with a fixed exponential saving, and provides a basis for lower bounds on familiar sequence problems.

cards.title: Directed unweighted APSP below \(n^{5/2}\)
cards.formal:
Do there exist real constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) and \(K>0\), an integer \(d\ge4\), and one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A\) such that, for every explicitly given unweighted directed graph \(G\) on \([n]\), \(n\ge2\), every execution uses at most
\[
 K n^{5/2-\varepsilon}
\]
instructions, outputs an explicit \(n\times n\) matrix \(D\), and satisfies
\[
 \Pr\bigl[\forall u,v\in[n],\ D[u,v]=\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\bigr]\ge\frac23?
\]
The machine has word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\); distances, unreachable pairs and all charged costs use the conventions below. The claim has no matrix-multiplication or other computational hypothesis.
cards.why: Determine whether direction alone enforces a central exponent barrier for exact distances when every edge has unit length. The target concerns all algorithms and an explicit matrix, making it a basic test of fine-grained graph complexity.

cards.title: Consequences of linear-time Orthogonal Vectors
cards.formal:
Does essentially-linear deterministic time for Orthogonal Vectors in every fixed polylogarithmic dimension regime imply failure of the Exponential Time Hypothesis? With \(\mathsf{EL}_{\mathrm{OV}}\) and \(\mathsf{ETH}\) defined below, the proposition is
\[
\mathsf{EL}_{\mathrm{OV}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \neg\mathsf{ETH}.
\]
Equivalently, does \(\mathsf{ETH}\) imply that some such dimension regime lacks deterministic \(O(N^{1+\varepsilon})\)-time algorithms for at least one \(\varepsilon>0\)? Here \(N\) is the complete binary input length. The target is a logical implication about algorithm existence, not a request to assume that the premise already holds. The explicit dimension quantifiers and binary encodings below complete the source's informal polylogarithmic-dimension formulation, while retaining its deterministic multitape Turing-machine model.
cards.why: A proof would base some polynomial-time hardness on ETH rather than the stronger SETH assumption, clarifying how much exponential hardness is needed for a widely used fine-grained benchmark. A refutation would expose a substantive separation between these algorithmic barriers. The importance lies in the relationship between two major hypotheses, beyond an improvement to one OV algorithm.

cards.title: Does logarithmic-dimension OV hardness imply Hitting Set hardness?
cards.formal:
Does the implication
\[
\mathrm{OVH}_{\log}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{HSH}_{\log}
\]
hold for the randomized logarithmic-dimension hypotheses defined below?

These are the hypotheses used in TCS-6596 and TCS-6599: the dimension is \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\), and a refutation of either hypothesis may use a separate uniform algorithm for each fixed \(c\), with one common positive exponent saving. Equivalently, does failure of the Hitting Set hypothesis imply failure of the Orthogonal Vectors hypothesis?
cards.why: Orthogonal Vectors asks for one disjoint pair, while Hitting Set asks for one candidate that intersects every set in the other list. Understanding whether their hardness assumptions imply one another would connect two different sources of fine-grained lower bounds, particularly for graph distance problems.

cards.title: Exact-Weight k-Clique hypothesis
cards.formal:
Is the following hypothesis true?

For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\) and every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\), there is no bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm that decides Exact-Weight \(k\)-Clique on all \(n\)-vertex inputs in worst-case time \(O(n^{k-\varepsilon})\).

An input is a simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\ge k\) and integer edge weights
\[
w:E\longrightarrow\{-n^{100k},\ldots,n^{100k}\}.
\]
The required output is YES exactly when there is a set \(S\subseteq[n]\) of \(k\) distinct vertices such that
\[
\binom S2\subseteq E,\qquad
\sum_{e\in\binom S2}w(e)=0.
\]
The algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. Its time bound applies to every random outcome. The explicit machine and input conventions are given below.
cards.why: Requiring the edge weights of a clique to cancel exactly couples all its edges in a way that ordinary clique detection does not capture. The hypothesis asks whether this numerical constraint prevents a fixed polynomial improvement over enumeration.
