Its consequences connect the cost of finding weighted structures with output-sensitive enumeration and other fine-grained lower bounds.

cards.title: Balanced dense NFA Acceptance Hypothesis
cards.formal: For the balanced dense binary NFA acceptance problem and word-RAM model below, is it true that for every constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) no uniform randomized algorithm has worst-case running time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) and error at most \(1/3\) on every input?
cards.why: This is a central unresolved barrier for general automata simulation with consequences across language processing and fine-grained complexity.

cards.title: A fine-grained reduction from logarithmic-dimension Hitting Set to 3SUM
cards.formal:
Is there a bounded-error randomized fine-grained Turing reduction from logarithmic-dimension Hitting Set to integer 3SUM, with a common exponent saving across all fixed dimension constants? Precisely, is the following true?

For every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there is a rational \(\delta\in(0,1)\) such that, for every integer \(c\ge1\), there exist a uniform classical randomized oracle algorithm \(\mathcal R_{\varepsilon,c}\) and constants \(K,B\ge1\) with this guarantee: on every Hitting Set input consisting of two lists of \(n\ge2\) subsets of \([\lceil c\log_2n\rceil]\), the algorithm, with an exact 3SUM oracle, gives the correct answer with probability at least \(2/3\), and on every execution has charged cost
\[
T+\sum_{j=1}^{q}m_j^{\,2-\varepsilon}\le K(n+2)^{\,2-\delta}.
\]
Here \(T\) counts all local word-RAM instructions and \(m_j\) is the number of integers in its \(j\)-th oracle query. The exact problems and all cost conventions are below.
cards.why: Hitting Set and 3SUM underpin different families of conditional lower bounds. A reduction preserving fixed exponent savings would connect their hardness assumptions despite the universal quantifier over the second Hitting Set list.

cards.title: Time exponents for multiple-string LCS over fixed alphabets
cards.formal: Determine the optimal deterministic polynomial-time exponent function \(\tau(\sigma,k)\) for longest common subsequence of \(k\) strings over an alphabet of size \(\sigma\), on the entire domain \(D=\{(\sigma,k)\in\mathbb N^2:\sigma\ge2,\ k\ge2\}\). For each fixed pair, let \[\tau(\sigma,k)=\inf\bigl\{c\ge0:\ \exists A\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \forall(s_1,\ldots,s_k)\in(\{1,\ldots,\sigma\}^{\le n})^k,\ A\text{ outputs an LCS within }Cn^c\text{ operations}\bigr\},\] where \(A\) ranges over the correct uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithms defined below, and \(n,n_0\) are integers. Supply a function \(g:D\to\mathbb R\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|g(\sigma,k)-\tau(\sigma,k)|\le1/100\) for every \((\sigma,k)\in D\). This explicitly broadens the source’s proposed constant-fraction exponent improvement into determination of the underlying exponent function; it is not claimed to be equivalent to that yes/no question.
cards.why: Multiple-string alignment has a rapidly growing dependence on the number of sequences, even though it is polynomial-time solvable when that number is fixed. A small alphabet may constrain the combinatorial choices enough to change the leading exponent. Determining the full exponent function would separate the cost of coordinating many strings from the expressiveness supplied by a growing alphabet, and would sharpen the fine-grained limits behind exact sequence comparison.

cards.title: Subgraph detection with a sublinear treewidth exponent on some unbounded class
cards.formal:
Does there exist a recursively enumerable class \(\mathcal H\) of finite simple undirected graphs with unbounded treewidth, a computable function \(f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), a computable rational-valued function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge2}\) with
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{g(t)}t=0,
\]
and one uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every pattern \(H\in\mathcal H\) with \(k\ge1\) vertices and every host graph \(G\) with \(n\ge1\) vertices, decides whether \(G\) contains a subgraph isomorphic to \(H\) in at most
\[
f(k)(n+2)^{g(\operatorname{tw}(H))}
\]
bit operations? This is unweighted, uncolored, non-induced subgraph detection. The multiplicative factor may depend arbitrarily but computably on pattern size; the exponent must be sublinear in its treewidth.
cards.why: Treewidth controls the exponent of the generic dynamic-programming algorithm for subgraph detection. Finding an unbounded pattern class with a sublinear exponent would reveal a structural source of tractability that treewidth by itself misses.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm P.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
cards.why: This asks whether independent random bits increase the set of total decision problems solvable efficiently. An equality would identify deterministic and randomized polynomial-time decision power; a separation would exhibit an inherent benefit of randomness even when a different deterministic algorithm is allowed.

cards.title: L versus BPL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, is it true that
\[\forall S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \Longrightarrow\ S\in\mathrm L?\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPL}\) consists of total decision languages recognized with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by one uniform randomized machine using logarithmic work space and polynomial time on every input and every random tape. The target is a uniform deterministic logarithmic-work-space decider for each such language.
cards.why: This asks whether randomness adds computational power when an algorithm can remember only logarithmically many bits of an arbitrarily long input. An equality would permit deterministic bounded-memory decision whenever bounded-error randomized decision is possible; a separation would show an inherent memory advantage of randomness.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic finite-program algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,D\ge1\) with the following property? For every \(n,w\ge2\) and \(p\ge1\), all integers, the algorithm specifies an integer seed length \(s=s(n,w,p)\ge0\) and a function
\[G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}\]
with \(s\le Cq\), where \(q=\lceil\log _2 n\rceil+\lceil\log _2 w\rceil+p\), such that every length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program \(B\) satisfies
\[\left|\Pr_{u\sim U_s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\sim U_n}[B(z)=1]\right|\le 2^{-p}?\]
Here \(U_k\) is the uniform distribution on the \(2^k\) binary strings of length \(k\). Require \(A\) to compute both \(s(n,w,p)\) and any requested bit \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), in at most \(Dq\) work bits and \((nw2^p)^D\) steps per call, in the model below. The same algorithm, constants and generator family must work for every parameter triple and every permitted program.
cards.why: A solution would give a uniform optimal-seed pseudorandom distribution for arbitrary small-memory computations and imply L = BPL. It would close the central gap between the existence of short seeds and their computation in small space, beyond the structural restrictions and weighted approximations covered by current results.

cards.title: P versus RP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\)? In other words, can randomness be removed from every polynomial-time decision algorithm that never accepts a false instance and accepts each true instance with probability at least one half?

Let \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) be any language for which there is one probabilistic Turing machine \(A\), with a polynomial worst-case time bound on every random tape, such that
\[x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr[A(x)=1]\ge\tfrac12,\qquad x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr[A(x)=1]=0.\]
Must there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(D\) and constants \(C>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every binary string \(x\),
\[D(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)\qquad\text{within }C(|x|+1)^a\text{ steps}?\]
The machine and constants may depend on the language, but not on its particular input.
cards.why: This is a central question about whether random choices enlarge efficient decision power even when false acceptances are forbidden. It tests a basic source of randomized algorithmic speed and connects the construction of deterministic algorithms with strong circuit lower bounds and the broader boundary between finding and verifying solutions.

cards.title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
cards.formal:
Do there exist universal constants \(C,B\ge1\), an integer \(b\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(\mathcal A\) with the following property? For every integer pair \(N\ge2\), \(2\le s\le N\), given the pair in binary, \(\mathcal A\) outputs an explicitly listed rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times N}\), with an integer row count \(m\ge1\), in at most \(BN^b\) Turing-machine steps, such that
\[m\le C s\ln(eN/s)\]
and
\[\forall x\in\mathbb R^N\text{ with }|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\le s,\qquad \frac23\|x\|_2^2\le\|Ax\|_2^2\le\frac43\|x\|_2^2?\]
The complete binary output must also have length at most \(BN^b\). The constants and the algorithm are common to every pair \((N,s)\).
cards.why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.

cards.title: AM versus NP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm{AM}=\mathrm{NP}\)? Equivalently, does every language having an Arthur–Merlin protocol admit polynomial-length certificates checked deterministically in polynomial time?

For a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), an Arthur–Merlin protocol is specified by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and polynomially bounded lengths \(p(n),q(n)\). Arthur draws a uniform public string \(r\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\); after seeing \(x\) and \(r\), Merlin may choose a reply \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\). With \(n=|x|\), require
\[x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\ge\tfrac23,\]
\[x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\le\tfrac13.\]
Must there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) and a polynomially bounded length \(s(n)\) such that, for every binary string \(x\),
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(|x|)}:\ W(x,z)=1?\]
The resulting verifier and its polynomial bounds may depend on \(L\), but must work uniformly at all input lengths.
cards.why: This asks whether short randomized interaction gives more verification power than static certificates. It is a fundamental derandomization question beyond decision algorithms, with consequences for certifying graph nonisomorphism and with close links to nondeterministic circuit hardness.

cards.title: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}\) unconditionally? Here the subexponential class is the intersection
\[\mathrm{SUBEXP}=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(2^{n^{1/k}}\right).\]
Thus, for every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decidable with two-sided bounded error in randomized polynomial time, and for every integer \(k\ge1\), must there exist a deterministic algorithm deciding \(L\) on every input in time \(O(2^{n^{1/k}})\)? The algorithm and the constant in its time bound may depend on \(L,k\). The target selects the subexponential question in the source's Open Problem 3.4; its separate quasipolynomial-time question is stronger.
cards.why: This asks whether randomness can provide a much larger speedup than the usual derandomization conjectures predict, even after allowing deterministic time far beyond polynomial. An unconditional simulation would move the general worst-case upper bound into the source’s much smaller subexponential class. A counterexample would establish a major separation between randomized and deterministic computation.

cards.title: Does arithmetic formula hardness derandomize identity testing?
cards.formal: Does \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\Rightarrow D_{\mathrm{form}}\) hold over \(\mathbb Q\)? Here \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\) asserts that there exists an explicit family \(f_m\in\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_m]\) of multilinear polynomials with \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)=m^{\omega(1)}\), in the precise sense below. The assertion \(D_{\mathrm{form}}\) is that, for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), polynomial identity testing for unrestricted arithmetic formulas has a uniform deterministic algorithm taking time \(2^{O(N^{\varepsilon})}\), where \(N\) is the input's bit length. This card selects the hardness-to-derandomization branch of the source's two-direction question; it asks for subexponential time, without requiring polynomial time.
cards.why: This asks whether hardness against arithmetic computation without shared subexpressions already suffices to remove randomness from identity testing in that same fundamental model. A resolution would clarify whether the central circuit hardness–randomness principle survives the restriction to formulas, connecting algebraic lower bounds with deterministic symbolic computation.

cards.title: Pseudorandom generators from hitting-set generators
cards.formal:
Does the existence of a polynomial-time hitting-set generator secure against all polynomial-size Boolean circuits imply the existence of a polynomial-time pseudorandom generator secure against all such circuits, in the cryptographic regime defined below? In symbols, decide
\[
\bigl(\exists H\;\operatorname{HSG}(H)\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\exists G\;\operatorname{PRG}(G)\bigr).
\]
Both generators must be uniform, have a seed shorter than their output, and meet their respective security conditions with negligible error. Their seed lengths, negligible functions and polynomial running-time bounds may differ. This is an implication between existence statements; it does not require an algorithm that compiles a given hitting-set generator into a pseudorandom generator.
cards.why: This asks whether hitting dense sets and reproducing acceptance probabilities have the same existential power when a uniform efficient generator must withstand arbitrarily stronger polynomial-size tests. Pseudorandom generators are foundational cryptographic objects connected to one-way functions, while the weaker hitting guarantee arises naturally from errorless average-case hardness. A resolution would clarify whether these two notions represent distinct assumptions about computational randomness, rather than merely improve the parameters of one construction.

cards.title: Uniform PRGs from exponential-time hardness
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPSUBEXP}\) imply the following generator statement? There are integers \(C,k,a\ge1\), a constant \(A\ge1\), and a single deterministic generator algorithm which, for every \(m\ge2\), maps \(d(m)=C\lceil\log_2m\rceil^k\) seed bits to \(m\) output bits in time at most \(A(m+2^{d(m)})^a\), and has this security property: for every fixed uniform probabilistic distinguisher \(T\) running in time \(O(m)\), there are infinitely many \(m\) such that \[\left|\Pr[T(G_m(U_{d(m)}))=1]-\Pr[T(U_m)=1]\right|\le \frac1m.\] The generator is independent of \(T\), and the infinitely many successful lengths may depend on \(T\).
cards.why: Hardness against algorithms is a weaker kind of premise than hardness against arbitrary circuits. A generator with only polylogarithmically many seed bits would turn strong uniform hardness into correspondingly fast average-case derandomization. The remaining gap tests how much of the familiar nonuniform hardness-versus-randomness tradeoff survives with uniform assumptions.

cards.title: Explicit near-optimal vertex expanders
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every rational \(\delta>0\), there exists an integer \(d_0\ge3\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge d_0\), there exist a rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), real \(K>0\), integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) which, for every integer \(j\ge1\) supplied in unary, outputs a finite simple undirected \(d\)-regular graph \(G_j\) within \(K(j+1)^a\) bit operations, with strictly increasing vertex counts \(n_j=|V(G_j)|\), and such that \[|\Gamma_{G_j}(S)\setminus S|\ \ge\ (d-2-\delta)|S|\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V(G_j)\text{ with }1\le |S|\le\eta n_j?\]
cards.why: Random regular graphs have almost the largest possible external neighborhood for every small set. Matching that additive guarantee by deterministic constructions would sharpen a central benchmark for expanders, with consequences for combinatorial structures underlying coding, routing and pseudorandomness.

cards.title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
cards.formal:
Does there exist an integer \(C\ge0\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) defining functions
\[
E_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
such that, for every \(n\) and every two independent probability distributions \(X,Y\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\) with
\[
H_\infty(X),H_\infty(Y)\ge\log_2 n+C,
\]
we have
\[
\left|\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]-\frac12\right|\le\frac1{100}?
\]
The algorithm receives only \(n\) and the two strings. The same additive constant, finite program and polynomial running-time bound must work for all lengths and all eligible distributions.
cards.why: The additive threshold asks whether polynomial-time evaluation can match the entropy scale available without an efficiency restriction, including its leading coefficient. It is a basic question about converting two independent imperfect sources into a nearly unbiased bit and has consequences for explicit Ramsey constructions.

cards.title: Seeded extraction with constant total entropy loss
cards.formal:
Do there exist an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors and absolute constants \(C,\Delta\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\), the family supplies a function
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
with
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad 0\le k+d(n,k)-m(n,k)\le\Delta,\]
and, for every distribution \(X\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) with min-entropy at least \(k\),
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). Explicitness means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(n\), with the same algorithm and polynomial for all \(n,k\). This is the constant-total-entropy-loss question in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.41.
cards.why: This asks whether an efficient general randomness purifier can preserve all but a constant number of the available random bits while using only a logarithmic seed. In applications that enumerate seeds or pay exponentially for entropy loss, the additive loss determines a multiplicative cost. Resolving the question would distinguish information-theoretic feasibility from the achievable efficiency of explicit extraction.

cards.title: Extraction with log n plus constant seed length
cards.formal:
Is there an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors with error at most \(1/100\), a rational constant \(\gamma\in(0,1]\) and an integer constant \(C\ge0\) such that, for all integers \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\),
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\to\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)},\qquad d(n,k)\le\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+C,\qquad m(n,k)\ge\lfloor\gamma k\rfloor?\]
For every distribution \(X\) on \(n\)-bit strings satisfying \(H_{\infty}(X)\ge k\), and a uniform seed independent of \(X\), the required guarantee is
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100.\]
The family, \(C\), \(\gamma\) and its polynomial evaluation bound must be uniform across \(n,k\). This selects the main \(m=\Omega(k)\) target in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.42, retaining its weaker polynomial-output alternative as context.
cards.why: A logarithmic seed is often enumerated over all possibilities. Fixing its leading coefficient at one makes that enumeration linear in the source length up to a constant factor, instead of an unspecified polynomial. Achieving substantial output at that seed length for arbitrary min-entropy would sharpen a central resource bound in explicit randomness extraction.

cards.title: Promise-BPP derandomization implying EXP circuit hardness
cards.formal: Does complete deterministic derandomization of bounded-error polynomial-time promise problems force a deterministic exponential-time language to require superpolynomial Boolean circuits? Precisely, is the implication \[\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\] true?
cards.why: Determine whether full promise-problem derandomization necessarily yields deterministic exponential-time circuit hardness, closing a central gap between efficient algorithms and nonuniform lower bounds.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{NEXP}\) circuit hardness from promise derandomization
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true?
\[
\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists L\in\mathrm{NEXP}\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N:
\operatorname{CC}_L(n)>2^{\,n^{1/k}}.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{CC}_L(n)\) is the minimum size of an unrestricted deterministic Boolean circuit computing membership in \(L\) on every binary input of length \(n\). One language and one positive exponent must work for infinitely many lengths. There is no restriction on circuit depth and no uniformity requirement on the circuits.
cards.why: This would sharpen a central converse in hardness versus randomness: removing efficient randomness would force a substantially stronger kind of circuit hardness than is presently supplied by the standard implication. The distinction matters because quantitative hardness controls the strength of pseudorandom constructions, and nonuniform circuits can exploit information unavailable to a single uniform program.

cards.title: Pseudodeterministic construction of primes at every length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a constant \(c\), and a sequence of primes \((p_{n})_{n\geq2}\), with \(2^{n-1}\leq p_{n}<2^{n}\), such that \(A\) runs in time \(O(n^{c})\) on input \(1^{n}\) and \[\Pr[A(1^{n})=p_{n}]\geq 2/3\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq2?\]
cards.why: A canonical prime construction tests how far efficient randomized search can be made reproducible without fully removing randomness. It is a prominent concrete problem connecting derandomization, explicit constructions and computational number theory; extending the infinitely-often theorem would close its remaining length-coverage gap.

cards.title: Subpolynomial-seed pseudorandom generators for \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[2]\)
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), is there an unconditional, mildly explicit generator family
\[
G_{k,m}:\{0,1\}^{d_k(m)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m}\qquad(m\ge1)
\]
whose integer seed length satisfies \(d_k(m)=m^{o(1)}\), and which fools every depth-at-most-\(k\), size-at-most-\(m\) \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[2]\) circuit on \(m\) input bits with error at most \(1/4\)?

Precisely, for every such circuit \(C\),
\[
\left|\Pr_{s\sim U_{d_k(m)}}[C(G_{k,m}(s))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_m}[C(x)=1]\right|\le1/4.
\]
The generator for a given \(k,m\) must work simultaneously for all the indicated circuits and cannot depend on \(C\). “Mildly explicit” means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(m\) and \(2^{d_k(m)}\), with the polynomial permitted to depend on \(k\).
cards.why: Adding parity gates is a basic step beyond constant-depth AND/OR circuits, yet existing worst-case lower bounds do not supply the strong average-case guarantees used by standard generator constructions. A generator with the requested seed would permit deterministic seed enumeration in subexponential time for the entire fixed-depth class. The question probes a central gap between proving circuit lower bounds and turning them into useful pseudorandomness.

cards.title: Deterministic linear representations of transversal matroids
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm that, given any finite bipartite graph with its two sides specified, constructs a rational matrix representing its transversal matroid in polynomial bit time?

Precisely, let \(a,b\) be nonnegative integers and let
\[
G=([a],[b],E),\qquad E\subseteq[a]\times[b],
\]
where the two labeled sides are disjoint copies and \([0]=\varnothing\). Let \(r(G)\) be the maximum size of a matching in \(G\). The required output is one explicit matrix
\[
M\in\mathbb Q^{\,r(G)\times a}
\]
whose column \(j\) corresponds to vertex \(j\) on the first side, such that
\[
\forall S\subseteq[a]\quad
\left[\exists\text{ injective }f:S\to[b]\ 
       \forall j\in S\ (j,f(j))\in E\right]
\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\left[\text{the columns }(M_{\ast j})_{j\in S}
       \text{ are linearly independent over }\mathbb Q\right].
\]
The same matrix must satisfy this equivalence for all subsets simultaneously.

With the encodings and deterministic machine model below, the algorithmic assertion is
\[
\exists A\ \exists C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ 
\forall a,b\in\mathbb N\ \forall E\subseteq[a]\times[b]\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,\operatorname{enc}(G),y,C(L(G)+1)^d)
\land \operatorname{Correct}(G,y)
\bigr).
\]
Here \(A\) is one fixed finite deterministic program, \(L(G)\) is the input's bit length, and \(\operatorname{Correct}\) checks the full matrix requirement above. The constants do not depend on the graph or its rank. This formulation makes explicit the rational-field and bit-complexity setting surrounding the source question; it does not ask for representations over every finite field or permit unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded numbers.
cards.why: This asks whether randomness can be removed from a basic translation between matching constraints and linear algebra. Such representations support matroid algorithms and, through related gammoid representations, several central preprocessing and cut-representation results. A polynomial-time construction would supply one exact algebraic representation of all independence relations without random choices. A negative result would establish a computational obstruction to this widely used translation, despite the existence of small rational representations.

cards.title: Universal determinant evaluations for bipartite matching
cards.formal:
Can one construct, in uniform deterministic NC, an integer table
\[\alpha^{(m)}=(\alpha_{i,j}^{(m)})_{i,j\in[m]}\in\{0,1,\ldots,m2^{m^2}\}^{m^2}\]
for each integer \(m\ge1\), such that the same table works for every simple bipartite graph \(G\) with labeled vertex classes \([m]\) and \([m]\)? Precisely, define the integer matrix
\[A_G(\alpha)_{i,j}=\begin{cases}\alpha_{i,j}&\text{if }(i,j)\in E(G),\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
The requirement is
\[\forall G,\qquad \det A_G(\alpha^{(m)})\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G\text{ has a perfect matching}.\]
The construction receives only \(1^m\), not \(G\). This card selects the NC construction explicitly proposed in Vadhan's Open Problem 3.7; its more permissive request for an efficient or even subexponential sequential construction is not an equivalent target.
cards.why: A universal evaluation table would give a reusable deterministic replacement for all random entries in the classical determinant test for bipartite matching. The same polynomial-size data would preserve every matching-existence test at a given graph size. The source uses NC construction as a particularly strong form of explicitness, connecting this algebraic derandomization object to efficient parallel computation.

cards.title: Optimal-size highly unbalanced lossless expanders
cards.formal:
Do there exist two fixed deterministic algorithms \(P,Q\) and positive integers \(C,c\) with the following properties for every pair of integers \(N,K\) satisfying \(N\ge2\) and \(1\le K\le N\)? Write \(L_{N}=1+\lceil\log_{2} N\rceil\). Algorithm \(P\), on input \((N,K)\), must output positive integers \(D=D(N,K)\) and \(M=M(N,K)\) such that
\[
D\le C L_{N}^{c},\qquad M\le CKD.
\]
Algorithm \(Q\), on input \((N,K,x,j)\) with \(x\in[N]\) and \(j\in[D]\), must output an element \(\Gamma_{N,K}(x,j)\in[M]\). Both the parameter computation and each neighbor computation must take at most \(C L_{N}^{c}\) steps in the uniform bit model defined below. The resulting bipartite multigraph must satisfy
\[
\forall S\subseteq[N],\quad |S|=K\ \Longrightarrow
\left|\{\Gamma_{N,K}(x,j):x\in S,\ j\in[D]\}\right|
\ge\frac{99}{100}DK.
\]
Thus the target is a fully explicit family with polylogarithmic left degree, a right side of size at most a constant times \(KD\), and expansion for every left set of size exactly \(K\). The algorithms and constants are chosen before \(N,K\); they must work uniformly over the entire stated parameter range. Prove this existence statement or its negation.
cards.why: Lossless expansion preserves almost all distinct choices made from an arbitrary input set while compressing their range. A construction with this right-side size and fast neighbor computation would provide lossless condensers with constant entropy overhead, improving a basic resource used in randomness extraction, coding and related algorithms.

cards.title: Lossless condensers with constant output overhead
cards.formal:
Is there an explicit family of functions
\[\operatorname{Con}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\to\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
and absolute integer constants \(C,\Delta\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\),
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad k+d(n,k)\le m(n,k)\le k+d(n,k)+\Delta,\]
and for every distribution \(X\) on \(n\)-bit strings with \(H_{\infty}(X)\ge k\), there is a distribution \(Y_X\) on \(m(n,k)\)-bit strings satisfying
\[H_{\infty}(Y_X)\ge k+d(n,k),\qquad \operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Con}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),Y_X\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). The family must have one deterministic polynomial-time evaluator for all parameters. This is the lossless-condenser formulation of Vadhan's Open Problem 6.35, paired in the source with the expander question 5.36.
cards.why: A lossless condenser compresses an arbitrary weak source while preserving its available randomness. Constant output overhead would leave that randomness concentrated in a string only a constant number of bits longer than its entropy, using a short seed. In graph terms it asks for nearly collision-free expansion with an almost minimal number of right vertices, a useful resource in extraction and data structures.

cards.title: Nontrivial PRGs for logarithmic-degree binary polynomials
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform explicit generator family
\[
G_n:\{0,1\}^{s(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}
\]
and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\),
\[
s(n)\le n-1
\]
and every polynomial \(p:\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb F_2\) of total degree at most \(d(n)=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor\) satisfies
\[
\left|\Pr_{Y\sim U_{s(n)}}[p(G_n(Y))=1]
-\Pr_{X\sim U_n}[p(X)=1]\right|\le\frac1{10}?
\]
The same generator must fool all such polynomials at that length. The seed saving is required at every sufficiently large length, not merely infinitely often.
cards.why: Binary polynomial tests describe algebraic correlations of increasing order. At logarithmic degree the standard seed bounds stop giving a guaranteed saving, even though they are very effective at fixed degree. Resolving the selected minimal saving would cross that precise boundary without assuming the much stronger goal of a polylogarithmic seed.

cards.title: Sub-log-squared seeds for width-four ordered branching programs
cards.formal:
Does there exist a function \(s:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to\mathbb N\) and a uniform explicit family
\[
G_n:\{0,1\}^{s(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}
\]
such that
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{s(n)}{(\log_2 n)^2}=0
\]
and, for every \(n\ge2\) and every width-at-most-four, length-\(n\), standard-order read-once branching program \(B\),
\[
\left|\Pr_{Y\sim U_{s(n)}}[B(G_n(Y))=1]
-\Pr_{X\sim U_n}[B(X)=1]\right|\le\frac1{10}?
\]
The same \(G_n\) must work for all such programs \(B\).
cards.why: Four states are enough to make the best general seed bound resist the improvements known for three states. Resolving this precise transition would clarify a central obstacle in pseudorandomness for sequential, space-limited computation. The question is significant even though its constant-width formulation alone is not an assertion that all randomized logarithmic-space computation can be derandomized.

cards.title: Sub-log-squared seeds for polynomial-size CNFs and DNFs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform explicit family of generators
\[
G_{n,m}:\{0,1\}^{s(n,m)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}
\qquad(n\ge2,\ m\ge n)
\]
such that both of the following hold?

For every \(n,m\) and every CNF or DNF formula \(F\) on \(n\) Boolean variables with size at most \(m\),
\[
\left|\Pr_{Y\sim U_{s(n,m)}}[F(G_{n,m}(Y))=1]
-\Pr_{X\sim U_n}[F(X)=1]\right|\le\frac1{10}.
\]
For every integer \(c\ge1\),
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\max_{\substack{m\in\mathbb N\\n\le m\le n^c}}
\frac{s(n,m)}{(\log_2 n)^2}=0.
\]
Thus every fixed polynomial size regime has sub-log-squared seed length. The generator depends on \(n,m\), but not on the particular formula.
cards.why: CNFs and DNFs are basic Boolean tests with only two layers, but variables can participate in many overlapping constraints. A seed below the log-squared scale would improve unconditional derandomization for this core model and reduce the cost of enumerating all generator outputs to estimate satisfying fractions.

cards.title: Simultaneously optimal averaging samplers
cards.formal:
Do there exist universal constants \(C,D\ge1\) and an explicit family of averaging samplers that simultaneously use an optimal-order number of random bits and samples?

Precisely, for every three integers \(m,a,b\ge1\), set \(\varepsilon=2^{-a}\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\). The family must give integers \(r\ge0,t\ge1\) and a deterministic map
\[
\operatorname{Samp}_{m,a,b}:\{0,1\}^{r}\longrightarrow(\{0,1\}^{m})^{t}
\]
such that
\[
r\le C(m+a+b),\qquad t\le D\,4^{a}b.
\]
For every function \(f:\{0,1\}^{m}\to[0,1]\), with
\(\mu_f=2^{-m}\sum_{z\in\{0,1\}^{m}}f(z)\), require
\[
\Pr_{s\sim U_r}\!\left[
\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^{t}f\!\left(\operatorname{Samp}_{m,a,b}(s)_i\right)
>\mu_f+2^{-a}
\right]\le2^{-b}.
\]
The sampler must satisfy the uniform indexed explicitness convention below, without any computational hardness assumption. The same constants and algorithms must work for all \(m,a,b\).
cards.why: Averaging is a basic way to estimate a large domain using few queries, and reusable sampling constructions also support extractors, codes and interactive proofs. Independent samples have the desired sample count but spend too many random bits, while correlations can save randomness at the cost of more samples. Achieving both bounds in one explicit construction would remove a long-standing loss in this general primitive.

cards.title: Fully explicit bipartite vertex expanders with constant additive loss
cards.formal:
Does there exist an integer \(C\ge1\) with the following property? For every integer \(D_0\ge1\), there is a fixed integer \(D\ge\max\{D_0,C+2\}\) and a fully explicit infinite family of bipartite multigraphs with \(N\) vertices on each side, left degree exactly \(D\), and
\[
 |\Gamma(S)|\ge(D-C)|S|\qquad
 \text{for all }S\subseteq[N]\text{ with }|S|\le\alpha_D N,
\]
where \(\alpha_D>0\) is independent of the family member? The available sizes \(N\) must be unbounded but need not include every positive integer. Full explicitness and all parameter dependencies are defined below.
cards.why: These graphs would spread every small group of left vertices to nearly as many distinct neighbors as its edge budget permits, losing only a fixed amount per vertex even as the degree grows. Computing each neighbor locally would make this structure usable without first constructing a large graph.

cards.title: Optimal PRGs for high-dimensional combinatorial rectangles
cards.formal:
Do there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) and a uniform explicit family
\[
G_{n,d,q}:\{0,1\}^{s(n,d,q)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}
\]
such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every positive divisor \(d\) of \(n\), and every integer \(1\le q\le n\),
\[
s(n,d,q)\le C\left(\frac nd+q+L(n)\right),
\qquad L(n)=1+\left\lceil\log_2\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil,
\]
and every \(d\)-dimensional combinatorial rectangle \(R\) on \(n\) bits satisfies
\[
\left|\Pr_{Y\sim U_{s(n,d,q)}}[G_{n,d,q}(Y)\in R]
-\Pr_{X\sim U_n}[X\in R]\right|\le 2^{-q}?
\]
The constant and the algorithms are independent of all parameters and of \(R\). This is the source’s seed target \(O(n/d+\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log\log n)\), with dyadic error \(\varepsilon=2^{-q}\).
cards.why: Combinatorial rectangles express simultaneous constraints on separate blocks and occur in pseudorandomness, hashing and communication. The question asks for the full dependence on alphabet size, dimension and error, so removing an extra factor would improve a reusable construction across several parameter regimes.

cards.title: Sublinear-seed generators for AC0 with parity gates
cards.formal:
Do there exist two deterministic multitape Turing machines \(R,G\) with the following properties? For all integers \(d,a,n\ge1\), the machine \(R(1^n,1^d,1^a)\) outputs an integer \(r(n,d,a)\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), and, for each seed \(z\in\{0,1\}^{r(n,d,a)}\), the machine \(G(1^n,1^d,1^a,z)\) outputs a string \(G_{n,d,a}(z)\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). For each fixed pair \(d,a\), both computations take at most \(K_{d,a}(n+1)^{b_{d,a}}\) bit steps for some constant \(K_{d,a}>0\) and integer \(b_{d,a}\ge1\), uniformly over all seeds. The seed length satisfies
\[
\forall d,a\ge1\ \forall\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:
\qquad r(n,d,a)\le\eta n.
\]
For every \(n,d,a\ge1\) and every circuit \(C\) on \(n\) input variables with depth at most \(d\), at most \(n^a\) gates, and the gate types defined below, require
\[
\left|\Pr_{z\sim U_{r(n,d,a)}}[C(G_{n,d,a}(z))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[C(x)=1]\right|\le\frac1{10}.
\]
Here \(U_t\) is the uniform distribution on \(\{0,1\}^{t}\). The constant distinguishing error is the documented interpretation of the source question.
cards.why: This asks whether an explicit generator can save an asymptotically complete fraction of the random bits against shallow circuits that freely combine Boolean operations and parity. It isolates a substantial gap between lower bounds for a well-studied circuit class and unconditional, efficiently generated pseudorandomness for that same class.

cards.title: Super-bits from demi-bits
cards.formal:
Does existence of a demi-bit imply existence of a super-bit?

Let \(\mathcal G\) be the set of nonuniform polynomial-size Boolean circuit families \(G=(G_n)_{n\ge1}\) with
\[
G_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n+1}.
\]
For a nondeterministic circuit \(D\) on \(n+1\) ordinary input bits, write
\[
\alpha(D)=\Pr_{y\sim U_{n+1}}[D(y)=1],\qquad
\beta(D,G_n)=\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[D(G_n(x))=1].
\]
Define the two positive-integer hardness measures
\[
H_{\mathrm{dh}}(G_n)=\min\{s:\exists D,\ |D|\le s,\ 
\alpha(D)\ge1/s,\ \beta(D,G_n)=0\},
\]
\[
H_{\mathrm{nh}}(G_n)=\min\{s:\exists D,\ |D|\le s,\ 
\alpha(D)-\beta(D,G_n)\ge1/s\}.
\]
Is the following implication true?
\[
\bigl[\exists G\in\mathcal G\ \exists\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\
\forall n\ge N:\ H_{\mathrm{dh}}(G_n)\ge2^{n^\varepsilon}\bigr]
\ \Longrightarrow\
\bigl[\exists H\in\mathcal G\ \exists\delta>0\ \exists N'\
\forall n\ge N':\ H_{\mathrm{nh}}(H_n)\ge2^{n^\delta}\bigr].
\]
The premise defines a demi-bit and the conclusion a super-bit. The two families, hardness exponents and cutoffs may differ.
cards.why: The problem compares two basic notions of pseudorandomness against nondeterministic tests. Resolving the implication would determine whether a hitting requirement with no false positives on generated strings can yield the stronger distributional guarantee used in nondeterministic natural-proof barriers. It connects foundational generator assumptions, circuit lower-bound methods and proof complexity, rather than only improving a parameter in one construction.

cards.title: A general oracle conversion from two-source extractors to non-malleable extractors
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(C,K,d\), a rational constant \(a\in(0,1]\), and one deterministic oracle algorithm \(T\) with the following property? For every choice of integers \(n\ge1\), \(1\le k\le n\) and \(t\ge1\), set
\[
\varepsilon=2^{-t},\qquad
\kappa=C\bigl(k+\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+t\bigr),\qquad
\eta=C\varepsilon^a.
\]
Whenever \(\kappa\le n\) and \(\eta\le1/10\), every one-bit two-source \((k,\varepsilon)\)-extractor \(E:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), supplied only as an evaluation oracle, yields a one-bit two-source non-malleable \((\kappa,\eta)\)-extractor
\[
N_E(x,y)=T^E(1^n,k,1^t,x,y),
\]
where each evaluation of \(T^E\) takes at most \(K(n+2^t+2)^d\) bit operations and oracle queries as specified below?
cards.why: A general conversion would explain when improvements in ordinary extraction automatically survive adversarial changes to independent weak sources. It would replace similarities between individual constructions by a reusable relation between the two notions.

cards.title: Polynomial-stretch PRGs for depth-two threshold circuits with superlinear gate count
cards.formal:
Do there exist a rational constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\), positive integers \(a,K,n_0\), and one deterministic algorithm \(G\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), writing \(r(n)=\lfloor n^{1-\delta}\rfloor\), the map
\[
G_n:\{0,1\}^{r(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^n,\qquad G_n(s)=G(1^n,s),
\]
is computed in at most \(K(n+2)^a\) bit operations and, for every depth-at-most-two linear-threshold circuit \(C\) on \(n\) input bits with at most \(\lfloor n^{1+\delta}\rfloor\) gates,
\[
\left|\Pr[C(G_n(U_{r(n)}))=1]-\Pr[C(U_n)=1]\right|\le\frac1{10}?
\]
Here \(U_j\) is the uniform distribution on \(j\) independent fair bits. The size bound counts gates, with no separate restriction on their fan-in or the number of wires.
cards.why: Depth-two threshold circuits are a central frontier between individually tractable threshold gates and powerful shallow computation. Fooling a superlinear number of unrestricted-fan-in gates would address a gate-complexity barrier not covered by current sparse-wire derandomization.

cards.title: Does exponential circuit hardness derandomize amplified relational computation?
cards.formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[
\mathsf H_{\rm circ}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathsf{FBPP}_{\log}=\mathsf{FP}.
\]
The hypothesis \(\mathsf H_{\rm circ}\) asserts that some language decidable in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) requires Boolean circuits of size \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) at every sufficiently large input length. The relation classes are defined below on the same universe of polynomially bounded, possibly partial relations. In particular, membership in a relation need not be efficiently verifiable or even decidable.
cards.why: For general search outputs there may be no efficient way to verify a candidate or combine several candidates. This tests whether strong error reduction restores deterministic simulation under a familiar circuit-hardness assumption despite that obstruction.

cards.title: Promise-ZPP versus Promise-BPP derandomization
cards.formal:
Does deterministic polynomial-time solvability of every zero-error randomized promise problem imply deterministic polynomial-time solvability of every bounded-error randomized promise problem?

More precisely, for every probabilistic polynomial-time machine \(M\) and every binary string \(x\), let \(p_i^M(x)=\Pr[M(x)=i]\), for \(i\in\{0,1\}\), and define
\[
Y_Z(M)=\{x:p_1^M(x)\ge1/2,\ p_0^M(x)=0\},\qquad
N_Z(M)=\{x:p_0^M(x)\ge1/2,\ p_1^M(x)=0\},
\]
\[
Y_B(M)=\{x:p_1^M(x)\ge2/3\},\qquad
N_B(M)=\{x:p_1^M(x)\le1/3\}.
\]
For \(S\in\{Z,B\}\), let \(\mathcal D_S\) be the statement that, for every such \(M\), there exists a deterministic polynomial-time decider \(D_M\) satisfying
\[
x\in Y_S(M)\Longrightarrow D_M(x)=1,\qquad
x\in N_S(M)\Longrightarrow D_M(x)=0
\]
for every binary string \(x\). Is the implication \(\mathcal D_Z\Longrightarrow\mathcal D_B\) true?
cards.why: Zero-error computation can certify an answer when it produces one, while bounded-error computation may return a wrong answer. The question asks whether eliminating randomness for all promised certification tasks already removes its power for every efficient randomized decision task. It tests the strength of a broad derandomization principle and the role of promises in transferring that principle.

cards.title: Universal traversal sequences under arbitrary labels
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(C,b\) such that, for every pair of integers \(n,d\ge1\), on input \((1^n,1^d)\) the algorithm outputs in at most \(C(n+d+2)^b\) steps a word \(w=w_1\cdots w_T\in[d]^T\), with \(T\le C(n+d+2)^b\), satisfying the following universal property? For every connected undirected \(d\)-regular port-labeled multigraph on \(n\) vertices in the convention below and every starting vertex \(s\), the walk that successively takes absolute port numbers \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\) visits all vertices.
cards.why: A universal traversal sequence replaces all random choices in a walk by one short deterministic instruction list, without inspecting the graph. Efficient construction under arbitrary local labels would expose how far randomness can be removed when a walker cannot use information about its incoming edge or leave memory on vertices.

cards.title: Linear-seed hardness-to-randomness sampling
cards.formal:
Does there exist one explicit family of point samplers
\[H_{\ell,s}:\{0,1\}^{d(\ell,s)}\to(\{0,1\}^{\ell})^{m(\ell,s)}\]
and absolute constants \(C\ge1\) and rational \(\beta\in(0,1)\) with the following property for every pair of integers \(\ell\ge1\), \(s\ge2\)? The lengths obey
\[d(\ell,s)\le C\ell,\qquad \max\{1,\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\}\le m(\ell,s)\le s.\]
For every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{\ell}\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying
\[\forall B\text{ of size at most }s,\quad\Pr_{x\sim U_{\ell}}[B(x)=f(x)]\le\tfrac12+\tfrac1s,\]
form the \(m\)-bit generator
\[G_f(z)=f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_1)\,f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_2)\cdots f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_m).\]
Must it then satisfy
\[\forall D\text{ of size at most }m,\quad\bigl|\Pr_{z\sim U_d}[D(G_f(z))=1]-\Pr_{u\sim U_m}[D(u)=1]\bigr|\le1/m?\]
The circuits, explicitness and probability spaces are defined below. The sampler is chosen independently of \(f\); each output bit of \(G_f\) is exactly one evaluation of \(f\) at the corresponding sampled point.
cards.why: This asks whether strong average-case hardness can be converted into many pseudorandom bits while using a seed only a constant factor longer than one input to the hard function, and preserving an especially simple evaluation form. Such a result would make the hardness-to-randomness connection more modular and usable across different computational classes. The restriction concerns the structure of the transformation, not merely the final existence of a short-seed generator.

cards.title: Polynomial-time derandomization of randomized \(\mathrm{AC}^0\)
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\subseteq\mathrm P\) hold for polynomial-time-uniform circuit families? Equivalently, must every Boolean function on finite binary strings that is computed with error at most \(1/3\) on each input by a uniform polynomial-size, constant-depth randomized AND–OR circuit family admit an exact deterministic polynomial-time algorithm?
cards.why: Constant-depth AND–OR circuits are a central restricted model for which strong lower bounds are known, yet fully eliminating their randomness in uniform polynomial time remains a distinct challenge. The question tests whether those structural restrictions suffice to remove random choices while allowing a much more flexible deterministic simulator.

cards.title: Promise-AM derandomization via targeted hitting sets
cards.formal: Is the following equivalence true? \[\mathrm{prAM}=\mathrm{prNP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{a uniform nondeterministic polynomial-time targeted hitting-set generator exists for co-nondeterministic Boolean circuits.}\] The promise classes and generator are defined below. The generator receives the full description of the circuit it must hit. It must have at least one successful computation branch on every valid circuit, and every successful branch must output a hitting set whenever the circuit accepts at least half of its ordinary inputs. The target permits multiple distinct valid outputs but no input-dependent advice.
cards.why: Derandomization removes the need for public random challenges in efficient proof protocols. A targeted hitting set is a concrete finite object tailored to a verifier. An equivalence would determine whether eliminating randomness necessarily gives such tailored objects in the Arthur–Merlin setting, extending a known structural characterization of ordinary randomized computation.

cards.title: Derandomization from almost-all-inputs uniform hardness
cards.formal:
Does the following uniform hardness assumption imply \(\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\)?

For every integer \(c\ge1\), there is a total length-preserving function
\[
f_c:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad |f_c(x)|=|x|,
\]
computable by a deterministic polynomial-time machine, such that every probabilistic machine \(A\) running in time \(O((n+1)^c)\) succeeds in producing \(f_c(x)\) on only finitely many individual inputs. Precisely,
\[
\forall c\ge1\ \exists f_c\in\mathrm{FP}\ 
\forall A\in\mathrm{RTIME}((n+1)^c)\ \exists N_A\
\forall x\ (|x|\ge N_A\Longrightarrow
\Pr_r[A(x;r)=f_c(x)]<2/3).
\]
Here \(\mathrm{RTIME}\) denotes the time-bounded randomized string-output machines defined below, without an additional correctness promise. The conclusion means that every bounded-error randomized promise problem has a deterministic polynomial-time solver correct on all of its promised inputs.
cards.why: Classical worst-case derandomization uses hardness against arbitrary small circuits. This question asks whether hardness against uniform randomized algorithms, strengthened to cover almost every individual input, already suffices. A positive answer would characterize full promise derandomization through an algorithmic hardness assumption without requiring a circuit lower bound or a shallow implementation of the hard function.

cards.title: Circuit hardness from inverse-polynomial-error BPP heuristics
cards.formal: Does the uniform-distribution heuristic assumption \[\forall L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \forall k\ge1\ \exists A_{L,k}\in\mathrm P\ \exists N_{L,k}\ \forall n\ge N_{L,k},\quad \Pr_{x\sim U_n}[A_{L,k}(x)\ne\mathbf1_L(x)]\le n^{-k}\] imply \[\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\quad\text{or}\quad\operatorname{Perm}\text{ has no polynomial-size arithmetic circuits over }\mathbb Z\] in the constant-free arithmetic-circuit model below?
cards.why: Would clarify whether substantially weakening derandomization to allow a small set of bad inputs still forces nonuniform computational hardness. It probes the reach of the hardness-versus-randomness connection beyond exact or extremely low-error simulations.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

cards.title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
cards.formal:
Does exact symmetric weighted travelling salesman admit a classical algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two, allowing bounded-error randomization and polynomial dependence on the input bit length?

Precisely, do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), positive integers \(K,c,B\) with \(B\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(\mathcal A\) such that, for every \(n\ge3\) and every complete undirected graph on vertices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with nonnegative integer edge weights encoded as below, both of the following hold?
\[\Pr[\mathcal A\text{ outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle}]\ge\frac23,\]
\[\text{number of charged operations on every random execution}\ \le\ K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+L)^c.\]
Here \(L\) is the total bit length of the explicit input, and the machine model is fixed below using \(B\). All constants and the algorithm precede the quantifiers over the graph, its weights and its encoding length. A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.
cards.why: Exact weighted TSP is a basic test of whether optimization over all orders of a set fundamentally requires base-two exponential time. A fixed reduction of that base would save an exponential factor for every sufficiently large instance, even when costs have arbitrary binary representations. Understanding this boundary would distinguish the difficulty of selecting an optimal tour from the already faster task of merely detecting a tour.

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

cards.title: Subset Sum below the meet-in-the-middle exponent
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), \(c\ge1\) and a uniform classical bounded-error randomized algorithm deciding whether a subset of \(n\) positive integers sums to a nonnegative integer target in \(O(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^{c})\) worst-case time, where \(L\) is the total binary input length?
cards.why: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.

cards.title: Set Cover conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
cards.why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.

cards.title: Strictness of the W-hierarchy
cards.formal:
Is the \(W\)-hierarchy strict at every positive level?
\[
\forall\,t\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\qquad
W[t]\subsetneq W[t+1].
\]
The classes use uniform deterministic fixed-parameter many-one reductions and exact-weight satisfiability of bounded-depth Boolean circuits, as defined below. Equivalently, for every \(t\ge1\), is there a parameterized decision problem in \(W[t+1]\) that does not belong to \(W[t]\)?
cards.why: Parameterized completeness places many natural problems into different levels of a common hierarchy, but a level label alone does not prove a difference in computational power. Establishing strictness would show that these levels capture distinct forms of parameterized intractability. An equality would instead identify a new general reduction principle connecting problems currently treated as having different complexity.

cards.title: Polynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut
cards.formal:
Does undirected Edge Multiway Cut, parameterized only by the allowed number \(k\) of edge deletions, admit a randomized polynomial kernel? Specifically, do there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(R\) and positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that for every explicitly encoded instance \(I=(G,T,k)\) of length \(N\), on every random tape \(R\) halts within \(C(N+1)^a\) steps and outputs a well-formed instance \(I'=(G',T',k')\) of the same problem with
\[|I'|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad k'\le C(k+1)^b,\]
and
\[\Pr_R[I\text{ is a yes-instance}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ I'\text{ is a yes-instance}]\ge2/3?\]
A yes-instance has a set of at most \(k\) edges whose removal leaves no connected component containing two terminals. The number of terminals is unbounded and is not an extra parameter. The constants, including the exponent \(b\), must be independent of \(|T|\).
cards.why: Kernelization asks whether the information relevant to a small cut budget can be compressed before solving the remaining hard instance. Edge Multiway Cut is a central test of that principle because it combines many terminal-separation requirements while parameterizing only the number of removed edges. A polynomial kernel would replace arbitrarily large graphs by uniformly small equivalent instances without fixing the number of terminals.

cards.title: Polynomial compression versus polynomial kernelization
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed parameterized language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\) such that its unary-parameter encoding \(\widetilde Q\) is NP-complete and \[\operatorname{PC}(Q)\ \land\ \bigl(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\bigr)?\] Here \(\operatorname{PC}\) means deterministic polynomial compression to an arbitrary fixed language, and \(\operatorname{PK}\) means deterministic polynomial kernelization back to \(Q\), with the exact definitions below. Thus the requested compression is unconditional, while its separation from kernels uses the explicitly stated hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).
cards.why: Kernelization asks whether small equivalent instances can remain in the original problem language, while compression permits a different representation. A separation would expose a fundamental limit of preprocessing back into the same NP-complete problem even when short decision-equivalent information is computable.

cards.title: General Formula-SAT with a fixed exponential saving
cards.formal:
Do there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), constants \(K\ge1\), an integer \(d\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that every explicitly given Boolean formula \(F\) over AND, OR and NOT is correctly decided for satisfiability in at most
\[
K\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}\bigl(L(F)+1\bigr)^d
\]
Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(n(F)\) is the number of distinct variables occurring in \(F\), \(L(F)\) is its full binary encoding length, and no restriction is placed on its size or depth. The same algorithm, positive saving and constants must work for every formula.
cards.why: Boolean formulas are more general than bounded-width CNF instances while still lacking arbitrary circuit sharing. A fixed exponential saving across all formula sizes would reveal algorithmic structure beyond exhaustive search and would also improve every fixed-width SAT problem with one common saving.

cards.title: Single-exponential Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm and constants \(A,c>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which decide Directed Feedback Vertex Set on every \(n\)-vertex directed graph and deletion budget \(0\le k\le n\) within \(A\,2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) bit-computation steps? The answer must be YES exactly when deleting at most \(k\) vertices makes the graph acyclic. The exponential dependence is solely on the solution-size budget, and the polynomial exponent is independent of \(k\).
cards.why: Deleting a small number of vertices to destroy every directed cycle is a basic model of repairing cyclic dependencies. Fixed-parameter algorithms make small deletion budgets tractable in principle, but the known factorial dependence is much larger than a fixed exponential base. The target asks whether directed cycle structure inherently causes that additional parameter cost.

cards.title: Exact recognition of bounded clique-width
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A_{k}\) and constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\ge 1\) such that \(A_{k}\) decides whether \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) for every finite simple undirected graph G in at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps, where N is the bit length of G’s adjacency-matrix encoding?
cards.why: Tests whether a major dense-graph width parameter admits efficient exact recognition at every fixed value.

cards.title: FPT approximation of twin-width
cards.formal:
Do there exist total computable functions \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) and \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), an integer constant \(c\ge1\), and one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) such that, for every nonempty finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices and every integer \(k\ge0\), the machine halts within
\[
 f(k)(n+1)^c
\]
bit operations and either correctly reports \(\operatorname{tww}(G)>k\), or outputs a contraction sequence of \(G\) of width at most \(g(k)\)? Only the graph and \(k\) are supplied, with no helpful vertex order, decomposition or contraction sequence.
cards.why: Many algorithms exploiting twin-width need a low-width contraction sequence as part of their input. Finding such a certificate from an ordinary graph would make these methods applicable without requiring the structural witness in advance.

cards.title: Directed Hamiltonicity
cards.formal:
Do there exist one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(c\in(1,2)\), and constants \(K\ge1\) and integer \(B\ge2\) such that the following holds for every \(n\ge2\) and every directed graph \(G\) on \([n]\)?

In the RAM model below, using \(Bn\)-bit words, \(A\) halts within \(Kc^n\) operations on every random tape and correctly decides whether \(G\) has a directed Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least \(2/3\). The same algorithm and constants must handle all such graphs.
cards.why: Direction prevents the symmetric treatment of cycle traversals available in undirected graphs. A fixed improvement in the exponential base for arbitrary digraphs would cross a long-standing boundary of exact graph algorithms, beyond modular counting and speedups restricted to particular structures.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for forbidden-minor vertex deletion
cards.formal: Does vertex deletion to exclude any fixed finite family of graph minors admit a polynomial kernel, parameterized by the number of vertices allowed to be deleted? Precisely, for every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\), is there a deterministic polynomial-time transformation of \((G,k)\) into an equivalent instance \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same \(\mathcal F\)-deletion problem whose total encoding length and parameter are bounded by \((k+1)^{O_{\mathcal F}(1)}\)?
cards.why: Would give a general guarantee that graphs close to a minor-closed class can be reduced efficiently to a polynomial amount of relevant information. It unifies preprocessing questions for vertex cover, feedback vertex set, bounded-width deletion and planarization.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.formal:
Does Directed Feedback Vertex Set admit a deterministic polynomial kernel parameterized solely by the deletion budget? More precisely, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(K\), constants \(C,c>0\), and a polynomial \(p\), such that for every finite digraph \(D\) and nonnegative integer \(k\), \(K\) runs in at most \(p(L)\) steps on the explicit input of bit length \(L\), and outputs one instance \((D^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same problem satisfying
\[
D\text{ has a directed feedback vertex set of size at most }k
\iff
D^{\prime}\text{ has one of size at most }k^{\prime},
\]
with the entire output encoding having at most \(C(k+1)^{c}\) bits? The constants and algorithm must work for all inputs. No additional structural parameter or promise on the input or the remaining acyclic graph is permitted.
cards.why: Directed Feedback Vertex Set is a central test of how much efficient preprocessing can compress a fixed-parameter tractable cycle-hitting problem. A polynomial kernel would reduce every large instance with a small deletion budget to a polynomial amount of relevant information. A rigorous obstruction would distinguish directed cycle constraints from many successful kernelization settings.

cards.title: Chromatic number in \(2^{n}\) time and polynomial space
cards.formal:
Is there one uniform deterministic algorithm that computes the chromatic number of every \(n\)-vertex finite simple undirected graph in time \(O^{*}(2^n)\) and polynomial space?

Precisely, do there exist a deterministic machine \(A\) and fixed integers \(K\ge1,c,d\ge0\) such that, for every such graph \(G\), the machine outputs \(\chi(G)\), halts after at most
\[
K\,2^n(n+1)^c
\]
transitions, and uses at most
\[
K(n+1)^d
\]
work-tape cells throughout its computation? The graph encoding and computation model are defined below. Both bounds must hold for the same algorithm on the same input.
cards.why: Fast exact coloring algorithms illustrate the power of storing information for all vertex subsets, but that table has exponential size. The question asks whether the time advantage survives when the algorithm can retain only polynomially many bits. A resolution would clarify a central time-space tradeoff in exact algorithms for graph partitioning problems.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial kernels for Almost 2-SAT
cards.formal:
Does clause-deletion Almost 2-SAT admit a deterministic polynomial kernel parameterized by the number \(k\) of permitted clause deletions?

Precisely, do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(K\), an integer \(C\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\ge0\) such that, on every encoded instance \((F,k)\) of length \(L\), the algorithm runs for at most \(C(L+1)^a\) bit-machine steps and outputs an instance \((F',k')\) of the same problem satisfying
\[
(F,k)\in\mathcal A_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(F',k')\in\mathcal A_2,
\qquad
|\operatorname{enc}(F',k')|\le C(k+1)^b?
\]
Here \(\mathcal A_2\) and the encoding are defined below. The algorithm and constants must work for every formula and every nonnegative budget.
cards.why: A kernel compresses a large instance to a size governed only by its distance from satisfiability. Randomized algebraic methods provide this guarantee for Almost 2-SAT, but removing randomness while retaining polynomial preprocessing time is a central test of those methods. A resolution would clarify whether an important family of efficient data-reduction guarantees inherently depends on random choices.

cards.title: Fixed-parameter tractability of graph isomorphism by rank-width
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge1\) such that, for every pair of finite simple undirected graphs \(G,H\), \(A\) decides whether \(G\cong H\) within \[f(k)(|V(G)|+|V(H)|+2)^c\] bit operations, where \(k=\max\{\operatorname{rw}(G),\operatorname{rw}(H)\}\)? Graphs are supplied by their explicitly encoded adjacency matrices; neither a rank decomposition nor a width bound is supplied.
cards.why: Rank-width captures dense graphs with structured adjacency cuts, extending the reach of graph decomposition beyond sparse settings. A uniform fixed-parameter isomorphism test would make the polynomial exponent independent of this structural complexity and settle a central boundary in parameterized graph isomorphism.

cards.title: ETH barrier to single-exponential treewidth computation
cards.formal: Assuming the deterministic Exponential-Time Hypothesis (ETH) defined below, is an exact single-exponential parameterized algorithm for Treewidth impossible? Specifically, let \(\mathrm{FastTW}\) mean that there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\), constants \(C\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\ge1\) such that, for every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices and every integer \(0\le k<n\), \(A(G,k)\) decides whether \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le k\) correctly within \(C\,2^{ak}(n+2)^b\) steps. Under the assumption ETH, determine whether \(\neg\mathrm{FastTW}\) or \(\mathrm{FastTW}\) holds. This selects the explicit single-exponential example in the source’s broader request for lower bounds.
cards.why: Treewidth is a central measure of how close a graph is to a tree, and a decomposition is often the prerequisite for running efficient parameterized algorithms. The cost of finding the optimum can therefore dominate the cost of using the structure. Establishing whether a single-exponential dependence is compatible with ETH would locate a major boundary between structural preprocessing and algorithms that work once a decomposition is already known.

cards.title: Does ETH rule out subexponential constant-gap Max-Clique?
cards.formal:
Does deterministic ETH imply that there exists a rational constant \(\gamma>1\) for which no uniform deterministic algorithm solves the following promise problem in time \(2^{o(n)}\)? Given an \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\) and an integer \(1\le k\le n\), distinguish
\[
\omega(G)\ge k\qquad\text{from}\qquad\omega(G)<k/\gamma,
\]
where \(\omega(G)\) is the maximum number of pairwise adjacent vertices. The exponent parameter \(n\) is the total number of graph vertices, not the requested clique size \(k\).
cards.why: Exact Clique has an ETH barrier at the exponential-in-vertices scale. Preserving that scale under even one fixed approximation gap would explain whether coarse approximation escapes the barrier without assuming gap hardness at the outset.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{W}[2]\)-hardness of bounded-VC-dimension Hitting Set
cards.formal:
Is there a fixed integer \(d\ge0\) such that Hitting Set on finite set systems of VC dimension at most \(d\), parameterized only by the allowed hitting-set size \(k\), is \(\mathrm{W}[2]\)-hard under deterministic fixed-parameter many-one reductions?

Use the explicit encoding, source problem and reduction convention below. The precise proposition is
\[
\exists d,c\in\mathbb N_{0}\ \exists R\
\exists f:\mathbb N_{0}\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists g:\mathbb N_{0}\to\mathbb N_{0}\
\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \forall k\in\mathbb N_{0}\
G(d,c,R,f,g;x,k),
\]
where \(R\) is one deterministic Turing transducer and \(f,g\) are total computable functions. The predicate \(G\) requires that, on input \(\langle x,k\rangle\), the transducer halts within \(f(k)(L(x,k)+1)^{c}\) transitions and outputs \(\langle y,k'\rangle\) such that \(y\) encodes a finite set system \(\mathcal F_{y}\),
\[
\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal F_{y})\le d,\qquad
k'\le g(k),\qquad
\operatorname{HS}(x,k)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\operatorname{HS}(y,k').
\]
All witnesses are chosen before the input. In particular, the VC bound \(d\) cannot grow with \(k\), the source system or its encoding length. The question asks for some constant bound, not specifically the bound two.
cards.why: This asks whether a broad restriction on combinatorial complexity preserves the full parameterized difficulty of general covering. A positive answer would show that bounded shattering complexity, despite its role in approximation and sampling, still supports \(\mathrm{W}[2]\)-hard exact covering. A negative answer would separate \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) from \(\mathrm{W}[2]\), because the dimension-two problem is already \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. The question therefore connects a widely used structural measure to a central distinction in parameterized complexity, beyond the already established failure of fixed-parameter tractability under standard assumptions.

cards.title: A DAG-treewidth dichotomy for homomorphism counting in degenerate graphs
cards.formal:
Is the following dichotomy true for every computable isomorphism-closed class \(\mathcal C\) of finite nonempty simple undirected graphs? For exact homomorphism counting \(\#\mathrm{Hom}_d(\mathcal C)\), parameterized by \(|V(H)|+d(G)\):

If \(\sup_{H\in\mathcal C}\tau_1(H)<\infty\), the problem is fixed-parameter tractable; if \(\sup_{H\in\mathcal C}\tau_1(H)=\infty\), it is \(\#\mathsf W[1]\)-hard under deterministic fixed-parameter Turing reductions.

Here \(d(G)\) is the degeneracy of the host graph and \(\tau_1\) is the maximum generalized DAG-treewidth over all acyclic orientations, with the exact definitions below. The bounded-width direction is known; the target includes the unbounded-width hardness direction.
cards.why: This would identify the structural boundary of exact homomorphism counting when the host is sparse in the degeneracy sense. It would extend known classifications for subgraph and induced-subgraph counting and link acyclic-orientation width to parameterized counting hardness.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for minor-free edge deletion
cards.formal: Does every fixed finite family \(\mathcal H\) of finite simple undirected graphs admit a deterministic polynomial kernel for \(\mathcal H\)-Minor-Free Edge Deletion, parameterized only by the number \(k\) of edges that may be deleted? An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\ge0\). It is a yes-instance if there exists \(F\subseteq E(G)\) with \(|F|\le k\) such that \(G-F\) contains no graph from \(\mathcal H\) as a minor. The kernel must return one equivalent instance of this same problem with total encoding length and output parameter bounded by a polynomial in \(k+1\), as specified below.
cards.why: A polynomial kernel would bound all information relevant to the deletion decision by a polynomial in the allowed number of changes, irrespective of the size of the original graph. This would make minor exclusion a broad source of effective preprocessing for edge repair. The distinction from vertex deletion matters because deleting a few edges can leave all vertices present and does not provide the same structural control as removing a small set of vertices.

cards.title: Graph homomorphism parameterized by both treewidths
cards.formal:
Do there exist one deterministic Turing-machine algorithm \(A\), a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), and an integer constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every pair of explicitly given finite simple undirected graphs \(G,H\), \(A\) decides whether there is a graph homomorphism \(G\to H\) in at most
\[
f(k)(L+2)^C\quad\text{bit operations},\qquad
k=\max\{\operatorname{tw}(G),\operatorname{tw}(H)\},
\]
where \(L\) is the full binary encoding length? Both graphs vary with the input. The exponent \(C\) must be independent of \(k\), the vertex counts and both graphs.
cards.why: Bounding the source graph alone permits dynamic programming whose exponent can depend on its treewidth. The question asks whether simultaneously controlling the target graph removes that dependence from the exponent, a basic structural tractability boundary for homomorphism and query evaluation.

cards.title: Near-logarithmic FPT inapproximability of Set Cover under Gap-ETH
cards.formal:
Does sparse deterministic Gap-ETH imply that, for some rational constant \(c>0\), no uniform deterministic FPT algorithm can distinguish
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(U,\mathcal S)\le k
\quad\text{from}\quad
\operatorname{OPT}(U,\mathcal S)>\rho_c(n)k,
\qquad
\rho_c(n)=\max\{1,c(\log_2(n+2))^{99/100}\},
\]
where \(n=|U|\) is the number of universe elements, \(\mathcal S\) is an explicitly given family of subsets of \(U\), and \(k\) is the parameter? FPT means time \(f(k)(L+1)^d\) for some computable function \(f\) and fixed exponent \(d\), with \(L\) the full input bit length. The two alternatives are promised; the definitions below fix the hypothesis and model.
cards.why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question asks for a sharp boundary or for a concrete gap to be closed. Such a bound identifies the attainable guarantee and provides a target for new techniques.

cards.title: Fixed-parameter tractability of coloring graphs with no induced P5
cards.formal:
Do there exist a computable function \(f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), an integer constant \(C\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(A\) which, for every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices and every integer \(1\le k\le n\), halts in at most
\[
f(k)(n+2)^C
\]
bit operations and, whenever \(G\) contains no induced path on five vertices, decides correctly whether \(G\) has a proper coloring using at most \(k\) colors?
cards.why: Coloring on P5-free graphs is tractable for each fixed number of colors, but the known polynomial exponent can depend on that number. Removing that dependence would distinguish structural fixed-parameter tractability from the weaker fixed-k phenomenon in a basic hereditary graph class.

cards.title: Shortest common superstring in \(O^*(1.99^n)\) time
cards.formal: Do there exist one uniform deterministic classical word-RAM algorithm \(A\), a constant \(K>0\), and integers \(d\ge2\) and \(a\ge1\) such that, for every list of \(n\ge0\) explicitly given finite strings over any finite alphabet, \(A\) outputs a shortest common superstring within \(K(199/100)^n(L+1)^a\) machine steps? Here \(L\) is the total binary input length, and words have \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil)\) bits. The constant base \(199/100\) is fixed, independently of all string lengths and alphabet sizes.
cards.why: The problem asks whether the classical exponential cost of ordering many overlapping strings can be reduced by a fixed factor in the exponent. It is a central exact-algorithm question for sequence assembly and helps distinguish the complexity of string overlap from more general ordering problems.
