If there exist an explicit family of multilinear polynomials \(f_n\in\mathbb F_2[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), a real constant \(\alpha>0\), and an integer \(n_0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{size}_{\mathbb F_2}(f_n)\ge 2^{\alpha n}\qquad(n\ge n_0),
\]
then there exist an explicit family of univariate polynomials \(g_d\in\mathbb F_2[t]\) of degree at most \(d\), a real constant \(\beta>0\), and an integer \(d_0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{size}_{\mathbb F_2}(g_d)\ge d^\beta\qquad(d\ge d_0).
\]
Explicitness means coefficient computation in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) for the first family and \(d^{O(1)}\) for the second, with one uniform coefficient algorithm for each family.
cards.why: Low-characteristic derandomization can use hard polynomials with very few variables. Understanding whether conventional multivariate hardness already supplies such polynomials would connect two presently different hardness assumptions and clarify what variable compression can preserve.

cards.title: Does real Zariski-closure membership belong to ∃R?
cards.formal:
Does the following language belong to \(\exists\mathbb R\)? An input is a quantifier-free Boolean formula \(\varphi\) in real variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), with explicitly encoded integer polynomial equations and inequalities. It is accepted exactly when
\[
0\in\overline{S_\varphi}^{\,Z},\qquad
S_\varphi=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\varphi(x)\}.
\]
Here \(\overline{S_\varphi}^{\,Z}\) is the real Zariski closure. The target is a deterministic polynomial-bit-time many-one reduction to the existential theory of the reals, for arbitrary input dimension and polynomial degree.
cards.why: This asks whether algebraic consequences of a real feasible region have existential real certificates of polynomial description length. It isolates a concrete boundary in real algebraic complexity that is not determined by the known classification for ordinary metric limits.

cards.title: Beyond the n log n barrier for unrestricted noncommutative circuits
cards.formal: For every field F, does the minimum size s_F(n) of a fan-in-two noncommutative arithmetic circuit computing Pal_{n,n}(X,Y)=∑_{(i₁,…,iₙ)∈{1,…,n}ⁿ}x_{i₁}⋯x_{iₙ}y_{iₙ}⋯y_{i₁} satisfy s_F(n)=ω(n log n), with no homogeneity or syntactic-degree restriction? Yes: the accepted 2026 result of Raz implies Ω(n^(3/2)), and Shastri’s concurrent preprint states the stronger Ω(n²).
cards.why: Historically isolates the obstruction to stronger lower bounds for unrestricted arithmetic computation when multiplication is noncommutative. The 2026 advances show that the n log n barrier can be crossed without constraining intermediate degrees or preventing reuse of intermediate results.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.

cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

cards.title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), and integers \(C,c\ge1\), such that \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps on every binary input of length \(L\) and every sequence of its random bits, and has the following correctness property? For every prime \(p\), every generator \(g\) of the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), and every \(h\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), given the binary encoding of \((p,g,h)\) specified below, it outputs the unique integer \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-2\}\) satisfying \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\) with probability at least \(2/3\).
cards.why: Discrete logarithms expose a basic gap between efficient modular exponentiation and our ability to invert it. A uniform classical polynomial-time solver would defeat the corresponding finite-field discrete-logarithm assumptions and solve computational Diffie–Hellman in this setting. An unrestricted impossibility proof would establish a fundamental classical lower bound for a concrete arithmetic problem already solvable in quantum polynomial time.

cards.title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), a real constant \(K>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly encoded \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, every run halts in at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit operations and returns a nonzero \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23?\]
The input length \(N\) includes all matrix entries. The lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1\) is its shortest nonzero Euclidean length. Randomness consists of independent fair bits on that fixed input. The program and all constants are chosen once, before any input.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient classical computation can find short vectors in every Euclidean lattice with a loss bounded by one fixed power of rank. The gap between known general algorithms and this regime is a basic obstacle in lattice complexity. Resolving it would clarify the relation between lattice geometry, efficient approximation and worst-case hardness assumptions used in cryptography; its consequences for particular schemes still depend on the exact problem and parameters.

cards.title: Vinogradov’s least quadratic nonresidue conjecture
cards.formal:
For an odd prime \(p\), let \(n(p)\) be the least positive quadratic nonresidue modulo \(p\), defined below. Is it true, unconditionally, that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists P_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_\varepsilon\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)\le p^{\varepsilon}?\]
Equivalently, is \(n(p)=p^{o(1)}\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through the odd primes? The threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the prime. No unproved analytic hypothesis is assumed.
cards.why: A small quadratic nonresidue is a basic witness used in finite-field arithmetic, and its size measures how long the initial integers can all behave like squares modulo a prime. The conjecture asks for uniform cancellation strong enough to beat every fixed power of the modulus. It would cross a long-standing barrier in character sums and bound the range of deterministic searches for such witnesses; subpolynomial size in the modulus is not the same claim as polynomial size in its bit length.

cards.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in BQP
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform quantum algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every integer matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Z} ^{m\times d}\) with \(m\ge d\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns, the algorithm outputs \(z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}\) satisfying ||\(Bz||_{2}=\min _{y\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}}||\)By||\(_{2}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p(\mathrm{L})\) elementary steps on every execution? L is the total binary encoding length of m, d and all entries of B.
cards.why: A central test of quantum algorithms against worst-case lattice hardness.

cards.title: Quantum polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), a real constant \(K>0\), and one uniform quantum algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly given matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, the algorithm terminates within \(K(N+1)^k\) charged operations on every execution and outputs a nonzero integer vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23.\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length, \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1(L(B))\) is the length of its shortest nonzero vector. The probability is over the computation’s measurement outcomes on this fixed classical input. All constants and the program are chosen before the input; the approximation exponent depends on neither rank nor coefficient size.
cards.why: This isolates whether quantum computation changes the polynomial-time approximation boundary for unrestricted Euclidean lattice search. A positive answer would improve the guarantee from a superpolynomial loss to one fixed power of rank on every lattice. A negative answer would establish an unconditional limitation on general quantum computation, far beyond the failure of any particular quantum lattice algorithm. Its cryptographic implications depend on the exact lattice task and approximation exponent.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time construction of a prime of a given bit length
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that constructs a prime of every requested bit length in polynomial bit time?

The input is the unary string \(1^n\), for any integer \(n\ge2\). The output must be the binary expansion of some prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
2^{n-1}\le p<2^n.
\]
The prime may be any one in this interval; no particular choice, such as the smallest prime, is prescribed.

With the finite machine model and output predicate below, the precise assertion is
\[
\exists A\ \exists C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ 
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,1^n,y,Cn^k)
\land \operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)
\bigr).
\]
One fixed deterministic program and one polynomial bound must work for every requested length. This retains the source's unary-input prime-construction question and makes its bit-computation convention explicit.
cards.why: Prime generation is a canonical example where recognizing a suitable object is efficiently possible but constructing one deterministically remains unresolved. A positive answer would remove randomness from this basic number-theoretic construction at every bit length. A negative answer would establish an unconditional computational lower bound for a concrete total search problem. The connection with succinct descriptions of primes also makes the question central to research on derandomization and time-bounded information.

cards.title: Deterministic NP-hardness reductions for Euclidean SVP
cards.formal:
Is the exact decision version of the Euclidean shortest vector problem NP-hard under a uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction?

An instance consists of a positive integer \(n\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), and a positive rational squared-radius threshold \(b\), all explicitly encoded in binary as specified below. Its lattice and Euclidean minimum are
\[
L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^{n}\},\qquad
\lambda_{1}(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^{n}\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_{2},
\qquad \|x\|_{2}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The answer is YES if \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}\le b\), and NO if \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}>b\). Thus the geometric radius is \(\sqrt{b}\), represented exactly by its rational square.

Precisely, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(M\) and integers \(a,k\ge1\) such that, on every encoded 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\), it outputs a valid instance \((B_{\varphi},b_{\varphi})\) within \(a(|\varphi|+1)^{k}\) steps and
\[
\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\mathbb Z^{n_{\varphi}}\setminus\{0\}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\varphi}}(B_{\varphi}z)_{i}^{2}\le b_{\varphi}?
\]
The same machine and constants must work for every input length. It must have the same time bound on malformed input strings, mapping them to valid NO instances.

This is the exact endpoint \(\gamma=1\) expressly allowed by the source's request for hardness of exact or approximate GapSVP under a deterministic Karp reduction. No approximation factor greater than one is required; a valid stronger gap reduction would also settle this endpoint.
cards.why: The shortest vector problem is a central lattice problem whose basic hardness theorem historically required randomized reductions. Removing randomness establishes its ordinary NP-hardness and separates the foundational exact worst-case question from approximation regimes and average-case assumptions used in lattice cryptography.

cards.title: Polynomial-factor Euclidean SVP hardness assuming NP is not contained in RP
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true?
\[
\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{RP}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q,\ 0<\varepsilon<1/2:
\operatorname{GapSVP}^{(2)}_{n^\varepsilon}\notin\operatorname{PromiseBPP}.
\]
Thus the target is a fixed positive power of the lattice rank in the Euclidean norm, with no classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm under the specified standard assumption. The exponent may be arbitrarily small but must be independent of the input.
cards.why: Constant-factor Euclidean lattice hardness does not explain whether even a small fixed power of the rank remains difficult to approximate. Establishing this from the standard randomized NP-hardness assumption would close a major qualitative gap in the approximation landscape.

cards.title: Quantum-ETH hardness of cryptographic-factor GapSVP
cards.formal:
Does the quantum Exponential Time Hypothesis defined below imply that, for some fixed integer \(k\ge1\), there is no bounded-error uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm for Euclidean
\[\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k},\qquad \gamma_k(n)=n^{3/2+1/k}?\]
Equivalently, the target is the conditional assertion
\[\mathrm{QETH}\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k}\notin\mathrm{PromiseBQP}.\]
The source asks for hardness at \(n^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) under a standard complexity assumption, without selecting that assumption. This card explicitly selects quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT; it is an editorial variant of that research direction, not a claim that the source stated this particular implication.
cards.why: This question asks whether a familiar quantum satisfiability assumption can support hardness of lattice approximation at a scale relevant to worst-case-to-average-case cryptographic reductions. That scale is much larger than constant-factor approximation, and hardness at a small factor does not automatically persist as the promise gap grows. A proof would connect lattice-based security foundations to a separate complexity assumption while addressing quantum algorithms explicitly.

cards.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
cards.formal:
Do there exist one randomized classical algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,d\ge1\) such that, for every rational lattice basis \(B\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) with linearly independent columns and total binary encoding length \(L\), the algorithm finds an exact shortest nonzero vector of \(\Lambda(B)\) with probability at least \(2/3\), while using simultaneously at most
\[
2^{Cn}L^d\quad\text{bit operations}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
L^d\quad\text{bits of working space}?
\]
Both bounds must hold on every random tape. The exponent parameter \(n\) is lattice rank, and every \(m\ge n\ge1\) and every valid coefficient encoding are included.
cards.why: The problem asks whether exact lattice search can retain a single-exponential time bound while avoiding an exponentially large stored collection. It separates two major resource regimes in lattice algorithms and helps clarify which memory assumptions matter when interpreting lattice-based computational hardness.

cards.title: Polynomial-factor approximation of cyclotomic ideal SVP
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that finds a polynomial-factor approximate shortest nonzero vector in every ideal of every power-of-two cyclotomic ring?

More precisely, do there exist one probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,C,d\) such that, for every \(n=2^k\) with integer \(k\ge1\), and every nonsingular matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) whose column lattice \(I_B=B\mathbb Z^n\) is an ideal of \(R_n=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^n+1)\), the following holds? On the explicit binary input \((n,B)\) of length \(L\), every run of \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and
\[\Pr\!\left[A(n,B)\text{ outputs }v\in I_B\setminus\{0\}\text{ with }\|v\|_2\le n^c\lambda_1(I_B)\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad
\lambda_1(I_B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2.\]
The constants and program are chosen before the dimension and ideal. The approximation factor depends on dimension, not on coefficient bit lengths. The output must be the full integer coefficient vector \(v\).
cards.why: The central issue is whether the algebraic structure used to make lattice cryptography compact also makes a core worst-case search problem efficiently solvable at polynomial approximation. The selected family is a standard cyclotomic family with growing dimension, not a collection of hand-picked easy ideals. Resolving the question would clarify the computational strength of these structured hardness assumptions. An efficient ideal-SVP algorithm would not, merely by reversing a known security reduction, constitute an attack on every ring-LWE or ring-SIS distribution.

cards.title: A classical reduction from semiprime factoring to polynomial-gap SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist an absolute rational constant \(\varepsilon>0\) and one classical randomized polynomial-time oracle algorithm that factors every integer \(N=pq\), where \(p\ne q\) are primes, using an oracle for Euclidean \(\operatorname{GapSVP}_{n^{2+\varepsilon}}\)?

Here \(n\) is the rank of the lattice in each oracle query, and the algorithm must output the two prime factors with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised input \(N\). The oracle may answer arbitrarily inside its approximation gap.
cards.why: This would connect two major sources of computational hardness: factoring integers and approximating shortest lattice vectors by a large polynomial factor. The selected approximation regime is strong enough to connect onward to classical worst-case-to-average-case reductions used for lattice cryptography.

cards.title: A classical same-dimension reduction from SIVP to polynomial-modulus LWE
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge3\), do there exist constants \(C,K,a>0\), an integer \(b\ge0\), and one uniform classical randomized oracle algorithm \(\mathcal R_c\) with the following property?

For all \(n\ge2\), all admissible parameters \(q,\alpha,m,t\) below, every rank-\(n\) integer lattice basis \(B\), and every admissible search-LWE oracle \(A\), the algorithm \(\mathcal R_c^A(B,q,\alpha,m,t)\) outputs \(n\) linearly independent lattice vectors of length at most
\[
\gamma(n,\alpha)\lambda_n(\mathcal L(B)),\qquad
\gamma(n,\alpha)=C\frac n\alpha\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b,
\]
with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input basis, using at most \(K(L+m+t+1)^a\) bit operations and oracle calls on every run? Every LWE query must have dimension exactly \(n\), modulus exactly \(q\), and exactly \(m\) samples with the noise parameter \(\alpha\) in the oracle guarantee. Here \(L\) is the complete binary input length, and the constants and algorithm may depend on \(c\), not on the instance.
cards.why: LWE is a classical noisy linear problem, yet the strongest known worst-case connection to SIVP uses quantum computation. Matching that connection classically at polynomial modulus and unchanged dimension would clarify which parts of the hardness foundation actually depend on quantum operations.

cards.title: Classical ideal-SVP hardness of ring-LWE in power-of-two cyclotomic rings
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge3\), do there exist constants \(C,K,a>0\), integers \(b\ge0,n_0\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized oracle algorithm that, for every power of two \(n\ge n_0\), reduces worst-case ideal-SVP in \(R_n=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^n+1)\) to the same-ring search-LWE problem defined below, with approximation factor
\[
\gamma(n,\alpha)=C\frac{\sqrt n}{\alpha}\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b?
\]
The reduction must succeed with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input ideal basis, for every admissible oracle, and use at most \(K(L+m+t+1)^a\) classical bit operations and oracle calls on every run. Its queries must retain the degree \(n\), modulus \(q\), noise-family bound \(\alpha\) and sample count \(m\). The constants and algorithm may depend on \(c\), but not on the ideal or the other parameters.
cards.why: Ring structure makes LWE-based constructions more compact, but the useful worst-case ideal-lattice connection uses quantum computation. A classical reduction at comparable approximation and modulus scales would strengthen the theoretical understanding of that connection.

cards.title: Scholz–Brauer conjecture
cards.formal: For every positive integer n, is \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell (n)\), where \(\ell\)\((m)\) is the minimum length of an addition chain for m?
cards.why: The conjecture predicts a precise relationship between optimal multiplication plans for an exponent and for its associated all-ones binary integer. Its restricted-chain theorem shows that the unresolved issue concerns how the freedom to reuse older values affects the best possible length.

cards.title: Baillie–PSW pseudoprimes
cards.formal: Does there exist a composite integer n that passes the strong base-2 probable-prime test and the strong Lucas probable-prime test with Selfridge’s Method A, including the parameter-search rejection rule specified below?
cards.why: Tests the mathematical reliability of a widely used primality-testing combination.

cards.title: NP-hardness of Euclidean unique SVP with a fixed gap greater than one
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute rational constant \(\gamma>1\) such that the search problem \(\gamma\text{-uSVP}_2\) is NP-hard under classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reductions?

The input is an explicitly encoded integer lattice basis \(B\), promised to satisfy
\[
\lambda_2(\mathcal L(B))>\gamma\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B)).
\]
The required answer is an exact shortest nonzero lattice vector. The uniqueness gap \(\gamma-1\) must be a positive constant independent of the input dimension and bit length.
cards.why: A constant separation between the shortest lattice direction and every independent competitor is a strong geometric promise. Proving NP-hardness despite that promise would show that isolating a shortest vector does not remove the worst-case difficulty of Euclidean lattice search.

cards.title: Dimension-preserving search-to-decision reductions for SVP
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction that, using only \(\gamma\)-GapSVP queries on lattices of the same dimension \(n\), solves SVP with approximation factor polynomial in \(n\) and \(\gamma\)? Concretely, do there exist absolute positive integers \(C,a,b\) and one randomized oracle machine \(R\) such that for every \(n\ge1\), every nonsingular \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), every rational \(\gamma\ge1\), and every admissible oracle \(O_\gamma\) below, \(R^{O_\gamma}(B,\gamma)\) runs in at most \(C(N+2)^b\) steps and outputs \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) with \[ \Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\le C(n\gamma)^a\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\ge2/3? \] Here \(N\) is the bit length of the encoded input, and the probability is over the reduction’s random bits.
cards.why: Search returns a short lattice vector, whereas a decision oracle only certifies which side of a length gap the lattice lies on. Bridging these versions with polynomial approximation loss and no dimension increase would sharpen a basic computational relationship at the center of lattice algorithms and worst-case hardness assumptions in cryptography.

cards.title: A classical SIS reduction from sublinear-factor GapSVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(C\ge1\), polynomially bounded computable modulus parameters as defined below, and a classical randomized polynomial-time worst-case-to-average-case reduction
\[
\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma(n)}\ \longrightarrow\
\operatorname{SIS}_{n,m(n),q(n),\sqrt{m(n)}},
\qquad \gamma(n)=\max\{1,Cn^{1-\varepsilon}\},
\]
in the Euclidean norm? The reduction must solve every promised rank-\(n\) GapSVP instance from a SIS oracle that succeeds on only an inverse-polynomial fraction of uniformly random matrices. It must have polynomial overhead in the inverse of that success probability.
cards.why: Current worst-case guarantees for SIS rely on roughly linear approximation factors when parameters support nontrivial compression. A fixed exponent improvement would base average-case short-integer-solution hardness on a weaker worst-case lattice assumption.

cards.title: NP-hardness of Euclidean covering radius
cards.formal: Is exact Euclidean lattice covering radius NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time map sending each Boolean 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a rational full-column-rank matrix \(B\) and a positive rational threshold \(r\), such that \[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu_2(L(B))\le r?\] Unsatisfiable formulas must map to instances with \(\mu_2(L(B))>r\). This is the exact decision problem, with approximation factor one and no promised gap between the two cases.
cards.why: The covering radius measures how far a point can be from its nearest lattice point. It is a central lattice invariant with connections to integer programming and to worst-case lattice problems used in cryptography. Establishing even exact Euclidean NP-hardness would close a basic gap in the complexity classification of lattice problems, without requiring the stronger approximation-hardness results known in other norms.

cards.title: Downward self-reducibility of integer factoring
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic oracle Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every integer \(N\ge 2\) of binary length n, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N within \(p(n)\) steps, using a factoring oracle only on integers \(M\ge 2\) whose binary length is strictly less than n?
cards.why: Downward self-reducibility of integer factoring asks whether a canonical arithmetic search problem has the recursive structure common to complete problems.

cards.title: coNP certificates for GapSVP at the square-root n/log n scale
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(C\ge2\) such that Euclidean \(\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_C(n)}\) belongs to coNP, where
\[
\gamma_C(n)=C\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log_2(n+2)}}\ ?
\]
Concretely, must every input lattice whose shortest nonzero vector has length greater than \(\gamma_C(n)r\) admit a polynomial-length, deterministically polynomial-time verifiable certificate, with no accepted certificate when the lattice has a nonzero vector of length at most \(r\)?
cards.why: A short certificate that no sufficiently short lattice vector exists would strengthen the known upper bounds on lattice complexity. Matching the better approximation scale of interactive proofs with a single classical certificate would clarify the role of interaction in certifying lattice distance.

cards.title: SVP hardness for fixed-rank cyclotomic modules
cards.formal:
Does exact Euclidean shortest-vector decision remain NP-hard on cyclotomic module lattices when the module rank is an absolute constant?

For each fixed integer \(r\ge1\), let \(\mathcal D_r\) be the decision problem defined below. A valid instance consists of a conductor \(m\ge3\), finitely many generators \(y_1,\ldots,y_s\in R_m^r\) spanning \(K_m^r\) over \(K_m\), and an integer squared threshold \(S\ge0\), where
\[K_m=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m),\quad R_m=\mathbb Z[\zeta_m],\quad M=\sum_{j=1}^s R_m y_j.\]
It is a YES instance exactly when \(\lambda_1(M)^2\le S\), using the canonical product norm below.

The target is the existence of a fixed \(r\), a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(F\), and positive integer constants \(C,d\) such that \(F\) runs in at most \(C(N+1)^d\) bit steps on every input string of length \(N\), and for every well-formed 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\), it outputs a valid instance of \(\mathcal D_r\) satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda_1(M_{F(\varphi)})^2\le S_{F(\varphi)}.\]
Thus one rank and one uniform polynomial-time many-one reduction must work for all formulas; the conductor, generators and threshold may depend on the formula.
cards.why: Module lattices retain algebraic structure while permitting much larger families than single ideals. Establishing hardness with a fixed number of module coordinates would show that this compact structure can support a fundamental worst-case geometric obstruction as the field degree grows. The problem tests the boundary between algebraic organization and computational difficulty; exact worst-case hardness alone does not establish the security of cryptographic parameter distributions.

cards.title: ETH hardness of constant-factor shortest-vector approximation for \(1\le p\le 2\)
cards.formal: Does deterministic ETH imply that for every fixed real \(p\in [1,2]\) there is a constant \(\gamma >1\) for which the gap shortest-vector problem \(SVP_{p,\gamma}\) has no deterministic algorithm running in time \(2^{o}(d)N^{O}(1)\), where d is the ambient lattice dimension and N is the explicit input bit length?
cards.why: Would strengthen the fine-grained hardness basis for constant-factor lattice approximation in the most familiar norm range, using an ordinary satisfiability assumption. It separates a genuine exponential obstruction from lower bounds relying on a stronger gap or randomized premise.

cards.title: A quantum 2^(0.2075n) lower bound for exact Euclidean SVP from QSETH
cards.formal:
Does the Quantum Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis defined below imply that there are no constants \(K,a>0\) and no uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm which, for every explicitly given integer lattice basis of rank \(n\) and total binary input length \(L\), outputs an exact shortest nonzero vector using at most
\[
K\,2^{83n/400}(L+1)^a
\]
elementary operations on every execution? The exponent is the exact rational number \(83/400=0.2075\), and the norm is Euclidean.
cards.why: Quantum attacks on lattice problems are often estimated from particular sieving algorithms. A rank-sensitive exponential lower bound under an independent SAT hypothesis would provide a much firmer basis for those estimates and would have to overcome substantial limitations of current reductions.

cards.title: Unconditional exponential hardness of \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP
cards.formal: Do there exist explicit positive constants c and \(\varepsilon\) such that no uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm solves Euclidean \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP on n-dimensional rational lattices in time \(O(2^{cn} N^{k})\), for any fixed k, where N is the input bit length? The lower bound must be unconditional; deterministic and randomized classical algorithms are included among the algorithms ruled out.
cards.why: Combines worst-case exponential hardness, a cryptographically relevant approximation gap and resistance to quantum computation in one unconditional theorem. A resolution would turn a central type of lattice-security assumption into a proved complexity bound and would go well beyond establishing \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

cards.title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance function
\[R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n},\qquad 0<\delta<\frac12,\]
where \(A_2(n,d)\) is the largest cardinality of any nonempty binary code of length \(n\) whose distinct codewords have Hamming distance at least \(d\). Supply an unambiguous real-valued approximation \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall\delta\in(0,1/2),\qquad |g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The error is absolute rate error in information bits per transmitted bit. Codes may be nonlinear and have no construction, encoding or decoding efficiency requirement. The same error bound must hold on the entire real domain.
cards.why: This function is the intrinsic packing limit for binary information protected against worst-case substitutions. Determining it to a certified rate accuracy would quantify the necessary redundancy independently of how a code is represented, constructed or decoded. Exact determination would settle a foundational coding-theory question; the selected tolerance is a distinct, weaker benchmark target.

cards.title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
cards.formal:
Determine the weighted capacity function
\[F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), \(P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). The real memoryless channel is
\[Y_{1,t}=X_{1,t}+aX_{2,t}+Z_{1,t},\qquad Y_{2,t}=bX_{1,t}+X_{2,t}+Z_{2,t}.\]
The region \(C\) uses two independent private messages, deterministic separate encoders, average power over messages and time, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing joint average decoding error, as defined below. The required absolute accuracy is \(1/100\) bit per real channel use everywhere on this domain.
cards.why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.

cards.title: Capacity of the general broadcast channel
cards.formal:
Determine the function
\[F(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for every finite discrete memoryless broadcast channel \(W\) with a rational transition table and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]\). Here \(C(W)\) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, deterministic codes, vanishing joint average decoding error, and no feedback, as defined below. The required accuracy is absolute \(1/100\) bit per channel use throughout this entire domain.
cards.why: One of the smallest communication networks whose full capacity region is unknown. It asks for the basic law governing simultaneous transmission of independent information to different receivers, with consequences for coding methods and converse techniques throughout network information theory.

cards.title: Li–Li conjecture
cards.formal:
For every network instance \(I\) defined below, is
\[\mathcal C(I)=\mathcal R(I)?\]
Here \(\mathcal C(I)\) is the closure of the rate vectors supported by finite deterministic causal zero-error network codes, with an entropy capacity shared between the two directions of every undirected edge. The region \(\mathcal R(I)\) consists of all rates supported by fractional multicommodity routing. The quantification includes every finite network size, every positive rational capacity vector, every finite list of independent unicast sessions, every finite message and symbol alphabet, every causal schedule and every nonlinear local encoding function.
cards.why: Asks whether computation inside an undirected network can increase the throughput of independent unicast messages, with direct connections to multicommodity flow and major computational lower bounds.

cards.title: Capacity of the general two-user interference channel
cards.formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{IC}}(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{IC}}(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-user interference channel \(W\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), with independent private messages and no feedback.
cards.why: A canonical unresolved network-information-theory model in which independent communications compete through interference.

cards.title: Binary codes beyond the Gilbert–Varshamov bound
cards.formal:
Do binary error-correcting codes have an asymptotic rate strictly above the Gilbert–Varshamov bound at some fixed positive relative Hamming distance?

Precisely, do there exist real constants \(0<\delta<1/2\) and \(\eta>0\) such that for every integer \(N\ge1\) there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a nonempty code \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying
\[\forall x,y\in C,\quad x\ne y\ \Longrightarrow\ d_H(x,y)\ge\lceil\delta n\rceil,\]
\[\frac{\log_2|C|}{n}\ \ge\ 1-H_2(\delta)+\eta?\]
The constants precede the block length and code. Codes may be nonlinear, and neither an efficient construction nor an efficient decoder is required.
cards.why: A binary code trades the amount of information stored in each symbol against the number of adversarial substitutions that can be tolerated. This question asks whether the ubiquitous random-coding rate is an actual information limit or whether binary codebooks can carry a fixed additional amount of information per symbol at the same relative distance. It concerns what codes can exist, independently of implementation efficiency.

cards.title: Polynomial-length constant-query locally decodable codes
cards.formal:
Do there exist an integer \(q\ge1\), real constants \(C\ge1\), \(d\ge1\) and \(0<\delta<1/2\), such that for every integer message length \(k\ge1\) there are an integer \(n\) with \(k\le n\le Ck^d\), an injective encoding
\[
 E_k:\{0,1\}^k\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^n,
\]
and randomized local decoders \(D_{k,i}\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), satisfying
\[
 \Pr[D_{k,i}^{\,z}=x_i]\ge\frac23
\]
for every message \(x\in\{0,1\}^k\) and every received word \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\) differing from \(E_k(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) coordinates, while each decoder reads at most \(q\) bits of \(z\) on every execution?
cards.why: Determine whether a constant number of bit probes can recover any requested message bit despite a constant fraction of adversarial corruptions using only polynomial storage. This is a central locality-versus-redundancy question with connections to private information retrieval and complexity theory.

cards.title: Decidability of unconditional entropy inequalities
cards.formal:
Does one deterministic Turing algorithm exist that always halts and decides the following problem? Its input is an integer \(n\ge1\) and rational coefficients \(a_S\) for the nonempty subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\). It must answer YES exactly when
\[
 \sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n]}a_S H(X_S)\ge0
\]
holds for every joint distribution of \(n\) finite-valued discrete random variables. The finite alphabet sizes are unrestricted, and the inequality has no premises or affine constant.
cards.why: A basic computability question about the laws of Shannon information, with consequences for automated proofs, network and coding bounds, and database query reasoning.

cards.title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(r\in\)(0,1], \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) and \(A>0\) such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with \(k\le n\le k/r\), an encoding \(C:\{0,1\}^{k}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), and randomized local decoders \(Dec_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,k\}\), satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word \(z\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) differing from \(C(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) positions, and every requested index \(i, Dec_{i}\) with oracle access to z outputs \(x_{i}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) while making at most \(\lceil A \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bit queries on every execution.
cards.why: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.

cards.title: Capacity of the general two-way channel
cards.formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{TW}}(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{TW}}(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-way channel \(W\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), with both terminals allowed to adapt their transmissions to past received outputs.
cards.why: Determines the fundamental value of interaction in simultaneous bidirectional communication.

cards.title: Computability of graph Shannon capacity
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A such that, for every finite simple undirected graph G and every integer \(k\ge 1, A\) on input \((G,k)\) halts and outputs integers a and \(b>0\) with |\(a/b- \Theta (G)|\le 2^{- k}\)? No bound on running time is imposed.
cards.why: Asks whether a finite zero-error communication model has an effectively approximable asymptotic information rate.

cards.title: Efficient explicit constant-rate tree codes
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed finite output alphabet \(\Sigma\), constants \(0<\delta<1\) and \(0<\alpha<\delta/2\), and uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms for binary tree codes of every height \(N\ge1\), with relative tree distance at least \(\delta\) and decoding from suffix error fraction at most \(\alpha\)? Both \(|\Sigma|\) and the two positive distance parameters must be independent of \(N\). The binary information rate \(1/\log_2|\Sigma|\) is therefore a positive constant. The precise causal and decoding requirements are specified below.
cards.why: Tree codes protect communication whose later symbols depend on earlier interaction. A constant alphabet and positive tree distance would keep redundancy bounded while maintaining distinguishability after every possible divergence. Efficient deterministic encoding and decoding would supply a central explicit object in the theory of reliable interactive communication.

cards.title: Explicit binary codes with efficient list decoding up to capacity
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\delta,R\) satisfying
\[
 0<\delta<\frac12,\qquad 0<R<1-H_2(\delta),
 \qquad H_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t),
\]
there are uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and list-decoding algorithms for binary codes
\[
 E_m:\{0,1\}^{m}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{N(m)}
 \quad(m\ge1),\qquad \frac{m}{N(m)}\ge R,
\]
such that every \(E_m\) is injective and the decoder, on every received word \(y\in\{0,1\}^{N(m)}\), outputs exactly
\[
 \{x\in\{0,1\}^{m}:d_H(E_m(x),y)\le\lfloor\delta N(m)\rfloor\}?
\]
The binary alphabet is fixed even as the gap to capacity tends to zero. The algorithms may depend on the two fixed constants but must handle all message lengths.
cards.why: Explicit binary codes with efficient adversarial list decoding throughout the capacity region would close a central gap between information-theoretic existence and deterministic usable constructions. Fixing the smallest alphabet prevents larger-symbol constructions from bypassing the main difficulty.

cards.title: Positive-rate binary codes against adversarial deletions
cards.formal:
Determine the real zero-rate threshold
\[
p^*=\sup\{p\in[0,1]:\operatorname{Ach}(p)\},
\]
where
\[
\operatorname{Ach}(p)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\exists r\in(0,1]\ \forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[n\ge N\ \land\ |C|\ge 2^{rn}\ \land\
\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)\right].
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Correct}(C,t)\) means that every codeword in \(C\) can be recovered uniquely, with zero error, after any choice of at most \(t\) deleted positions. Deleted positions are not revealed, and the adversary may know the entire code and transmitted word. The positive rate \(r\) may depend on \(p\), but must remain fixed along the unbounded sequence of block lengths. This is a question about arbitrary code families, with no efficiency, linearity or uniform construction requirement. Benchmark acceptance is absolute error at most \(1/100\) in \(p^*\).
cards.why: This threshold is a basic information-theoretic limit for synchronization errors over the smallest nontrivial alphabet. It links the geometry of large code families to unavoidable common subsequences in binary words and separates worst-case synchronization loss from substitution and erasure models. Determining it would settle the maximum deletion fraction compatible with nonvanishing binary communication rate, independently of implementation constraints. The numerical question remains significant after the qualitative discovery that the threshold is strictly below one half.

cards.title: Do nonlinear binary codes have a strictly better asymptotic rate?
cards.formal:
Does there exist a fixed real \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) such that
\[
R_2(\delta)>R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta),
\]
where these are the optimal asymptotic rates of arbitrary binary codes and binary linear codes, respectively, at relative minimum Hamming distance \(\delta\), as defined below? Any fixed strictly positive gap qualifies.
cards.why: Linearity makes coding algebraically tractable, but it is unknown in this regime whether it sacrifices a positive fraction of information per transmitted bit. Resolving the comparison would distinguish a fundamental cost of linearity from limitations of known constructions and bounds.

cards.title: Linear-length locally testable proofs for CircuitSAT
cards.formal:
Does CircuitSAT have binary locally testable proofs of length linear in the circuit size? More precisely, do there exist an integer \(K\ge1\) and a polynomial-time decidable proof relation \(P\) such that, for every Boolean circuit \(C\) of size \(N\), the set
\[
\Pi_C=\{\pi\in\{0,1\}^{KN}:P(C,\pi)=1\}
\]
is nonempty exactly when \(C\) is satisfiable, and this one family of proof sets has the following property: for every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there is a uniform randomized verifier that makes a constant number of nonadaptive bit queries to \(\pi\), accepts every \(\pi\in\Pi_C\) with probability one, and rejects every \(\pi\) at relative Hamming distance at least \(\varepsilon\) from \(\Pi_C\) with probability at least \(1/2\)? The computational and randomness bounds are specified below.
cards.why: The question asks whether satisfiability witnesses can have only constant-factor redundancy while remaining testable through a constant number of inspected bits. It connects the economy of proof representations with robust local verification and strengthens the ordinary linear-size PCP target.

cards.title: Rate–distortion tradeoff for distributed lossy source coding
cards.formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{RD}}(P,d_1,d_2,D_1,D_2,\lambda)=\inf_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal R(P,d_1,d_2,D_1,D_2)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet memoryless source pair, finite distortion tables, feasible distortion targets and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), where \(\mathcal R\) is the rate region for separate encoders and a joint decoder.
cards.why: The basic unresolved limit of compressing correlated information without coordination between encoders.

cards.title: Polyhedrality of linear-rank inequality cones
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge6\), is the cone \(L_n\) of linear rank inequalities valid over every commutative field polyhedral? Equivalently, for each fixed \(n\ge6\), do finitely many valid coefficient vectors generate every universally valid homogeneous linear inequality on the dimensions of all nonempty sums of \(n\) subspaces by nonnegative real linear combination? The finite generating family may depend on \(n\); no common bound on its size as \(n\) varies is assumed.
cards.why: Dimensions of subspace sums describe the information profiles available to linear coding and linear secret-sharing systems. Finite generation would give a finite complete system of universal linear constraints for each fixed number of subspaces. Nonpolyhedrality would show an intrinsic need for infinitely many constraints even after that number is fixed.

cards.title: Full-length Reed–Solomon list decoding beyond Johnson
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(\varepsilon,\rho\in(0,1)\) with \(\varepsilon<\sqrt{\rho}\), a constant \(K\ge1\), an integer \(c\ge1\), and infinitely many prime powers \(q\), such that for every function \(r:\mathbb F_q\to\mathbb F_q\), \[\left|\left\{f\in\mathbb F_q[X]:\deg f\le\lfloor\rho q\rfloor,\;\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb F_q:f(x)=r(x)\}\bigr|>\varepsilon q\right\}\right|\le Kq^c?\] The zero polynomial is included among the degree-bounded polynomials. All four constants are fixed independently of \(q\) and of the received function \(r\). This is the combinatorial full-length Reed–Solomon question from Open Problem 5.20, without a requirement for an efficient decoding algorithm.
cards.why: Reed–Solomon codes are a central algebraic code family, and their list size expresses an intrinsic information limit even when computation is unrestricted. The full-length requirement fixes the evaluation set completely. Determining whether any constant-rate infinite family surpasses the Johnson threshold would resolve a basic distinction between this rigid algebraic family and the punctured variants for which capacity results are known.

cards.title: Entropic matroid approximations approaching unit ratio
cards.formal:
Does every finite integer-valued entropic polymatroid admit entropic matroid approximations with retention ratio arbitrarily close to one?

Precisely, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every normalized, monotone, submodular function \(g:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) that is exactly the joint Shannon entropy function of finite-valued random variables in bits, and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1\), must there exist integers \(m,k\) and a set \(T\) satisfying
\[
m\ge1,\qquad 1\le k\le m,\qquad \frac{k}{m}>1-\varepsilon,
\qquad T\subseteq U_m,
\]
\[
|T\cap X_i|\ge k\,g(\{i\})\quad(i\in[n]),
\qquad \operatorname{EntMat}(T,r_m|_{2^T})?
\]
Here the disjoint blocks, their union and the free-expansion rank function are
\[
X_i=\{i\}\times[mg(\{i\})],\qquad U_m=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}X_i,
\]
\[
r_m(A)=\min_{S\subseteq[n]}
\left(mg(S)+\left|A\setminus\bigcup_{i\in S}X_i\right|\right)
\qquad(A\subseteq U_m).
\]
The predicate \(\operatorname{EntMat}\) below permits one common positive scaling of the entropy function. In contrast, the input polymatroid \(g\) must be exactly entropic without a scaling factor. The ratio measures how many elements survive in each block of a free expansion; it is not a relative error in approximating a rank table. The integers, retained set and entropy representation may depend on \(g\) and \(\varepsilon\).
cards.why: The question asks whether information represented by a finite entropy function can be organized into exact matroid dependencies while losing an arbitrarily small fraction of each expanded coordinate. Such a bridge would connect entropy constraints with combinatorial independence and clarify the expressive power of entropic matroids beyond linear representations. Its approximation notion preserves the specific free-expansion structure, making it substantially more demanding than membership in the closure of an entropy region.

cards.title: Explicit positive-rate codes below the Plotkin point
cards.formal: For every fixed finite adversarial channel \(A\) with rational polyhedral input and noise constraints, and every fixed integer \(L\ge2\), does the existence of a nonconfusable completely positive order-\(L\) distribution with admissible input marginal imply a uniform deterministic polynomial-time encodable family of positive-rate \((L-1)\)-list-decodable codes for that same channel? The alphabets, transition rule, constraints and list bound are fixed as blocklength grows; all terms and the allowed blocklength convention are defined below.
cards.why: The information-theoretic criterion identifies when a channel permits a linear amount of information with a fixed ambiguity bound. Making that criterion explicit would turn a broad existence theorem into efficiently usable encoders without changing the channel or relaxing the list bound.

cards.title: The maximal error fraction for constant-rate binary two-way codes
cards.formal:
Determine, with certified absolute error at most \(1/100\), the constant
\[
\rho_* = \sup\{\rho\in[0,1]:\ \rho\text{ is achievable by a constant-rate deterministic binary two-way code}\}.
\]
Here Alice must transmit an arbitrary \(n\)-bit string to Bob; the speaking schedule is fixed before communication, and an adversary can flip up to a \(\rho\) fraction of all bits sent in both directions. Achievability and the cost model are defined below.
cards.why: Interaction already allows binary message transmission beyond the classical one-way quarter-error threshold. Locating its ultimate constant-rate resilience measures the benefit of a dialogue when the feedback itself is costly and corruptible.

cards.title: Bounded-alphabet approximation of the β = 0 entropy face
cards.formal:
Does there exist an integer \(K\ge2\) such that every point \(z\) on the face
\[
F=\{(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)\in S:\beta=0\}
\]
can be approximated arbitrarily closely by points of the relative interior of \(S\) obtained from normalized entropy vectors of four jointly distributed variables, each taking at most \(K\) values? The body \(S\), its coordinates and normalization are defined below. One common \(K\) must work for the entire face and for every positive accuracy.
cards.why: This question tests whether the boundary geometry of a four-variable entropy region can be captured uniformly with bounded finite probabilistic models. It distinguishes genuine restrictions on alphabet size from gaps created by numerical exploration.

cards.title: Are characteristic sets of linear-rank inequalities finite or cofinite?
cards.formal:
For every integer \(r\ge1\) and every family of rational coefficients \((c_S)_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[r]}\), is the set
\[
P(c)=\left\{p\text{ prime}:\ \forall d\ge0\ \forall V_1,\ldots,V_r\le\mathbb F_p^d,\quad
\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[r]}c_S\dim_{\mathbb F_p}\!\left(\sum_{i\in S}V_i\right)\ge0\right\}
\]
either finite or cofinite in the set of all primes?
cards.why: Rank inequalities constrain what linear coding can accomplish over different alphabets. This question asks whether one such constraint can distinguish two infinite classes of prime characteristics, beyond the finite exceptional sets occurring in known constructions.

cards.title: The infimal normalized Ingleton score
cards.formal:
Determine, with certified absolute error at most \(1/100\), the real constant
\[
\iota_*=
\inf_{\substack{X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4\ \text{finite-valued}\\H(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)>0}}
\frac{I(X_1;X_2\mid X_3)+I(X_1;X_2\mid X_4)+I(X_3;X_4)-I(X_1;X_2)}
{H(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)}.
\]
The infimum ranges over all finite alphabet sizes and all joint probability distributions, with no common bound on the alphabets. Negative values represent violations of the Ingleton inequality.
cards.why: The normalized Ingleton violation measures how far general entropy vectors can depart from an inequality obeyed by linear-rank models. Locating its global infimum would give a concrete quantitative constraint on the poorly understood four-variable entropy region.

cards.title: Capacity of the binary deletion channel
cards.formal:
Supply a function \(g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) and prove
\[\forall\delta\in[0,1],\quad |g(\delta)-C(\delta)|\le\frac1{100},\]
where \(C(\delta)\) is the operational capacity of the binary independent deletion channel, measured in bits per input bit. The probability \(\delta\) is fixed as the block length tends to infinity. This retained benchmark is a formalization task at the stated accuracy: an unrestricted finite approximation scheme is already known. It does not require a new exact capacity formula.
cards.why: The binary deletion channel isolates the information cost of hidden synchronization errors. Its exact capacity curve remains a central coding question. This user-retained approximation task instead tests an end-to-end Lean formalization connecting reliable transmission to a certified finite description of the capacity curve.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on input a finite list \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple graphs, always halts and correctly decides whether \(\mathcal F\) has the polynomial sampling property below? The input is the finite list of forbidden induced patterns. No running-time bound is imposed on this classification algorithm. The constants in the sampling property may depend on the whole fixed list, but must hold simultaneously at every graph order and proximity parameter.
cards.why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
cards.why: A decision tester recognizes only a large violation, whereas a distance estimator measures the minimum repair needed at every distance scale. A general polynomial implication would transfer efficient sampling guarantees to quantitative assessment across the dense-graph model. A separating property would establish an information-cost distinction between these two basic tasks even when unlimited local computation is allowed.

cards.title: Sharp graph-removal bounds for fixed patterns
cards.formal: Determine the asymptotic order of the extremal copy-count function \(M_H(\varepsilon,n)\) defined below, for every fixed connected finite simple graph \(H\) with at least two edges. Both the proximity parameter \(\varepsilon\) and the graph order \(n\) vary. The requested precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(H\), uniformly over all feasible pairs \((\varepsilon,n)\). Thus the answer must specify bounds \(B_H(\varepsilon,n)>0\) and prove that, for each such \(H\), there are constants \(0<c_H\le C_H<\infty\) such that \[c_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\le M_H(\varepsilon,n)\le C_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\] for every feasible pair. The copies are ordinary subgraphs, with extra edges allowed.
cards.why: Removal bounds quantify how visible a forbidden configuration must become once a graph is globally far from avoiding it. Their dependence on the distance parameter controls the sampling cost of detecting violations and connects dense-graph testing to extremal and additive combinatorics. Distinguishing polynomial from superpolynomial dependence identifies a broad boundary, but does not determine the rate on either side of it.

cards.title: Polynomial-time density learning of Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that properly learns every mixture of at most \(k\) nondegenerate Gaussian distributions on \(\mathbb R^d\), to any fixed total-variation accuracy, in time polynomial jointly in \(k\) and \(d\)? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) in the arithmetic model below such that, for every integer \(t\ge3\), there are integers \(C_t,a_t\ge1\) for which the following holds for all integers \(k,d\ge1\) and all \(P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\)? Given \(k,d,t\) and independent samples from \(P\), the algorithm uses at most \(C_t(k+d)^{a_t}\) operations and outputs a description of \(\widehat P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\) satisfying \[\Pr[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,\widehat P)\le1/t]\ge2/3.\] The time bound holds on every execution and includes sampling and writing the output. Its constants are uniform over all mixture parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(t\) is required: this card asks the source's joint polynomial dependence on the number of components and dimension at each fixed accuracy.
cards.why: Gaussian mixtures are a basic example where enough observations can be available but extracting a useful distribution from them may remain computationally difficult. Joint dependence on dimension and component count distinguishes scalable learning from methods efficient only for a small fixed mixture. Resolving this target would clarify that statistical–computational gap in the absence of separation or conditioning assumptions.

cards.title: Polynomial-query submodularity testing
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error tester for submodularity of arbitrary real-valued set functions using a number of value queries polynomial in the dimension and reciprocal distance? Precisely, do there exist one tester \(A\) in the model below and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), and every function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\), the algorithm \(A^{f}(n,\varepsilon)\) halts and makes at most \(C((n+1)/\varepsilon)^{k}\) value queries on every execution, accepts with probability one if \(f\) is submodular, and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)\ge\varepsilon\)? The constants and program must work simultaneously for all parameters and functions.
cards.why: Submodularity formalizes diminishing returns and underlies many optimization and valuation models. Its value table has exponentially many entries, while algorithms using a submodular value oracle typically see only a small part of it. Polynomial-query testing would determine whether global consistency with that structural assumption can be checked from comparably limited information, with rejection guaranteed for functions requiring widespread changes.

cards.title: Planar graphs from local neighborhoods
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a positive integer \(D=D(\varepsilon)\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every pair of finite simple planar graphs \(G,H\) on \(n\) vertices, equality of their multisets of rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhoods implies \[\min_{\phi:V(G)\cong V(H)}\left|\phi(E(G))\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)\right|\le\varepsilon n?\] The minimum is over all vertex bijections, and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference of edge sets. There is no maximum-degree bound; the radius may depend only on \(\varepsilon\).
cards.why: This asks whether local structure determines approximate global structure throughout the planar family, even around vertices of very high degree. It isolates a structural obstruction behind extending sparse-graph testing beyond bounded-degree and outerplanar settings.

cards.title: Sublinear testing of bounded-degree graph isomorphism
cards.formal:
Can isomorphism between two arbitrary bounded-degree graphs be tested with a sublinear number of adjacency-list queries? Precisely, does there exist a uniform randomized tester \(A\), with explicit inputs \(n\ge1\), a degree bound \(d\ge1\), and an integer \(q\ge2\), satisfying the following guarantees for every pair of allowed \(n\)-vertex input graphs \(G_1,G_2\)?
\[G_1\cong G_2\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\]
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)\ge1/q\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ rejects}]\ge2/3.\]
For each fixed \(d,q\), its worst-case query bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) must satisfy
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{Q(n,d,q)}n=0.\]
Both graphs are given only through oracles. The graph model, distance and query accounting are specified below. The target retains the sublinear-existence question in the saved card, which is one part of the source’s broader request to determine the full query complexity.
cards.why: The problem asks whether two large sparse structures can be compared without reading a linear fraction of their neighborhoods. It isolates the information needed to recognize structural similarity when both objects are unknown. A resolution would locate a basic boundary of sublinear access and explain whether large connected components create an obstruction beyond the known distribution-like examples.

cards.title: Complexity of tolerant monotonicity testing
cards.formal: Determine, up to multiplicative constants for each fixed pair \(0<a<b<1\), the asymptotic randomized adaptive query complexity \(Q(n;a,b)\) of distinguishing Boolean functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\) at uniform Hamming distance at most \(a\) from monotonicity from those at distance at least \(b\). The nonadaptive complexity is a distinct comparison problem and is not silently identified with \(Q\).
cards.why: Tolerance changes monotonicity testing from detecting defects to estimating distance, exposing a large unexplained query gap.

cards.title: Polynomial testing of induced four-cycle freeness
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that the canonical sampling test below, with sample size \[s(\varepsilon)=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil,\] rejects every finite simple graph that is \(\varepsilon\)-far from having no induced four-cycle with probability at least \(2/3\), for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)? The constants must be independent of the graph order and of \(\varepsilon\). The test always accepts graphs with no induced four-cycle, so this asks for polynomial-query one-sided testing in the dense graph model.
cards.why: This is the unresolved concrete case, up to complementation, in the classification of polynomial testing for a single forbidden induced graph. It asks whether a globally expensive repair necessarily leaves violations visible in a polynomial-sized random sample. The answer would separate two very different quantitative regimes of dense-graph testing for one small and fully specified pattern.

cards.title: Query complexity of Max-CSP testing
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the randomized query complexity \(q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\) of distinguishing bounded-degree constraint instances with optimum satisfied fraction at least \(c\) from those with optimum at most \(s\). The target ranges over every fixed finite predicate template \((D,\Gamma)\), degree bound \(d\), density lower bound \(\alpha\), and gap \(0\le s<c\le1\), under the variable-query model defined below. Taking \(\alpha=0\) includes unrestricted bounded-degree inputs; positive \(\alpha\) includes the source’s density-bounded model.
cards.why: This asks for a general account of how much of a sparse constraint system must be inspected to distinguish high from low optimum value. It covers different predicates, value gaps and densities in one query model, and could identify broad structural boundaries between local testing and essentially complete inspection. Its complexity bounds are information-based and need not assume computational hardness conjectures.

cards.title: Efficient black-box testing of high-dimensional convexity
cards.formal: For each fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), is there a randomized adaptive membership-query tester that, for every dimension \(n\) and every Borel set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), distinguishes convexity from Gaussian distance at least \(\varepsilon\) to every convex set using at most \(C_\varepsilon n^{c_\varepsilon}\) queries and with error probability at most \(1/3\) on each promised input? This is ordinary two-sided testing, not tolerant testing.
cards.why: This asks whether a basic high-dimensional geometric property is accessible through a small black-box interface.

cards.title: Estimating sparse finite-field matrix rank with sublinear queries
cards.formal: For each fixed integer \(d\ge1\) and fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), determine up to constant factors the randomized adaptive row/column-query complexity \(Q_d(n,\varepsilon)\) of estimating \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}(A)\) within additive \(\varepsilon n\), for all \(n\times n\) binary matrices with at most d ones in every row and column, with success probability at least \(2/3\).
cards.why: Rank estimation tests whether a global algebraic invariant can be recovered from local sparse access.

cards.title: Efficient characterization of instance-optimal identity testing
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(\Phi\) and a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite rational probability vector \(q\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1\),
\[C^{-1}n_*(q,\varepsilon)\le\Phi(q,\varepsilon)\le Cn_*(q,\varepsilon)?\]
The integer \(n_*(q,\varepsilon)\) is the smallest fixed number of independent samples needed to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon\), with each error probability at most \(1/3\), when the reference \(q\) is known and the unknown distribution \(p\) is otherwise arbitrary. Computation of the statistical test is unrestricted. Polynomial time is required of the evaluator of the characterization, in the binary input length of \((q,\varepsilon)\), and the multiplicative constant must hold at the same input \(\varepsilon\).

This is the finite, explicitly encoded version of the efficient-computability branch of the source's Open Question 1. The source also allows countably infinite domains and leaves “succinct” open to a closed-form interpretation; this card makes its computational interpretation and finite rational input scope explicit rather than treating those broader interpretations as equivalent.
cards.why: Two reference distributions on the same domain can require very different numbers of samples to test. A computable characterization at the exact requested distance would identify the information needed for each reference profile, including distributions for which existing bounds disagree by unbounded factors. It would also separate the statistical cost of testing from the cost of evaluating that cost.

cards.title: A dimension-free directed \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) Poincaré inequality
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every Lipschitz function \(f:[0,1]^{n}\to \mathbb{R} , d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f) \le  C \int _{[0,1]^{n}} (\sum_{i=1}^{n} \max \{- \partial _{i}f(x),0\}^{2})^{1/2} dx\)? Here \(d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f)\) is the \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) distance to the coordinatewise nondecreasing functions. The same C must work for every dimension and every finite Lipschitz constant.
cards.why: Would connect local directional decreases to global distance from monotonicity with a universal constant, extending a central isoperimetric principle to real-valued functions on continuous cubes.

cards.title: Sample complexity of symmetric Markov-chain identity testing
cards.formal: Determine the minimax trajectory-length complexity \(M(n,\varepsilon)\) of identity testing for symmetric Markov chains in the model below, up to universal multiplicative constants. Both the state-space size \(n\) and reciprocal proximity \(1/\varepsilon\) vary. Give an explicit positive comparison function \(B(n,\varepsilon)\), a uniform tester attaining its upper bound, and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that \[cB(n,\varepsilon)\le M(n,\varepsilon)\le CB(n,\varepsilon)\] for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/4]\). Constants must be independent of the reference chain, the starting state, \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\); logarithmic factors in these parameters may not be suppressed. If the complexity is infinite on part of this domain, identify that part and prove infinitude there instead of assigning it a finite bound.
cards.why: This asks how much dependent data is needed to validate an entire stochastic transition rule when the experiment cannot be restarted or directed toward unvisited states. Sharp bounds would separate the intrinsic information cost of testing dynamics from the cost of fully exploring the reference chain, extending the foundations of distribution testing beyond independent samples.

cards.title: Polynomial accuracy dependence for sublinear LIS estimation
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm which, for every array \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) accessible by adaptive random-access queries and every rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), returns an estimate \(\widehat L\) with \(\Pr[|\widehat L-\operatorname{LIS}(a)|\le\varepsilon n]\ge2/3\) in \(C(\log(2+n))^c\varepsilon^{-c}\) total operations, for absolute constants C,c? Here LIS uses nondecreasing values.
cards.why: This tests whether global order can be estimated with efficient dependence on both input length and accuracy.

cards.title: Query complexity of conditional equivalence testing
cards.formal: Determine, up to multiplicative constant factors, the dependence on domain size \(n\) of the randomized adaptive conditional-query complexity \(Q(n,\varepsilon)\) of testing equality of two unknown distributions, for every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/4]\). The task is to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\ge\varepsilon\) with error at most \(1/3\), using the model below. The answer must give a positive comparison function \(F(n,\varepsilon)\), a uniform tester attaining its upper bound, and for every fixed permitted \(\varepsilon\) constants \(c_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon}>0\) and \(n_0(\varepsilon)\) such that \[c_{\varepsilon}F(n,\varepsilon)\le Q(n,\varepsilon)\le C_{\varepsilon}F(n,\varepsilon)\qquad(n\ge n_0(\varepsilon)).\] Multiplicative factors depending on \(n\), including iterated logarithms, must be resolved rather than suppressed.
cards.why: Conditional sampling exposes relative probabilities inside chosen parts of a domain and can dramatically reduce the amount of data needed for comparison. The remaining dependence on domain size measures the cost of comparing two wholly unknown laws even with this strong access. The central gap is now closed up to iterated-logarithmic factors; the exact growth requested by the source still requires distinguishing those factors.

cards.title: Query complexity of directed acyclicity testing with bidirectional access
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty\) for each fixed degree bound \(d\ge 1\) and fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), the minimum worst-case number \(Q(n,d,\varepsilon )\) of incidence-list queries needed by an adaptive randomized two-sided-error tester to distinguish acyclic n-vertex digraphs from digraphs more than \(\varepsilon dn\) edge deletions away from acyclic, when every indegree and outdegree is at most d and both incoming and outgoing queries are allowed.
cards.why: Measures how much local information is needed to certify the absence of global directed cyclic structure up to a proximity promise. It would clarify the power of adaptive two-direction exploration in sparse directed graphs.

cards.title: Optimal query cost of reducing testing adaptivity
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors over all integers \(q,k\ge1\) and \(0\le\ell<k\), \[F(q,k,\ell)=\sup\{q_\ell(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon):n\ge1,\ \varnothing\ne\mathcal P\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ 0<\varepsilon\le1,\ q_k(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon)\le q\},\] the worst query cost of reducing a Boolean property tester from \(k+1\) batches to \(\ell+1\) batches.
cards.why: Quantifies the general price of replacing sequential information gathering by fewer batches. A substantive universal bound would apply across Boolean property testing, beyond the behavior of one particular property.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic-query pattern-freeness testing
cards.formal: For every integer \(k\ge2\) and every permutation \(\pi\) of \([k]\), is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error value-query tester \(A_\pi\) such that, for each fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there are integers \(C_{\pi,\varepsilon},a_{\pi,\varepsilon}\ge1\) for which the tester uses at most \[C_{\pi,\varepsilon}\bigl(1+\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\bigr)^{a_{\pi,\varepsilon}}\] queries on every execution for every \(n\ge1\)? On input \(n,\varepsilon\) and access to any \(f:[n]\to\mathbb R\), it must accept with probability one if \(f\) is \(\pi\)-free, and reject with probability at least \(2/3\) if the normalized Hamming distance to \(\pi\)-freeness is at least \(\varepsilon\). No polynomial dependence on \(k\) or \(1/\varepsilon\) is required; those parameters are fixed when measuring the growth in \(n\).
cards.why: A fixed order pattern is a basic obstruction in sequences and generalizes monotonicity. The conjecture asks whether adaptive access makes every such obstruction testable from only a polylogarithmic number of values, despite large lower bounds for predetermined queries. Its resolution would clarify the reach of adaptivity in ordered property testing and its connection with sublinear sequence analysis.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
cards.why: This asks whether finite local constraint descriptions force a sharp complexity classification even when the accepted and rejected instances are separated by a promise. It encompasses approximate graph colouring and many relaxed feasibility problems. A resolution would determine whether the organizing principle of the finite CSP dichotomy extends beyond exact satisfaction, or whether a fixed finite promise can have intermediate decision complexity.

cards.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
